 history, and particularly cross-national comparative history, can help us understand why our cities are governed the way they are and how we can govern them better. Institutions and norms are powerful factors because they are relatively inflexible; in any given historical moment, they are parameters rather than variables. Taking a long historical view reveals their evolu- tion through the collision of social forces amid profound economic and technological change. As in the past, it is in this potential for change that the seeds of future forms of urban governance lie, and it is with these seeds that we may find ways to grow more successful cities. the end of this module students will be able to: 1. Differentiate between the concepts of sex, gender, gender identity, and gender role. 2. Assess the relative contributions of biology and environment in the development of gender and gender roles related to sexuality. 3. Identify the ways in which gender role socialization contributes to gender differences in sexuality. 4. Examine the ways that the traditional sexual script for sexual interactions contributes to gender inequality. 5. Understand the concept of transgender as a gender identity. Topic Overview Perhaps no issue related to sexuality garners as much discussion and debate as gender differences in sexuality. Are men and women fundamentally different in terms of sexuality? If they are different, what explains these differences? Is it simply a matter of basic biology? To what extent is it true that differences in male and female sexuality are the result of how our culture teaches us to behave as we grow up and live in Western culture? Before we get to these questions, there are some basic terms we need to define and clarify if we are to understand how gender shapes our sexuality. Often, people will use terms such as \"sex\", \"gender\", \"gender identity\", and \"gender role\" interchangeably as if they were all referring to the same thing. In fact, these terms have quite different meanings and developing a precise understanding of these and other relevant terms, and the differences between them, will help us gain a clearer picture of the relationship between sexuality and gender. Defining: Sex, Gender, Gender Identity and Gender Role Key Point The terms \"sex\", \"gender\", \"gender identity\", \"gender role\", \"transgender trans\", \"Two Spirit\", and \"Gender binary\" have distinct meanings that are important for understanding the relationship between gender and sexuality. The list below is not exhaustive. See Chapter 5 of your textbook for a more complete set of definitions and discussion of these terms. Sex refers to a person's biological status and is typically categorized as female, male or intersex. There are a number of indicators of biological sex, including sex chromosomes, internal reproductive organs and external genitalia. Gender: The behavioural, cultural, or psychological traits usually associated with one sex. Gender is distinct from sex which is based on the physical differences between females and males. Gender identity: A person's sense of being a boy or man, or a girl or woman, or another gender. Gender role: The expression of one's gender identity to others. Gender role may also refer to that culturally determined cluster of behavioral patterns and attitudes that members of different genders are socially expected to fill. Transgender Trans: A person whose gender identity is different from their assigned sex at birth. Two Spirit: A term that describes a person who has both masculine and feminine spirits used in some Indigenous communities. Gender binary: A social or cultural system that classifies sex and gender into two distinct, opposite forms of masculine and feminine. Sources: (APA, 2012; Rathus ., 2024) It is important to distinguish between terms such as sex, gender, gender identity, and gender role because they represent inter-connected but distinct aspects of the make-up of every individual and because they do not always line up in clear-cut rigid division between what our culture tells us it means to be a boy or girl or woman or man. For example, while a person's sex may be male or female, the extent to which their behaviour reflects stereotypical masculine or feminine gender roles can vary tremendously. As we are examining the social context of human sexuality, the concepts of gender and gender role are of particular importance. This is because it is clear that one's social role as a sexual person and the cluster of behavioral patterns and attitudes that members of one or another gender are socially expected to fill can change over time from one historical period to another, they can differ from one cultural group to another, and the extent to which a person conforms to these societal expectations for gendered behaviour also vary considerably. For example, the Indigenous Two Spirit identity is different from some of other the gender systems found in other cultures that predominately classify people within a gender binary. It is important to note that most of the research on gender and sexuality, including research discussed in this module tends to reflect a gender binary. That is, it narrowly classifies people into either a male or female category. As noted in Chapter 5 of your textbook, \" It is important to recognize that the gender binary represents a socially prescribed way of classifying gender in our culture, but it does not accurately reflect the diverse range of gender identities that actually exist\" . Key Point The concepts of gender and gender role are important for understanding the social context of human sexuality. Lets look at some basic gender and gender role differences between men and women related to sexuality and see how two of the theories we looked at in Module 2 (Sociobiology, Social Learning Theory) interpret and explain these differ
0|dashboard  | ences. As described in your textbook (Chapter 5), surveys of sexual attitudes and behaviours have consistently found gender differences. For example, Oliver and Hyde's meta-analysis of 177 studies examining gender differences in sexuality found that men were more likely than women to approve of casual premarital sex, extramarital sex, and men had a generally more permissive attitude towards sexual behaviour. Men were more likely to masturbate and had more sexual partners than women. Interestingly, when the meta-analysis was repeated almost two decades later these same gender differences continued to exist but to a lesser degree than in the previous analysis . A more recent meta-analysis indicated that men fantasized about sex more often, experienced desire for sex more often, and masturbated more often than women . The authors are careful to point out that although these group gender differences can still be found, on average, in the research, it is far from unusual for individual women experience higher sex drive than individual men. These gender differences in sexuality translate into what is called the \"traditional sexual script\" for heterosexual sexual interactions and gender roles related to sexuality (Recall the concept of \"sexual scripts\" from Module 2). The Traditional Sexual Script for Heterosexual Sexual Interactions and Gender Roles People with gay, lesbian, bisexual, or queer identities will develop sexual scripts that are unique to their identities. Also, we should note that scripts for sexual behaviours are subject to ethno-cultural influences. Thus, we will find considerable variation in the sexual scripts of people in Canada. One pervasive sexual script in North America, however, is a sexual script that confines people to very narrow and unequal scripts to guide sexual interactions between men and women. This is often referred to as the traditonal sexual script (Hyde, Delameter and Byers, 2009). Examining the traditional script is important not just because it is common but also because the traditional script is associated with gender inequality. It is argued, for example, because it places men in an assertive and directive role in sexual interactions, the traditional sexual script contributes to sexual violence by men against women. The traditional sexual script may also make it more difficult for women to negotiate condom use in sexual encounters with men. In addition, the traditional sexual script can be highly limiting for both women and men who are forced into roles that restrict ability for people to enjoy mutually pleasurable and respectful sexual relationships. It's not surprising then that many people, including both women and men, actively resist participating in the traditional script and hopefully it will fade away as society strives for gender equality. However, it is important for us to be aware of the existence of the traditional sexual script and the problems associated with it if we are to work constructively towards positive social change related to sexuality. The Traditional Sexual Script Sex Drive: Men are expected to have a stronger desire than women for frequent sexual activity. Motivations to engage in sexual activity: Women are expected to view partnered sexual activity as an expression of love, commitment, and intimacy whereas men are expected to view sexual activity in terms of physical pleasure. Number of Sexual Partners: Men are expected to be more likely than women to desire and seek out a variety of sexual partners. Initiation Patterns: Men are expected to initiate sexual activity whereas women are expected to be the \"gatekeepers\" who respond to or reject male advances. Sexual Interaction: Men are expected to take the lead in sexual interactions and direct sexual activity whereas women are expected to take a passive role. Double Standard: It is socially acceptable for men, but not for women, to be sexually assertive, and to engage in casual sex with multiple partners. We should emphasize that each of these elements of the traditional sexual script represent broad generalizations and that many men and women do not conform to them. Secondly, as discussed below, the sexual scripts for women and men are changing over time. Key Point Although gender roles related to sexuality are changing over time, the traditional sexual script continues to characterize the sexual interactions of many people. Theoretical Explanations for the Traditional Sexual Script In Module 2 we looked at essentialist and social constructionist theoretical explanations for human sexual behaviour. Recall that essentialist theories suggest that many aspects of our sexuality are the product of a basic and largely unchangeable human nature while social constructionist theories suggest that our sexual attitudes, motivations, and patterns of behaviour are determined by what we learn in the social environment that we grow up and live in. Sociobiology is an example of an essentialist theory and Social Learning Theory is an example of social constructionism. Let's look at how these two different types of theory explain gender differences in the traditional sexual script. According to the theory of Sociobiology, human beings, like all biological organisms, have a primary built-in motivation or drive to reproduce and pass on their genes to the next generation. This basic drive is necessary in order for a species to survive. In other words, humans are motivated, by nature, whether they are aware of it or not, to be reproductively successful. Because of basic biological differences between males and females, sociobiologists point out that effective strategies for reproductive success are quite different for men and women. First, they point out that sperm are plentiful (the male body manufactures millions per day) whereas the egg is comparatively rare (only one is produced per month) and therefore precious. Thus, it makes evolutionary sense for the male to inseminate many females but for the female to be careful about which genes are paired with hers in the rare egg. Second, they point out that the woman commits 9 months of her body's energy to gestation .leading her to want to continue to ensure the viability of the offspring by caring for them but also leading her to be highly selective in her choice of mate . In other words, in order to create the greatest chance of reproductive success (passing on your genes to the next generation) it would be in the best interest of the male to have intercourse with many different women and biologically father as many children as possible. Because women are limited in the number of children that they can give birth to, for the female, her chances of reproductive success are greatest when she is able to select a mate who is willing and able to commit to helping her care for her and her children. When it comes to explaining the existence of the traditional sexual script, sociobiologists argue that, for example, the desire for a variety of sexual partners on the part of men and the desire to have sexual intercourse within committed relationships on the part of women simply reflects men's and women's different strategies for reproductive success. This basic imperative for reproductive success would also explain other aspects of the traditional sexual script including the propensity for men to attempt to initiate sexual activity and for women to take on the role of either accepting or rejecting male advances. Although sociobiologists acknowledge that the culture and learning environment in which we grow up and live influences gender roles related to sexuality to some degree, they also point out, in defence of their theory, that elements of the traditional sexual script can be found in a number or cultures across the world and in many historical periods. Key Point The theory of Sociobiology suggests that some differences in sexuality between women and men are the result, at least in part, of differences in male and female strategies for reproductive success. As its name implies, Social Learning Theory takes a quite different approach to explaining the existence of the traditional sexual script. In basic terms, this theory suggests that the roles that women and men enact in the traditional sexual script are the result of what our society has taught us as we grow up about how men and women are supposed to behave. In other words, rather than being hard-wired into us, we learn these scripts through learning and imitation of what we see around us. In general social constructionist theories note that the traditional sexual script can be expected to exist in patriarchal, male dominated societies where men have more political, economic, and social power than women. Some suggest that the traditional sexual script is an expression of male dominance and it can be found in many cultures, in greater or lesser degrees, because there is an unequal distribution of power between men and women in most cultures and historical periods. In contrast to essentialist theories, social learning theory suggests that because the messages we receive as we grow up can change as society changes, the traditional sexual script can also change. According to Social Learning Theory, gender differences are shaped by positive reinforcements for gender-role-consistent behavior, whereas role inconsistent behavior is ignored or perhaps even punished, thereby becoming less frequent. At the same time, according to the theory, children differentially imitate same-gender adults, so that the gender role behavior of the previous generation perpetuates itself in the next generation Thus, social learning theory can readily account for change over time in patterns of gender differences in sexuality . In sum, Social Learning Theory suggests that the patterns of sexual attitudes and behaviour characteristic of the traditional sexual script are things that are taught to us by our culture and that we learn the script by observing, particularly when we are children and adolescents, how men and women interact with each other. According to this view, young people will imitate the behaviour of role models such as parents or media figures. In contrast, from the sociobiological perspective, the traditional sexual script is largely the product of millions of years of human evolution where males and females have developed patterns of sexual behaviour that maximize their potential for reproductive success. Key Point Social Learning Theory suggest that gender differences in sexuality are the result of messages that we absorb from our environment, particularly as we are growing up, about how society expects us to behave as men and women. Keep these different explanations for gender differences in sexuality in mind when we look at the developmental tasks related to sexuality at different phases of the life course. For example, in Module 10 we will be looking at the developmental tasks of adult sexuality and many of these tasks relate to how people in longer-term relationships relate to each other in the sexual component of their relationship. One way of looking at how people can resolve difficulties in their sexual relationships, is to examine how gender differences in the sexual script impact on their relationship. The Development of Gender Difference in Sexuality: The Role of Culture and Childhood Learning All theoretical explanations for gender differences in sexuality acknowledge that culture plays some role in shaping gender roles related to sexuality. Sociobiologists argue, for example, that while our behaviour is guided at a basic level by our quest for reproductive success, these predisposition's to behave in certain ways sexually are filtered through the gender role expectations of the specific culture in which we live. As your required textbook reading for this module demonstrates, these gender role expectations related to sexuality vary considerably from one ethno-cultural group to another. As noted above, the traditional sexual script is male dominated and contributes to inequality between men and women. If we, as a society, wish to create a social learning environment that contributes to a more egalitarian sexual script for men and women, it is important to understand the dynamics of how children and youth learn to enact the traditional sexual script. According to Ehrhardt , \"...the development of gender differences in childhood are of critical importance for the sexual interaction between adolescent girls and boys, and, subsequently, between women and men\" (). If the traditional sexual script is to change, the primary mechanism for change will be the socialization process whereby young people learn what is expected of them in terms of their gender specific behaviour. Your required textbook reading for this module outlines some of the ways the socialization process contributes to gender differences in sexuality. Transgender Trans Health and Identity Development In examining gender issues related to sexuality, it is important to consider people who are transgender. In looking at gender we often tend to think in terms of strict dichotomies between male and female. As suggested by the definitions of sex, gender, gender identity, and gender role given above, some individuals do not uniformly or consistently fit strict sex gender categories. For example, a person whose gender identity (sense of being a male or female) does not correspond to the gender they were assigned at birth is referred to as trans or transgender. Your textbook reading for this module will introduce you to key aspects of trans identity. Trans identity is an important topic to consider because it demonstrates the complex and distinct ways that sex, gender, gender identity, and gender role interact to create an individual's sexuality. People who do not conform neatly within the biological and social categories prescribed by Western culture s rigid gender binary are often the victims of discrimination and violence. Transgender and non- binary youth experience high rates of victimization including physical, sexual, and verbal harassment . (Non-binary or genderqueer people do not identify or express their gender within the gender binary). At school, trans and non-binary youth are frequently the targets of bullying which affects school attendance and access to education. As a result, trans youth have higher rates of mental health issues than non-trans youth and frequently report depression, self-harm, suicide ideation, and suicide attempts . The Trans PULSE Canada project surveyed 2,873 trans and non-binary people, presenting national data on the health and well-being of trans and non-binary youth in Canada . The survey data indicated that: 1 in 5 avoided schools in the past 5 years for fear of harassment or outing. The majority reported reliable health care access, with 77 having a primary health care provider. 2 in 5 considered suicide in the past year; 1 in 10 attempted suicide. 58 were told by their parents guardians that they were respected supported, and half were called by their correct name, pronouns, and gendered language by their parents guardians . Navarro note that acceptance of trans and non-binary identities is growing and the proportion of trans youth living day-today in their felt gender is increasing, which also supports their well- being (). A review article published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (link: Management of gender dysphoria in adolescents in primary care) notes that studies have shown that the mental health of adolescents with gender dysphoria improves when they receive gender-affirming care (Bonifacio, Maser, Stadelman, and Palmert, 2019). The authors recommend that \"Primary health care providers can support adolescents with gender dysphoria and their families by providing guidance on the timing of social transitioning, reviewing and overseeing the potential use of medical management, and connecting them with local community resources and supports\" (p. E69). (This article also provides a comprehensive glossary of commonly used terms related to gender identity.) In Module 5 we will look at stage models used to understand the identity development and coming out processes for lesbian, gay, and bisexual people. Here, we will briefly outline two models for identity development for transgender people. It should be noted that not all people follow these stage model trajectories. Some transgender people may progress through the stages in a different order and not all stages are necessarily experienced by all people. However, these models can be helpful in providing a basic general understanding of developmental milestones and processes among LGBTQ people . Key Developmental Milestones of Transgender People . Indeed, some key developmental milestones exist for many, if not most, transgender people. Childhood gender nonconformity may be a first indicator of transgender identity, but this is complicated by the fact that it is also strongly associated with future sexual minority orientation. Personal feelings of gender incongruence (i.e., mismatch between felt gender identity and that assigned at birth) and gender dysphoria (i.e., distress resulting from gender incongruence) often reach a critical point between ages 10 to 13, potentially driven by the onset of puberty, sexual desire and stronger gender role enforcement in school peer groups. These feelings are frequently the motivating force behind transgender self-identification, although recent critiques of gender dysphoria as a diagnosis required to receive gender-affirming healthcare have indirectly highlighted the lack of research on gender euphoria (i.e., positive feelings resulting from gender identity affirmation) and how it may also motivate transgender identity (Doyle, 2022, .) Developmental Stages of Transgender Identity Development . 1. Pre-coming Out: Feeling different from assigned sex gender. 2. Coming Out: Acknowledgement of transgender identity. 3. Exploration: Experimenting with alternative non-stereotypical notions of femininity and masculinity, personal attractiveness, and sexuality; developing pride. 4. Intimacy: Desire for intimacy and relationships in preferred gender role. 5. Identity Integration: Affirmation of gender identity ambiguity; Less focus on identity labels. Gender and Sexual Orientation You may have noticed that up to this point we have not addressed how concepts of gender relate to sexual orientation. While it is certainly true that various gender characteristics can contribute to the expression of a person's sexual orientation, it is important to keep in mind that gender, gender identity, and gender role are conceptually distinct from the concept of sexual orientation. Key Point gender, gender identity, and gender role are conceptually independent of sexual orientation. A commonly held assumption inherent within the traditional sexual script is that a truly \"masculine\" male or a truly \"feminine\" female are attracted to the \"opposite sex\". However, this is an assumption based on stereotypes that often do not reflect reality. Gay men and lesbian women often have gender, gender identity, and gender role characteristics that match societal expectations for the masculine man and feminine woman. Munk School of Global Affairs, University of Toronto 1 Devonshire Place Toronto, Ontario, Canada M5S 3K7 Copyright held by author, 2013 0-7727-0918-1 Executive Summary Many of the most explosive local controversies today spending scandals, service disruptions, political disputes share one thing: they involve local agencies, boards, and commissions (or ABCs). In Toronto, controversies about waterfront redevelopment, libraries, public housing, and transit planning have been complicated even caused by the ABCs in these fields. The same is true in many other Canadian cities. This should not come as a surprise. Everywhere we turn in municipal politics, from transit to housing, conservation to libraries, education to policing, we encounter ABCs: local or regional public agencies, with a single or limited set of functions, that receive their revenue partly or wholly from municipal governments, provincial governments, user charges, or some combination of these. These ABCs (or special-purpose bodies ) provide hugely important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. Yet we spend little time thinking about how they are governed. Supporters of local ABCs argue that some services should be kept at arm s length from municipal politics and that ABCs allow certain operations to be governed by those with an interest or expertise in the field, rather than by municipal politicians. Those who oppose ABCs argue that they keep local councils from coherent budgeting, priority-setting, and policymaking and that ABCs are nearly invisible to the public, making important decisions without sufficient local oversight and accountability. This paper poses three practical and important questions. The first concerns existence: do we need to have ABCs at all? The second is about scale: what is the appropriate geographic boundary (local, regional, provincial, etc.) for a particular policy task? The third is about personnel: who should sit on the board of the ABC and should they be appointed or elected? We consider each of these questions in light of experiences with local ABCs in Canada and abroad. IMFG Perspectives 1 Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada Introduction At the bottom of Cherry Street, on an ordinary summer morning, the city of Toronto seems a world away. Early risers walk dogs through the cool lakefront air. Gravel trucks rumble past. Tourists loiter at the water s edge, their cameras pointed at the skyline across the harbour. Standing in the sand at Cherry Beach, looking across at the morning roar of the city s downtown expressway, visitors could be forgiven for thinking that they had stumbled into a completely forgotten world. In August of 2011, however, this small corner of the city was anything but forgotten. That month, local media reported that members of the city s executive committee had plans to transform the city s waterfront redevelopment program. Naturally, the headlines focused on the striking new suggestions for the waterfront: a monorail link to the downtown, a massive shopping mall and waterfront hotel, and the world s largest Ferris wheel. But the real debate that summer and the question that Toronto s council was required in September 2011 to answer was whether responsibility for redevelopment in the Port Lands should be transferred from Waterfront Toronto, a tri-level redevelopment body, to Toronto Port Lands Co., a city agency. Waterfront Toronto, with four appointees each from the federal, provincial, and municipal governments, was criticized by some as being too distant from the city and too cautious for speedy action. A reorganized Port Lands Co., on the other hand, would have two municipal councillors on its board, along with two municipal bureaucrats and five council appointees, and would therefore be linked much more directly to Toronto s city council. For all the talk of shopping malls and Ferris wheels, the waterfront debate in summer 2011 was really a debate about special-purpose governance.1 Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada 2 When we refer to local ABCs, then, we are speaking about public agencies of limited purposes, operating locally or regionally, that are more or less formally separated from the ordinary council-committee structure. The best-known special-purpose bodies have been around for decades, even centuries: school boards, library boards, transit commissions, and boards of health. In many municipalities, however, special-purpose bodies have proliferated. In Toronto, for example, they range from the massive Police Services Board to much smaller operations like the William H. Bolton Arena Board of Management. The fiscal arrangements for local special-purpose bodies also vary widely. In councils have the final authority to approve the budgets of special- purpose bodies. But this authority is a matter of degree. In some cases, such as libraries, council can review and adjust the board s submitted budget.5 In other cases, like policing, council can approve or reject a budget, but it cannot specify particular items that the board should increase or decrease.6 And in the peculiar case of school boards in Ontario, council is required by law to levy taxes on behalf of the board, but has no control over the board s budget.7 In many cases, local boards also receive funding from the province, and particular tasks and services are often mandated and funded, wholly or in part, by the province. Whatever the fiscal arrangements, however, the money involved is no small matter: in many Canadian cities, more than a third of the city s operating budget is handed over to special-purpose bodies every year.8 Consider Vancouver. In 2012, of the city s 1.1-billion operating budget, 243 million more than a fifth of the budget was devoted to policing; a further 103 million was budgeted for parks and 42 million for libraries. These three policy areas are administered by special-purpose bodies and, in the case of parks, by a separately elected Park Board. The three ABCs alone represent more than a third of Vancouver s operating budget, not to mention thousands of its employees.9 Moreover, a full account of local spending by ABCs in Vancouver would include regional bodies such as Vancouver Coastal Health (health care) and TransLink (public transit). How ever we do the calculations, in other words, we find enormous public funds under the control of Vancouver s local and regional ABCs. The same is true in many other Canadian cities. ABCs provide very important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. This was not unusual. Everywhere we turn in municipal politics, from waterfront redevelopment to libraries, transit to housing, education to policing, we encounter a peculiar administrative animal: the special-purpose body. These ABCs of local government agencies, boards, and commissions are more than mere administrative quirks, confined to a few forgotten corners of the local landscape.2 They provide hugely important services, spend large sums of money, and raise serious questions about democratic accountability. But what are they? How do they operate? And why might we defend or deplore them? In this paper, we will provide a toolkit for thinking about local ABCs for anyone who wants to understand the strengths, weaknesses, and purposes of local special-purpose bodies in Canada. If our goal is to understand and improve Canada, we cannot afford to ignore these local special-purpose bodies. What are local special-purpose bodies? The first challenge in any discussion of local special- purpose bodies is that the enormous range and variety of ABCs, each with its own peculiar history, makes them difficult to summarize. When a group of Canada s leading experts on local ABCs met some years ago to write a book on the subject, they found that the task of defining the special- purpose body was more difficult than they had expected.3 Still, it is useful to have some definition of the ABC in mind. In my view, the best definition can be found in a decades-old report by Susan Dolbey of the Government of Ontario, who defined local special-purpose bodies as follows: (1) They are public bodies in that they are either elected by local voters or appointed by council(s), the provincial government, or other special- purpose bodies (2) They operate at the local or regional level, but outside the normal council structure (3) They have a single function or a limited range of functions (4) They receive at least part of their revenue from and or user charges.4 IMFG Perspectives 3 Thinking about Local ABCs: Three Key Questions Across Canada, thousands of local ABCs are performing important tasks in dozens of widely varying policy fields. Are they improving local governance, or worsening it? If we decide to create or reform local ABCs, where should we begin? To clarify our thinking on these issues, there are three general questions that we need to ask about special-purpose bodies. They concern existence, scale, and personnel. 1. Should the ABC exist? The first question is the simplest: should the ABC exist? While advocates and critics of special-purpose government have made many arguments for and against local ABCs through the decades, there are a few arguments to which those on both sides of the debate have returned again and again.1 Those who advocate local ABCs often claim that a particular service, such as policing, should be insulated from local politics, either because the service is too important or complex, or because it would create conflicts of interest or patronage if councillors were allowed to control the service directly. In some cases, this is cast as an argument for efficiency: by separating particular services from councillors who might impede or micromanage them, tasks like policing, utilities, or transit can be operated in a more efficient and businesslike manner.1 This argument emerged in Canada s urban reform era , but it is still alive and well today. Do not leave the future of our city to our city council, wrote Toronto columnist Royson James during the 2011 waterfront debate. Too many of the councillors too often don t know the details of an issue, fail to understand the core principles governing many policies and are like a political weather vane that spins in the direction of the prevailing political power source. 1 If we allow our politicians to get too involved, the argument goes, our policies will suffer from short-term, inefficient, and excessively political thinking.1 Better to entrust those areas to special-purpose ABCs. A second, related argument is that local ABCs provide an opportunity to recruit people into public service who might not otherwise be involved. There may be people with particular interests, acumen, or expertise who would not seek municipal office, but might be willing to sit on the board of a special-purpose body. Historically, this argument has been used to justify the recruitment of businesspeople for businesslike services (like utilities) and experts for scientific services (like planning). But it could as easily be used to justify the need for environmentalists on waterfront commissions, poverty activists on housing corporations, or What is central to the argument is the belief that some policy areas should be overseen by those with a special interest or expertise, rather than by uninterested or uninformed local politicians.1 Of course, many disagree with these arguments and not just the municipal politicians who are implicitly or explicitly besmirched by them. Those who oppose special-purpose bodies often begin with the problem of fragmentation. If we create local ABCs to administer particular tasks, they argue, no one body or agency will be able to make coherent decisions for the city as a whole. How, these critics ask, can a city like Toronto develop a coherent waterfront policy, when responsibility for the waterfront is divided among a conservation authority, a port authority, a tri-level waterfront commission, and three levels of government? The same criticism could be made of transit policy, urban homelessness, health care, and a range of other issues. For critics of local ABCs, it is better to empower a general-purpose government a municipal council, a regional government, or the province with enough authority to make policy decisions across a range of fields and to the basis of the needs of the community as a whole. A second common argument against ABCs concerns accountability. When a policy is the responsibility of council, the lines of praise and blame are usually clear. But the same cannot be said of local ABCs. If a conservation authority makes an unpopular decision, who should be held responsible? If local residents object to the sums being spent on policing, or transit, or housing, to whom should they complain? Recent research on the Toronto waterfront has suggested that special- purpose bodies can sometimes be so distant from ordinary lines of accountability that they virtually constitute a separate, unelected level of government.1 Even in less extreme cases, the lines of responsibility and accountability can be perplexing for careful observers and altogether bewildering for the general public. The result, according to critics, is a system of local policymaking that would score low on any reasonable evaluation of democratic accountability. In addition to these common arguments for and against local ABCs, there are many others, pertaining to particular services, in particular places, at particular times. Speaking generally, however, local ABCs are often supported by those If we allow our politicians to get too in- volved, the argument goes, our policies will suffer from short-term, inefficient, and excessively political thinking. Hidden in Plain View: Local Agencies, Boards, and Commissions in Canada 4 who are focused on a single local service, such as hydro, planning, or conservation, who hope that a local ABC will protect and insulate the policymaking process in their favoured domain. Those who care passionately about public libraries, say, but have little interest in municipal government in general, may defend the existence of their local library board. Those who are more concerned about the operation of local government in general, on the other hand, tend to be more skeptical.1 Advocates of localism, who believe that local communities should be empowered with more autonomy, tend to be critical of specialized ABCs. Ultimately, then, our answer to the first question about existence depends on our reaction to these broader arguments for and against local ABCs. But we must remember that there is nothing natural about the arrangement of local special- purpose bodies in Canada today. Some policy tasks that were once thought to require special-purpose administration, such as water distribution and urban planning, have been safely under the control of municipal councils for decades. In many jurisdictions, tasks like policing, education, and watershed management are carried out by general-purpose municipal, regional, and provincial or state governments rather than ABCs. When we compare ourselves to other jurisdictions, in other words, we quickly realize that our way is not the only way: we might choose to create ABCs similar to those being used effectively in other jurisdictions, or we may realize that certain ABCs can safely be eliminated. Like most organizations, public and private, special- purpose bodies are easier to create than to eliminate. When the legislation to permit library boards was first passed, for example, it provoked almost no debate or discussion. But legislation to abolish library boards would surely provoke a passionate reaction. Once they are created, special-purpose bodies quickly gain important resources that help them survive over time: local clients who become accustomed to interacting with an ABC rather than with council; inter- municipal and inter-provincial organizations in which members of local ABCs meet to discuss and coordinate their policies; provincial departments whose officials prefer to work directly with specialized local agencies; and, of course, politicians of every stripe who cry local autonomy! whenever reforms are proposed. When we are considering a new special-purpose body, therefore, we should ask ourselves if we want the new special-purpose body to persist for ten, twenty, even fifty years into the future. 2. What s the right scale? Suppose we decide that an ABC does deserve to exist. Our next question might concern scale: what is the best geographic boundary for the ABC? In theory, the possible answers are limitless, but in practice, the choice is restricted to three options. First, a special-purpose body might be located at the municipal scale, sharing a border with a single municipality. Many well-known ABCs, such as library boards and planning commissions, are organized at the municipal scale. If the local scale is too restrictive, we might consider the regional scale, larger than a single municipality but smaller than the province as a whole. In some cases, such as policing and education, a regional ABC might share a border with an upper-tier municipality like a county or a regional government. In other cases, like conservation or public health, the boundaries of the regional ABC might be drawn exclusively for the purposes of a particular policy task. The range of possibilities at the regional level are nearly limitless, from smaller ABCs that incorporate just two or three municipalities, like a small utilities commission, to huge ABCs, like Conservation Authorities, whose geographic territory sometimes includes dozens of Among the policy fields in which regional ABCs are employed, one recent area of innovation has been in public transit: in the past two decades, several of Canada s largest cities including Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal have created regional public transit agencies.1 The third scale is provincial. Many hundreds of ABCs operate at the provincial scale, performing a wide range of tasks, and we can occasionally find calls for a particular local service to be relocated to the provincial level. During recent debates on hydro distribution in Ontario, for example, some argued that the province should create a single distribution Like most organizations, public and private, special-purpose bodies are easier to create than to eliminate. IMFG Perspectives 5 utility to cover the entire province.1 Others have made similar arguments, with varying success, in the areas of public health, water treatment, and education. When it comes to scale, the story of the past century in many policy fields, such as education, public health, and policing, has been one of consolidation. In an attempt to capture economies of scale, to simplify the administrative system, and to build agencies with the capacity to carry out highly specialized modern services, local ABCs once bounded by a single municipality have been consolidated into much larger boards at the county, regional, or mega-regional level. In many cases, consolidation began as a voluntary local option, stimulated by funding incentives from the provinces. Provincial governments have often found it easier to introduce and defend a voluntary approach, rather than face the charges of centralization that inevitably accompany mandatory changes to entrenched local institutions.1 We must remember, however, that voluntary consolidation is rarely a panacea for policy problems, and the result is almost always a system that is more complicated than the one it replaced. No matter how attractive the incentive, some municipalities will choose not to consolidate, leaving some parts of the province under the old form of administration and others under the newer consolidated structures. In Ontario, for example, voluntary consolidation programs in education and public health resulted in adoption rates of roughly 50 percent that is, half of the province s local governments decided not to adopt the new structures which made governance, accountability, and funding all the more complicated. More recently, a voluntary consolidation program in hydro has resulted in a handful of very large utilities, a number of mid-sized utilities, and a few extremely small distributors. The current hydro system in Ontario is arguably as difficult to coordinate as the system it replaced. Consolidation is rarely painless. There is no easy path to regional ABCs, and if the process is to be completed, compulsory legislation will probably be necessary. If the goal in a consolidation process is to simplify the administrative landscape, only compulsory consolidation, with all of its political risks and challenges, is likely to make such simplification a reality. 3. Should ABC boards be elected or appointed? Finally, we must also ask: who should govern the ABC? Who should sit on its board? How and by whom should senior staff be appointed? Answering these questions requires that we decide, first of all, whether members should be elected or appointed. These days, with just a few exceptions such as school board trustees or the Vancouver Park Board most ABCs are governed by appointed board members. If we decide that an ABC should be elected, however, there will be further decisions to make. Will the board members be elected in wards, or at large? How many will be elected? For how many years will they serve? These questions could be answered in a thousand ways, but those who have supported elected ABCs throughout Canadian history have typically advocated at-large systems with relatively lengthy terms of office in an attempt to insulate the ABC from parochial and short-term thinking. If we decide that an ABC should be appointed, we also face a host of questions. First, we will need to decide who gets to make the appointments. In many cases, board members are appointed by municipal councils, but some appointments are also made by provincial governments (e.g., some boards of health), by outside associations (e.g., local heritage boards), and even by other ABCs (e.g., some library boards). A second councillors to serve on the board. Some local ABCs are composed entirely of making them very similar to committees of council; in others, one or two councillors are selected along with a handful of non- politicians; and sometimes, councillors are forbidden from These eligibility rules often appear poorly thought- out at one point, Ontario had two sets of provisions for creating local park boards, one requiring local councillors, and the other forbidding them and it is useful to think very carefully about the nature of the people who sit on the board. In general, provincial statutes have grown more flexible on this issue over time, giving local councils more freedom to decide whom to appoint to their local special-purpose bodies. The most obvious consideration to keep in mind when thinking about personnel is insulation: how closely should the ABC be linked to the municipal council? As we have seen, a common argument for local special-purpose bodies is that they insulate sensitive tasks from the local political sphere. In many cases, this claim is accurate: mayors and councillors often pay little attention to the day-to-day decisions of their conservation authorities, library boards, or transit commissions. When those bodies make more far-reaching or controversial decisions, however, the insulation provided by the ABC structure often proves to be very drafty indeed. When ABCs make more far-reaching or controversial decisions, the insulation provided by the ABC structure often proves to be very drafty indeed. And they raise ongoing questions about accountability and efficiency, flexibility and independence, fragmentation and oversight. Local ABCs have been with us, in Canada, for more than a century. The debate about the efficiency of local ABCs when compared to council is dif- ficult, controversial, technical, and ongoing. For an early negative statement in the Canadian case, see Harry Kitchen, Some Orga- nizational Implications of Providing an Urban Service: The Case of Water, Canadian Public Administration, , : 297 308; for a more positive view, see Mark Sproule-Jones, The Recent events in Toronto provide examples of this problem. On the one hand, local politicians rarely hesitate to get involved in a policy issue, even when the issue has been entrusted to an agency, board, or commission. From policing to transit to housing, local councillors feel free to make criticisms and suggestions, even when they are not directly involved with the relevant ABC. On the other hand, when controversies do arise within special-purpose bodies controversies from which local politicians might prefer to be insulated it is rare that they avoid blame. Controversies in Toronto about social housing, for example, have spilled over into council debates, despite the insulation that is supposedly provided by the Toronto Community Housing Corporation. The insulation provided by local ABCs often seems to break down precisely at the moments of heightened controversy for which it was created. If the goal is to insulate a policy arena from local politics, other options such as a transfer of responsibility to a regional or provincial government might do the job in a more lasting and effective way. A Final Observation At the end of September 2011, the waterfront controversy that had been boiling in the city of Toronto was back to a simmer. Despite their strenuous efforts, those who had advocated for the proposed changes failed to secure enough support to transfer responsibility for the Port Lands from Waterfront Toronto to the Toronto Port Lands Co. In the end, council voted only to speed up the redevelopment process along the waterfront. Although Waterfront Toronto survived, the debate in summer 2011 illustrated the accountability and governance challenges that are ever present in the relationship between municipal governments and ABCs. The story of Toronto s 2011 waterfront debate illustrates a final, very simple observation about local ABCs in Canada: each of them has its own story. The more that we investigate the history and organization of local ABCs, the more we realize that we are dealing with an extraordinary variety of very different species. Special-purpose bodies can be local or regional, elected or appointed, fiscally independent or dependent, publicly prominent or largely invisible. They can be large or small, permanent or temporary, prestigious or pilloried. While all of them might be accurately defined as special-purpose bodies, there is as much that differentiates these agencies, boards, and commissions as unites them. The role of special-purpose bodies in local governance is significant and under-appreciated in Canada. As provinces meddle more in municipal issues, cities raise concerns about political overreach . The Globe and Mail. The Municipal Corporations Act, or Baldwin Act, 1849 was the first legislation to focus on local government. It was followed by the British North America Act, 1867, which established Canada as a federal state with constitutionally defined and protected responsibilities shared between the federal and provincial levels of government. Municipalities were small and predominantly rural; only 16 of the population lived in urban areas in 1861 (Statistics Canada, 2018). We might imagine that discussions about municipalities and local government didn t take much time in the negotiations that led to Confederation in 1867. No doubt the situation would be different now with municipalities providing home to most Canadians and with more than 80 of Canadians living in urban municipalities. The British North America Act gave provinces and territories the authority to pass legislation about municipalities. Provincial municipal acts established different forms of municipalities as well as many of the other municipal institutions that are in place today. Provinces developed new institutions in response to their priorities, interests, and the issues and context at the time. For example, the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board (which was later renamed the Ontario Municipal Board) was established to deal with railway-municipal conflicts and to regulate basic infrastructure such as utilities, telephone systems, and gaswork
0|dashboard  | s. The Depression of the 1920 and 1930s left many municipalities in financial distress and by At the time, municipalities were also responsible for welfare and their expenditures had more than doubled in an eleven-year period. In response, the OMB was given additional authority to approve municipal debt, some municipalities were amalgamated, and Ontario established the Department of Municipal Affairs. As the population continued to grow in the post-war period, Ontario again introduced other structural, functional, legislative and financial changes in its relationship with municipalities. provided an overview of some of the more significant changes, including the creation of regional, two-tier structures and amalgamations and restructuring of existing municipalities. The overriding conclusion that can be drawn from the history of provincial-municipal relations in Canada concerns the importance of provincial initiative. For the most part, it has been provincial governments that have defined the municipal system and introduced the most important changes to it (Andrew, 1995, 147). An Important Relationship The municipal-provincial territorial relationship is a significant and ongoing relationship. Provinces are important to municipalities because they establish, enable, and control local government and many local agencies, boards, and commissions. Similarly, municipalities are important to provinces and territories: Municipalities play a key service delivery function they deliver local services based on local preferences that provinces could not easily deliver or are not interested in delivering. Municipalities also deliver delegated or downloaded provincial services on behalf of the provinces. Municipalities represent a vehicle for advancing provincial policy priorities provinces can set policy frameworks and program priorities that get implemented at the local level. Kristin Good argues that municipalities provide: a check on provincial power, encouraging citizen participation through decentralization to local communities, and providing a mechanism by which legislation and services can be tailored to local communities. They further the principles of democracy and federalism which underpin Canada s constitutional architecture. Municipalities are vibrant cultural and economic hubs that contribute tax revenues to the provincial coffers, attract businesses and visitors, and position the province to compete nationally and internationally. Each province territory develops the municipal structure to fit unique provincial needs. The nature and form of the relationship varies from jurisdiction and over time, and because municipalities are under provincial control, there may be little consistency in the structure of those relationships across the country. Changing Issues and Understandings The issues, demands, and expectations of local government have changed a lot since Confederation. In 1849, the local government issues were drunkenness, profanity, charivaries (post-wedding celebrations), the running of cattle or poultry in public places, itinerant salesman, and the prevention or abatement of noises or nuisances. Today, municipalities own and operate telecommunications systems, hydroelectric plants, public transportation, waste treatment plants, airports, toxic waste remediation facilities and other works or services never contemplated in 1849. (Lidstone, 2004, 2) In addition, there has been a shift in the understanding of local government with a greater appreciation for democratic self-government. In 1993, the International Union of Local Authorities published principles for local self-government that included adequate powers and financial resources, required consultation before other levels of government took action that might affect local government, and respect for areas of municipal jurisdiction. Canadian municipalities used these principles to lobby for change in the provincial-municipal relationship. The Association of Municipalities of Ontario proposed a bill of rights for local government in 1994. The Union of British Columbia Municipalities gave support to a 1991 policy paper called Local Government and the Constitutions, which argued that local governments must be recognized in the Constitution; this position was reaffirmed at subsequent meetings of the UBCM. By the mid-1990s, municipalities and municipal associations were intensifying their pressure on provincial governments for greater levels of local autonomy, including more scope and authority for decision-making and more sources and control over revenues. principles of self-government, including independence from outside forces. Some provinces responded by introducing legislation to give municipalities more flexibility and authority to act in certain broad areas. The mid- to late-1990s were also a time of provincial-led change and upheaval. David Siegel described the changes in Ontario between 1996 and 1999 as the most comprehensive reform of municipal government since 1849 (Siegel, 2004, 182). The 1990s reform included amalgamations in Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Kawartha Lakes, Temiskaming Shores, Haldimand County, and Norfolk. The amalgamations reduced the number of municipalities in Ontario from 815 to 447 nearly 100 fewer municipalities than were in place at the time of Confederation in 1867 . At the same time, the Ontario government reformed the property tax system, introducing different property classes, as well as the system for assessing property value. Further, an extensive who does what realignment exercise was undertaken that had significant implications for local services. Education was uploaded as part of this exercise and remains a provincial responsibility, although the education portion of the property tax continues to be collected at the same time as the municipal property tax. The relationship between municipalities and the Ontario Conservative government was understandably tense during this time. The Ontario Liberal government, elected in 2003, worked to rebuild the relationship with municipalities. Ontario phased out pooling for GTA social services whereby municipalities in the GTA contributed to a fund to offset higher social service costs experienced by Toronto with a grant. A new Municipal Act and the City of Toronto Act brought in a more permissive policy framework, flexibility, and natural Ontario negotiated a framework with the Association of Municipalities of Ontario that would guide future consultations regarding policy and program reform. The economy was healthy, and Ontario increased financial support to municipalities through grants like the permanent gas tax funding for municipalities while taking back some previously downloaded costs, including land ambulance and public health, and some other costs associated with Ontario Works and the Ontario Disability Support Program. At the same time, there were a growing number of issues that crossed municipal boundaries. For example, people worked in one municipality (using municipal infrastructure) and lived and paid taxes in another. Regional coordination and consistency continued to be a challenge. In 2006, the Greater Toronto Transportation Authority (which later became Metrolinx) was established in an effort to coordinate transit planning across the GTA. The Ontario Conservative government, elected in 2018, appointed two advisors to review regional (two- tier) municipal structures but advised in 2019 that they would not be proceeding with imposed changes to the structure of regional municipal government. Instead, Ontario encouraged municipalities to consider opportunities for efficiency and governance streamlining and made funds available to support local initiatives. Legislative Controls The Legal Relationship Provincial and territorial legislation controls all aspects of municipalities, including boundaries, size, election processes, roles, responsibilities, and funding sources. Legislation also establishes the categories or type of municipalities that can be created, including the designation of city or town; village, township, or improvement district; and regions. Similarly, legislation gives provinces and territories the power to eliminate municipalities, as evidenced in the restructuring discussion in Module 3, or to approve special charter legislation for certain municipalities. This section looks at the three main expressions of legislative control municipal legislation, other provincial legislation, and charter cities. : Legislative controls are a prime instrument by which provinces and territories establish the structure and role of local governments, and the Municipal Act is the main piece of provincial legislation that defines the purpose and powers of local government; provides the governance framework, including composition and decision-making procedures of local councils; and identifies areas of municipal responsibility. It establishes municipalities as corporations and not as levels of government. This is an important distinction. In 1909, a Manitoba Court of Appeal judge observed that a municipality under the traditional regime of provincial municipal acts is nothing more than a public corporation created by the government for political purposes and having subordinate or local powers of legislation (Lidstone, 2004, 4). Municipal acts vary in content from province to province they reflect the system of local government that has evolved in that province. Provinces can assign any matters identified as provincial authority in the Constitution to local government. Powers or issues not identified in municipal legislation were considered beyond the purview of the municipality unless the municipality negotiated specific authority with the province. Dillon s Rule is a term used to describe the situation where municipalities are limited to the powers given to them through legislation. As noted earlier, municipalities had been advocating for some time for changes to their role, responsibilities, and authority. Many provinces responded with amendments to their municipal legislation or with new legislation that included some or all of these features: Provision of natural person powers Module 1 talked about natural person powers, which allow municipalities to do what an adult person would be able to do, including hiring, entering contracts, and borrowing, without having to get provincial permission. Authorization to act within broad spheres of jurisdiction or areas where municipalities have designated authority to act. Spheres of jurisdiction are broader than the specific listed powers and areas of jurisdiction included in earlier municipal legislation. The Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, included natural person powers and sphere of jurisdiction powers in ten identified areas. Commitment to advance consultation prior to changes to municipal roles, authorities, or scope. Requirement for municipal approval before certain actions initiated by the province or territory (like amalgamation) could proceed. A commitment to provide resources commensurate with the municipal responsibilities being allocated. (Adapted from Tindal ., 2017, 145) The British Columbia Community Charter (or Municipal Act) goes further. It recognizes municipalities and their councils as an order of government within their jurisdiction that is democratically elected, autonomous, responsible and accountable (British Columbia, 2003, 1(1) and 1(1)(a)). The Community Charter sets out principles of municipal-provincial relations, including acknowledge ing and respect ing the jurisdiction of each (British Columbia, 2003, 2(1)(a)). Other Provincial Legislation In addition, municipalities are covered by hundreds of other pieces of provincial and territorial legislation that have implications for local government, including the Ontario Planning Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, Ontario Works Act, and the Municipal Elections Act. Others, like the Ontario Child, Youth and Family Services Act establish special purpose bodies such as children s aid societies to plan, develop, and deliver services in municipalities. Provincial legislation often adds responsibility for regulation, delivery, or compliance to local government with the associated costs. It may add requirements for collaboration, such as with provincially established special purpose bodies like children s aid societies, with the associated costs. Charter Cities Provincial legislation can also establish a charter city. As discussed in Module 3, charters were originally designed to deal with early, growing municipalities such as Montreal, Saint John, and Halifax. The practice of establishing charter cities became unpopular over time the number of potential charter cities were growing and the provinces realized that each new charter, and any subsequent changes to the charter, required a special provincial legislation. The desire to treat all municipalities consistently through a vehicle like a municipal act outweighed the local benefits from charter city legislation. Charter cities were promoted again in the late 1990s as a way to strengthen the scope, authority, and autonomy of municipalities. The mayors of Montreal, Calgary, Toronto, Winnipeg, and Vancouver met to develop strategies to increase the autonomy of large cities of regional and national importance and to develop a model framework for a city charter. They lobbied successfully for the establishment of new charter cities. Despite the effort at defining municipal authorities and jurisdictions through charters, city charters seem to have little effect on provincial decisions about cities. Silva found that the existing charters did not provide any protection from provincially imposed amalgamation and reorganization in Montreal, Halifax, or Winnipeg or from provincial plans for natural gas pipes under municipal roads in Saint John. City of Toronto Act The City of Toronto Act was the provincial response to years of intense lobbying that one size doesn t fit all municipalities in Ontario, and that Toronto needed enhanced powers and authority. The legislation is over 300 pages of detailed text, based heavily on the 2 Ontario Municipal Act (enacted in 2003). Sections 8 and 20 of the bill are unique to Toronto and attempt to create an entirely new legislative context for the city. describes the broad general powers assigned to the city: the city may provide any service or thing that the city considers necessary or desirable for the public. provides for delegation of decision-making by city council to committees, such as the community councils described in Module 4. Toronto was also given some limited new revenue tools, including the ability to impose taxes on alcohol, tobacco, and entertainment. And finally, and importantly, the act permits the city to enter into agreements with the federal government. All provincial laws, except the Municipal Act, continue to apply to the city. In addition, there are some limits and restrictions in the legislation. For example, Section 25 states that the provincial cabinet may make short-term (18-month) regulations imposing limitations and conditions in the power of the city. Section 8(2)1 states that the city can create its own governance structure, but Section 151 says that by regulation the province can require the mayor to enact a governance structure with particular characteristics. While the City of Toronto Act is seen as an important milestone in the municipal- provincial relationship, it has been criticized for not going far enough to give Toronto sufficient autonomy and authority. Supervisory and Control-Based Relationships In City Politics, Canada, James Lightbody describes the provincial relationship with local government as one of control and guidance. The Ministry of Municipal Affairs is the lead ministry, but others like Education, Transportation, Community and Social Services, and the Environment have a significant policy, program, and funding impact on municipalities, and they exercise control over municipalities through supervisory review. There are a variety of mechanisms embedded in provincial legislation and regulation that require provincial approval or review of local government decisions. A ministry of municipal affairs would have broad responsibility to assure municipal compliance with legislation. They must approve certain municipal policies before they can become legal. For example, in Ontario, the province must approve the official plans of municipalities. Ontario has exercised this power in the past by overruling a Toronto plan to build the Spadina Expressway in the early 1970s; a plan to introduce market value property tax system; approval of the Eglinton Avenue subway; and the decision to increase the size of Toronto city council in 2018. In addition, most provinces have appointed review boards to adjudicate complaints against local land use decisions. The Ontario Municipal Board and the Local Planning Appeal Tribunal, discussed in Module 5, are good examples. Other examples include the accountability officers, also discussed in Module 5, who are often appointed by the province to provide an oversight function based on provincial requirements for all municipalities in the province. Courts The provincial-municipal relationship may be exercised through the provincial court system. In the past, decisions were more heavily weighted in the province s favour, but Lidstone noted that this has changed: The courts have during the past decade declared that the law must respect the responsibility of elected municipal bodies to serve the people who elected them, and exercise caution to avoid substituting the courts views of what is best for the citizens for those of municipal councils. Unless a municipal decision is clearly beyond a council s powers, the courts generally will uphold the decision. Further the courts are willing to imply jurisdiction where powers are not expressly conferred. (Lidstone, 2004, 6) Nonetheless, courts continue play an important role in interpreting provincial legislation and supervisory actions. Fiscal Relationships Provinces and territories influence municipal revenues by: providing grants to municipalities for services and support, defining expectations, standards, and funding levels for mandated provincial programs to be delivered at the local level by municipalities, and setting legislation, which limits the revenue generation tools available to a municipality. Each is an important constraint on the financial position and capacity of a municipality. As we will learn in Module 8, municipalities collect funds in three ways through taxes, through user charges and other municipal revenue sources, and through grants and transfers, primarily from the province. The proportion of revenue from provincial sources has been declining over the years but the available revenue tools, set out in municipal acts, generally have not expanded to make up the loss of provincial support. In addition, provinces shape the local property tax system a main source of revenue for municipalities. Municipalities set the mill rate and levy the taxes within a provincially designed system. Ontario conducted a major reform to the property tax system in the late 1990s, shifting to a market value assessment system and establishing a new corporation (Municipal Property Assessment Corporation) to determine municipal property values across the province. Provincial and territorial governments exert control over local decision-making, leaving even the largest municipalities with limited flexibility on how to raise funds or how to spend them. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities has suggested that this has turned local governments into puppets on a shoestring (Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, 1976). Disentangling the Complex Relationship Over the past 25 years or so, most provinces have significantly altered the job descriptions of local governments by unilaterally changing their assigned responsibilities, often through a province-led process of disentanglement. There are frequent arguments for a separation of government responsibilities, claiming this would enhance local autonomy, eliminate overlapping jurisdictions, and both politicians and the public would be better off with a clear definition of which level of government was responsible for which types of service. Entanglement happens gradually over time as a result of many decisions, or it may be an intended part of a program or service design. For example, there may be provincial standards that municipalities have to meet in their provision of a service to residents of their municipality. The provincial standards ensure that all residents, regardless of where they live, can access roughly the same type and quality of service. There may also be funding entanglement, where a province will pay 50 of a service if a municipality pays the other 50 . Finally, there can be policy entanglement, where provinces or territories set a broad policy framework for an issue and municipalities can adapt or refine the policy framework based on unique local needs. As discussed on the Reform and Disentanglement page in Module 3, Graham, Phillips, and Maslove identified three types of downloading: Another level of government withdraws from a program area and mandates it as a municipal responsibility Transferring responsibility for a program without the associated funding or resources Assigning a new responsibility without associated funding or resources Some level of entanglement is expected and can be good. However, over time, and as relationships get more entangled, there can be negative consequences in terms of confusion, accountability, effectiveness, and efficiency. Efforts to disentangle roles, responsibilities, and funding have been guided by the principle of subsidiarity that assigns responsibility for policy and the delivery of services to the lowest level of government possible. As noted earlier in the module, Ontario engaged in a major municipal disentanglement exercise in the late 1990s, along with other significant municipal change. As with other disentanglement exercises, it was clear that controlling provincial costs was at least as important as clarifying the role of each government, establishing greater local autonomy, or distinguishing responsibility for services. Many of the disentangled programs that were shifted to the municipal level remained either cost-shared or entangled by provincial standards and an ongoing provincial role in policy setting. Twenty years later, fundamental questions are again being raised about the role and responsibilities of municipalities and provinces as a result of the COVID-19 crisis. What should provinces be What should municipalities be Who does what? Do we have the appropriate mix of what the province should be responsible for and what municipalities should be responsible for? Crises like these lay bare some of the systemic or underlying issues with the system we re in. So I think maybe not today, but in the future when : Entanglement can also be a result of downloading.
