(Slack as quoted by Gul, 2020) Looking Back and Looking Ahead This module has looked at the fundamentals of the intergovernmental relationship between provinces and municipalities. It is clear the pressures on that relationship are leading to ongoing calls for change. there is a mismatch between the size and role of cities in the economy compared to their lack of autonomy and provincially prescribed role, the increasing complexity of municipal-provincial relationships is getting in the way of effective and efficient governance, and municipalities don t have sufficient resources to address issues in their communities and they don t have the capacity to develop new sources of revenue. But there isn t a simple solution. Should all municipalities in a province be covered by the same legislation? Is there one size that fits all municipal-provincial relationships? In addition, provinces and municipalities are heavily entangled in different types of relationships, some of which may be productive and positive while others get in the way of accountability, effectiveness, and efficiency. Should there be a strict division of responsibilities, and if so, is it realistic to expect that all programs, funding, and policies can be disentangled? Informal but Important The discussion to this point has focused on the provincial-municipal relationship. This is largely because the federal government doesn t have a formal, constitutional relationship with municipalities in Canada. Nonetheless, federal policies, decisions, and programs have a direct impact on municipalities. Stoney and Graham describe this as the basic paradox at the centre of the federal and municipal relationship. Municipalities are important to the federal government and the federal government is important to municipalities. nearly everything the federal government does or spends money on has a direct or indirect impact on municipalities in Canada, but the federal government has no formal powers over local government. (Spicer, 2017, 291) The federal government owns a lot of land in municipalities, which can influence development. It is a large employer. Ottawa plays key roles in immigration, transportation, infrastructure, and housing that influence the connectedness, footprint, and composition of municipalities. The federal government is concerned about Canada s overall global competitiveness and positioning urban or municipal issues can have negative implications for Canada s growth and success. There are also political reasons why the relationship between the federal government and municipalities is important. While there are some unincorporated areas in Canada, most people live in some form of municipality. National political parties and candidates need to connect with those people in order to get or stay elected. With 80 of the population living in urban areas, it is in the best interest of the federal government and all the federal political parties to work with municipalities to address local issues and gain support for local candidates. In addition, provinces and territories don t have access to unlimited resources. Health, education, and social spending have stretched provincial budgets, and they may be more open to accepting federal funding and involvement at the municipal level than in the past. And while there isn t a formal relationship, there are connections and interactions that change based on the overall environment, the political parties in office federally and provincially, and the presence of a relationship window and relationship champions at both the federal and municipal levels. An Evolving Relationship Stoney and Graham described the evolving federal-municipal relationship as ad hoc and opportunistic. Let s look at why. In the early 1900s the federal government played a strong role in developing national programs to respond to the challenges of increasing urbanization, immigration, economic crisis, poverty, and war. Housing programs beginning with the 1 Housing Program, as well as national income support and medicare programs, contributed to quality of life in municipalities. We can also understand the relationships as having distinct phases (Stoney and Graham, 2009; Spicer, 2017). 1960 1 The 1960s were a time of urban growth, change, and development. With the growth came pressures against development, urban renewal, and major projects. Municipalities were ill-equipped to deal with the need for infrastructure and housing. The Reform and New Structures page in Module 3 described the amalgamations that began in the late 1950s (for example, the creation of Metropolitan Toronto) in an effort to better reflect urbanization patterns and provide municipalities with more capacity and tax revenue to address the challenges. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities lobbied for a stronger federal role in municipal affairs and, in 1971, Canada created the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs . Did You Know? The Federation of Canadian Municipalities was established in 1901 to advocate for municipalities with the federal government. It continues to be an important force in representing the interests of large and small, urban and rural municipalities with the government. In its nine years of existence, MUSA had four ministers and evolved its focus from policy planning and cooperation to project funding and coordination to project planning and delivery (Spicer, 2017, 298). Provinces were not happy with the new federal relationship with municipalities and opposed a federal role in urban planning, policy, and delivery. Although it didn t last long, MUSA was an important effort at a structured federal relationship with municipalities. 1979 1 The federal government s relationship with municipalities changed after MUSA. Instead of developing structures and programs, the government shifted its focus to regions and to tri-level federal, provincial, and municipal agreements related to regional development. Urban development, regional development, and community development partnerships were initiated with an emphasis on collaboration and cooperation. The federal role was lower key than in the first phase . The Relationship from 1 Onward Pressure grew in the late 1990s for a new relationship and a new deal for cities in Canada. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities initiated some quality of life studies, the group of five mayors (C5 mayors) advocated for more autonomy and funding, and external groups like the Board of Trade and the TD Bank encouraged the federal government to consider a new relationship. Federal involvement in municipalities in the late 1980s and 1990s focused on infrastructure funding, particularly through regional development grants and the Canada Infrastructure Works program that provided 2 billion over two years, with matching funding from the provinces and municipalities. Urban Development Agreements In addition to the initiatives described above, the federal government was also involved with municipalities and provinces through formally negotiated urban development agreements . The first urban development agreement was signed between the federal, provincial, and municipal governments in Winnipeg in 1981, for the five-year period from 1981 1986. The highly regarded Vancouver Agreement brought together the three levels of government with a shared focus on the Downtown Eastside and became a model for other tripartite urban development agreements that followed. There have also been UDAs in Saskatoon and Regina, and a committee in Halifax region provided a tri-level forum for discussion about the future of the Halifax Airport, the Port of Halifax, and the rail links in the area. Urban development agreements were tri-level collaborations on broad issues such as inner city revitalization, strengthened innovation, or sustainable economic development. They were flexible instruments that supported cooperation between the three levels of government and more collaborative and seamless service delivery. In signing the agreements, each level recognized the need for long-term commitment, collaboration, and coordination. These partnerships were broader than the three levels of government and include business, nonprofit organizations, communities, and residents. Other programs like the National Homelessness Initiative clearly positioned the federal government in communities and municipalities. The January 2 Speech from the Throne stated that the federal government would cooperate with provincial and municipal partners to improve public transit infrastructure and help stimulate the creation of more affordable rental housing . The budget included multi-year funding commitments for affordable rental housing and strategic infrastructure. The emphasis was on working with municipalities, provinces, the private sector, and nonprofits and charities through a new deal that included both funding programs as well as new revenue sources for municipalities. Ministry of State for Infrastructure and Communities In May 2001, the prime minister appointed a Task Force on Urban Issues, chaired by Judy Sgro, an MP from Toronto. Following research and extensive national consultations, the task force called for a federal urban strategy to include a national affordable housing program, a national transportation program, and an extension of the Infrastructure Canada program (with a focus on municipal water infrastructure). The task force commented on the need for all levels of government to collaborate to implement the urban strategy. Canada s Urban Strategy would provide a strategic framework for a collective approach, with the Government of Canada acting as the catalyst within a strengthened urban partnership. It offers an opportunity to establish a foundation for sustainable growth in collaboration with provincial, municipal and community partners. (Prime Minister s Caucus Task Force on Urban Issues, 2002) This message was echoed in the 2 Speech from the Throne, which stated: Competitive cities and healthy communities are vital to our individual and national well-being, and to Canada s ability to attract and retain talent and investment They require new partnerships, a new urban strategy, a new approach to healthy communities for the 21st century. The new deal recognized that while municipalities fell under provincial jurisdiction, greater coordination and partnership was needed between levels of government to address the needs of communities. Cities welcome this kind of direct relationship with the federal government because it generally means they will receive additional funding. But cities remain creatures of the provinces, and provincial governments have not been keen to cede any of this authority to the federal government. The federal government can give money to cities, but it cannot change their expenditure responsibilities or their revenue-raising tools. The federal government can say whatever it wishes about a new deal for cities, but any real deal will essentially depend on provincial involvement and consent. (Slack and Bird, 2008, 74) A number of new programs were introduced, including a transportation strategy to reduce congestion in cities and trade corridors; investments in affordable housing and to reduce homelessness; and an expansion of pilot programs directed at poverty among Indigenous Peoples living in cities. Infrastructure Canada was a six-year initiative aimed at fixing aging and building new municipal infrastructure with one- third contributions from the federal government, the province, and the municipality. A Cities Secretariat was established in the Privy Council Office and a Minister of State for Infrastructure and Communities was established in 2004 as part of an internal effort to coordinate federal programs and policy that affected communities. As well, the goods and services tax was eliminated for municipal expenditures and a portion of the federal gas tax was provided to municipalities on a temporary, and later permanent, basis to support transit and related programs. The Green Municipal Fund was originally established in 2000 it now has a nearly 1 billion endowment from the federal government to fund municipal projects, including energy efficiency, sustainable affordable housing, and brownfield renewal. The fund is administered by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and has supported more than 1,300 projects across the country. Bill Karsten, the President of FMC, celebrated it as a federal-municipal partnership at its practical best because it provided a long-term commitment that the federal government would support local communities to be more sustainable. And finally, it is important to note that Prime Minister Paul Martin established an External Advisory Committee on Cities and Communities in 2004, headed by Mike Harcourt, former premier of British Columbia and mayor of Vancouver to look into the state of Canada s cities and communities. A federal election intervened, and the advisory committee tabled their final report with Prime Minister Stephen Harper, elected in the 2006 federal election. Changing Politics, Changing Relationships The 2006 election brought in a federal Conservative government and a different federal relationship with municipalities. Prime Minister Harper recognized the formal relationship that the federal government had with provinces and expected provinces to deal with municipalities. There was no interest in or action on the Advisory Committee Report on Cities and Communities. Instead, Harper worked to clarify federal- provincial roles and responsibilities (Dunn, 2016, 3). The Canadian Constitution the very core of our country s success provides for a direct link between municipal institutions and provincial governments the federal government means to respect the letter and the spirit of this provision. (Friendly, 2016, 9) The Ministry of State for Infrastructure and Communities was amalgamated into a new Ministry of Transport, Infrastructure and Communities. The prime minister communicated that he would limit his contacts with provinces to ad hoc bilateral (one-on-one) meetings with premiers (Dunn, 2016, 2) and focus on fixing the fiscal imbalance and cutting taxes rather than introducing new programs. This period was marked by reducing the federal footprint through initiatives like the devolution of responsibility for labour market programs to provinces through labour market development agreements (Ibbitson as referenced in Dunn, 2016, 9). Another Change in Government In a speech to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in advance of the 2015 federal election, Liberal leader Justin Trudeau signalled a different federal relationship with municipalities: i t s time for a new arrangement between our municipalities, provinces and our federal government . Since the 2015 and 2019 elections, federal funding has provided for infrastructure, transit, and housing and other projects as part of the focus on investing in Canada. Nonetheless, the FCM continues its pressure for a new modernized relationship with the federal government. More recently, the FCM has called for federal funding as well as federal-provincial cooperation in making financial assistance available related to the COVID-19 crisis. Municipalities large and small have announced huge losses of revenue. In May 2020, the FCM estimated that 10 billion was needed in emergency federal funding . expressed concern about the situations faced by municipalities and eagerness to work with them but noted that the federal government would respect provincial jurisdiction over municipalities . Themes in the Federal-Municipal Relationship The federal-municipal relationship has varied over the years in fits and starts (Spicer, 2017, 291). It has taken place through political relationships with groups like the FCM and its committees, through tripartite partnership agreements negotiated with provincial and municipal governments, and at the staff or bureaucratic level. Stoney and Graham identified three distinct periods in the federal-municipal relationship: The early phase, from 1960 1978, emphasized internal coordination and getting the house in order by adding a minister of state to the political structure and a new ministry to the bureaucratic structure. Decisions on programs were top-down and made in Ottawa. The period from 1979 1993 emphasized building agreement on joint federal-provincial-regional priorities and programs. Decision-making was decentralized to the regional level with the establishment of regional development agencies. Since 1994, relationships have reflected tri-level partnership, often with the involvement of the private sector and civil society. Projects were locally identified through local decentralized decision- making processes, and additional financial resources were shared with municipalities through the gas tax and GST refund. The federal role has become more arms-length over time. In the absence of a formal role, the federal government has used its resources to get attention and action on federal priorities at the local level. Initially, these resources were short-term and subject to political change, but more recently they have been more stable and longer-term. In addition, there has been a shift from the early federal focus on social issues and infrastructure to the current focus on physical infrastructure, and a shift from reacting to problems to proactively supporting municipalities and cities as key elements of a competitive national economy . Role of Federal Courts Before we leave the discussion of the federal-municipal relationship, it is important to note the role played by the federal justice system in determining disputes about municipal roles and scope of authority. The Spraytech v. Hudson case was an important case that established core principles that would form the foundation for future decisions. Spraytech v. Hudson, 2 The municipality of Hudson, Quebec passed a bylaw that restricted the use of pesticides to certain activities and locations. A landscaping lawn care company, Spraytech, was charged with using pesticides in contravention of the municipal bylaw. Spraytech argued that the bylaw restricting pesticides was beyond municipal authority and that it conflicted with federal and provincial legislation both of which allowed the use of the pesticide. The Supreme Court denied the appeal. They determined that the municipal bylaw fell under the municipal responsibility to regulate for the general welfare of its community members. The Court noted some guiding principles in the case: Law-making is often best achieved at the level closest to the citizens affected (this reflects the principle of subsidiarity) So long as the municipality is not exceeding its delegated powers, it should be afforded wide discretion Later the Ontario courts rejected a challenge to Toronto s bylaws related to pesticides and Montreal won a Supreme Court case that confirmed that Montreal had the power to regulate the noise from a local night club. Options for New Relationships What can be done to address the ongoing issues in the municipal relationship with provinces and the federal government? Let s explore the choices. Constitutional Recognition for Municipalities Entrenchment of municipalities in the Constitution as a formal level of government would give all municipalities (large and small, rural and urban) recognition as a democratic level of government. Municipal scope, role, and responsibilities would be defined and not subject to provincial change, and municipalities would be able to negotiate directly with the federal government. However, constitutional recognition would be a long and challenging process. In addition, opening the Constitution for municipal recognition would bring pressures for reform in other areas that would prolong the negotiation process and potentially reduce the likelihood of success. Reform can only be undertaken with support of two-thirds of the provinces that have at least 50 of the Canadian population. Entrench Municipalities in Provincial Constitutions Kirstin Good argues that calling municipalities creatures of the provinces is a fallacy. In sum, municipalities, and the laws that establish them, are constitutional in nature. Municipalities fulfill functions similar to federalism by providing a check on provincial power, encouraging citizen participation through decentralization to local territorial communities, and providing a mechanism by which legislation and services can be tailored to local communities. They further the principles of democracy and federalism which underpin Canada s constitutional architecture. (Good, 2019, 11) Good dismisses the option of constitutional recognition and instead proposes legal recognition in provincial constitutions, which set the rules about decision-making that guide provincial processes. If restrictions were put on the process to amend municipal legislation perhaps by requiring a certain proportion of votes rather than the current simple majority requirement municipalities would have greater protection from unilateral provincial action. Constitutional Amendment Section 4 John McGrath has argued that Section 43 of the Constitution Act allows provinces to amend the Constitution in matters that are specific or unique to that province. McGrath suggests that a particular province could give their municipalities specific power and authority through a Section 43 amendment. The federal government would, of course, have to agree with the amendment, but the amendment wouldn t require approval of other provinces based on the amending formula that requires the support of two-thirds of the provinces representing at least 50 of the population of Canada. This may be a potential, albeit incremental, option for constitutional recognition for some municipalities in some provinces. City Charters As discussed earlier in the course, a city charter sets out the role, scope, and responsibilities of a particular municipality in provincial legislation. It is unique to a particular city. Current charters vary. The City of Toronto Act describes a provincial-municipal relationship based on mutual respect, consultation, and cooperation and notes that an ongoing consultative relationship is in the province s best interests (Good, 2019, 24). However, it stops short of requiring consultation. In contrast, the British Columbia Community Charter (similar to a provincial municipal act) includes It notes that consultation is needed on matters of mutual interest and in cases of changes of government legislation, financial changes in transfers to municipalities, or changes to other provincial legislation or programs that will affect municipalities. The Community Charter includes a process for resolving disputes between the province and municipalities. Proponents of city charters argue that they give cities clearer authority; critics reply that charters may still be subject to provincial change or intervention. Transform Large Municipalities to Provincial Status In 2008, Alan Broadbent argued that the province of Toronto should be established. This would give Toronto, which is larger than six provinces, the status and role that it deserves and remove it from provincial oversight and control. Key Point Each of the above options has clear advantages and disadvantages, but they all include clearer municipal responsibility and authority and provide for a more collaborative, stable, and predictable relationship with provinces. Other Options for New Relationships Increasingly, municipalities are looking to other types of intergovernmental relationships that don t involve legislative or formal change with significant negotiation and approval processes. These options are known by a number of terms, including multi-level, metagovernance, new regionalism. Regardless of the name, they are more flexible and adapt to changes in the environment and the partners. : Eager Beavers and the Mushy Middle Smith and Stewart argue that municipalities should move beyond the constitutional constraints and stop trying to negotiate changes to the formal municipal-provincial relationship. Instead, municipalities should use their ideas and local experience to engage others in working This requires a shift in how municipalities understand their roles and how they use their formal and informal power and relationships to work toward their goals. The ideal positioning for municipalities is as eager beavers that use their informal authority based on experience, knowledge, influence, and community support to work collaboratively with other levels of government. Smith and Stewart suggest that there is a lot of space in the mushy middle the space between current assigned authorities and areas where municipalities don t have assigned authority for this type of proactive initiative. The Vancouver Agreement is often cited as an example where a municipality acted as an eager beaver and engaged British Columbia and Canada in a multi-year agreement in the municipality s best interests, despite not having formal authority in all the areas covered by the agreement. New Regionalism New regionalism brings a focus on governance and process and emphasizes collaboration, partnerships, and cooperation involving different partners like business, the civil society, and communities in the process of governance. Instead of being constrained by municipal boundaries and structures, municipalities can engage others in addressing issues and challenges that cross municipal borders. Processes are more flexible and adaptive to changing context and move beyond the traditional municipal decision- making structures. Instead of formally defined regions and partners, the boundaries and actors may change depending on the issue. For example, employment and economic development may include different partners and geographic reach than a regional focus on arts and culture. Metro Vancouver British Columbia has 162 municipalities and 27 regional districts that cover the province. Regional districts are described as unique federations of municipalities Metro Vancouver describes itself as a federation that includes 21 municipalities, one Electoral Area, and one Treaty First Nation that collaboratively plans for and delivers regional-scale services such as water, wastewater, solid waste management, regional parks, affordable housing (Metro Vancouver, 2020). Member municipalities lend authority to the regional federation rather than being under its control; the regional district has limited formal powers but can be granted more authority by its members and voters . Greater Toronto Area The Greater Toronto Area (or GTA) is a term used to describe the urban area that includes Toronto and the regions of Durham, Halton, Peel, and York. From time to time, there are suggestions that there needs to be a regional government for the GTA to provide a more integrated approach to development, sustainability, and economic competitiveness. Toronto mayor Mel Lastman appointed a Greater Toronto Task Force, chaired by Anne Golden, to look at governance in the GTA. The 1996 report recommended an upper-tier GTA region governance structure. In 1998, the Ontario government established the Greater Toronto Services Board in an effort to address service coordination and financing issues in the GTA without structural change. The board had limited powers of coordination, its members disagreed on key directions, and it was terminated in 2001. In March 2006, the Ontario government established the Greater Toronto Transportation Authority , now called Metrolinx, with responsibility for integrated planning, coordination, and operation of the GO transit system. At the beginning, elected representatives from local and regional governments sat on the board of the GTTA, but this was later changed to appointed business and community representatives. New calls for regional governance are emerging from the COVID-19 crisis. C t , Eidelman, and Fenn have proposed a voluntary regional governance body that would be developed from the bottom-up by local municipalities. It differs from other examples of new regionalism in that the authors propose that it be developed and led by senior municipal staff in an effort to move past the politics that have got in the way of previous regional collaboration initiatives. The authors describe the model as built on a foundation of trust; flexible, letting partners opt in or out; allowing for business and civil society partners; and focusing on issues rather than municipal boundaries Meta-governance Metagovernance, an umbrella concept introduced in the mid-1990s, is described as a practice by public authorities that entails the coordination of one or more governance modes by using different instruments, methods, and strategies to overcome governance failures (Gjaltema, Beisbroek and Termeer, 2019, 1). Local government failures might include problems of coordination, engagement, and support, and challenges with deciding on and implementing change. Metagovernance overcomes these failures by bringing together a network of actors from different sectors around an issue. The network can be led by local government and can be advisory or have decision-making authority. Multi-level Governance Alan Broadbent argues that cooperation rather than coercion is a better way of governing our large city regions . More can be achieved, and at less cost and effort, than through amalgamations, privatization, and other traditional efforts to achieve efficiencies. The complex, multi-faceted challenges faced by municipalities can t be addressed on an ad hoc, piecemeal basis, and municipalities don t have the resources to address them independently. Broadbent argues that multi-level collaboration, across municipal, provincial, and federal levels as well as with community, nonprofit, and business interests is key to develop shared approaches. Roles and contributions will vary depending on the issue. Metro Vancouver Regional Steering Committee on Homelessness A study of collaborative decision-making related to homelessness in Vancouver concluded that almost half of the policy decisions made by the group would not have been made under typical processes . The collaborative, created in 2000 to implement the federal government s National Homelessness Initiative, included diverse government and civil society actors to develop priorities and allocate funding (Doberstein, 2016, 826). The development and maintenance of trust in the collaborative, through some early wins and clear rules developed by the group, was a key factor in its success. Key Point Each of the approaches described in this section differs significantly from the formal constitutional options described earlier. These approaches put aside questions of formal authority and emphasize municipal leadership in bringing multiple actors together, across municipal boundaries, to focus on issues of shared concern. They focus on positive change and multi- sector relationships without formal structural change. In addition to relationships with the federal government and provinces and territories, municipalities have relationships with each other. These relationships can be competitive, conflictual, or cooperative. Intermunicipal relationships often relate to infrastructure and hard services such as waste, sewage, and water. Some are longstanding relationships, like mutual aid agreements for fire service between neighbouring municipalities, while others are more recent, like a memorandum of understanding in Bruce County, Ontario, to launch a Municipal Innovation Council that will support seven partnering municipalities in finding and implementing smarter and more effective ways of delivering municipal services . Cooperative relationships take place when municipalities expect that there will be benefit to all parties of the agreement perhaps through efficiencies, new services that couldn t be provided by a single municipality, or a need to pool resources to address a significant shared problem. Spicer looked at inter-municipal agreements in Toronto, Regina, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Calgary, and Edmonton census metropolitan areas between 1995 and 2013 (as noted earlier in the course, the Toronto CMA includes the city of Toronto and the regions of Peel, Halton, York, and Durham). Only 354 relationships were identified in the 117 municipalities (Spicer, 2015, 139), leading Spicer to reflect that t he most obvious finding is that Canadian municipalities within large metropolitan areas are using interlocal agreements sparingly . The inter-municipal relationships took different forms, including informal networks, contracts, mandated agreements, working groups, partnerships, networks, councils of government, regional authorities (Spicer, 2015, 140). The relationships were small, with an average of 2.87 partners (Spicer, 2015, 141), and most were restrictive in the terms, conditions, expectations of the partners, and termination clauses. About 20 of the agreements were more open-ended and flexible (Spicer, 2015, 142). Example Stratford, Prince Edward Island Stratford, Prince Edward Island voted in favour of building a new sewage treatment plant and learned, shortly after the vote, that the province would not contribute its 50 share of the development. The provincial government preferred a sewage option that included building a pipeline and sharing in a waste treatment plant in Hillsborough River, Charlottetown. This option was considered by Stratford, but was discounted because it would cost the municipality about 1 million extra for the infrastructure, and the ongoing treatment costs would be higher than a municipally owned plant in Stratford. In the end, Stratford Council approved the pipeline project. The process took a number of years of study, more than six months of active discussion in Stratford, and involved funding negotiations and relationship management. This example shows that finances, relationships with neighbouring municipalities, and politics are often part of inter- Most agree on the need for improved cooperation between federal, provincial, and municipal governments to address the scale and complexity of issues facing Canada s municipalities, particularly the large cities. Whether this is through formal or informal means continues to be debated. Are municipalities well positioned to negotiate? Do they have a clear and strong position? In federal- provincial relations, the federal government negotiates with ten provinces and three territories. In provincial-municipal relations, the negotiating group is much larger and significantly more diverse. It includes towns, cities, rural municipalities, as well as single-tier, local, and regional governments. Organizations such as the Federation of Canadian Municipalities or provincial bodies such as the Association of Municipalities in Ontario struggle to reach positions on issues that reflect all their members perspectives. Over time, subgroups of municipalities have been established within these associations to advocate for issues specific to their size or unique characteristics. For example, the FCM has a Big City Mayors Caucus that meets a few times a year; it also has a Rural Forum and a Northern Forum, recognizing the unique issues faced by municipalities in these areas. Within municipalities, who has responsibility to develop strong relationships with other levels of government? Typically, municipalities are not well resourced or structured for this. While staff in program areas negotiate program, policy, or funding arrangements for approval by their municipal councils, few municipalities have the resources to take a big picture look at intergovernmental relations. Of course, there are exceptions, like the large municipalities and cities. In addition, the decision-making processes and the need to report to municipal council for approval or input complicates the process. Municipal elections every four years can also frustrate the development of a consistent municipal position on intergovernmental issues if there is significant change in the elected members. Municipalities benefit from the links they have with their citizens and communities. Provincial and federal governments need local governments as a vehicle of democracy and conduit of values, opinions, and needs, as well as for their delivery of delegated downloaded services and programs. In addition to the boundary, size, capacity, structure, and decision-making issues that muddy intergovernmental relationships, there are many municipally oriented special purpose bodies, like school boards, transportation bodies, or health service planning groups, that serve municipalities but have different boundaries. The Local Health Integration Networks established by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care did not reflect existing municipal boundaries and exacerbated the challenges of effective local health planning and service delivery. From a provincial or territorial perspective, the challenges of negotiating are significant. As discussed in this module, it is difficult for a province or territory to develop a generic, one size fits all policy for municipalities that effectively responds to the range of issues facing municipalities. In addition, the capacity of a province to provide leadership over municipalities is heavily influenced by the provincial ministry or departmental structure . Often referred to as silos, provincial ministries and decentralized program areas do not always work together and, consequently, there can be limited coordination in policy or direction as it relates to municipalities. The way this country works is that a lot of big decisions are made by federal and provincial governments, but the implementation of those decisions whether it s transit, whether it s housing, whether it s child care happens in local communities. (Mayor John Tory, as quoted by Patel and Blouin, 2020, May 18) The relationships between municipalities and provincial and federal governments are critical to the health and quality of life in Canada s municipalities. This module has provided an overview of some of the key points of tension and progress in the relationships. The module also highlighted that intergovernmental relations is a complex and challenging area of politics, finances, jurisdictions, and personalities. Did You Know? Alberta is the only province that contains two incorporated urban municipalities, Banff and Jasper, that are located in national parks. Lloydminster, a charter city, crosses into two provincial jurisdictions, Alberta and Saskatchewan. Think about the unique interjurisdictional challenges (and opportunities) that these multi- jurisdiction municipalities must face. You are encouraged to further explore the intergovernmental relationships in the module discussion by reflecting on a current intergovernmental issue affecting your municipality. Canadian federalism, and the 1 British North America Act, gives the provinces control over municipalities. The Municipal Act (or equivalent) is the primary instrument of provincial control over municipalities, although control is also exercised through other legislation, regulatory supervisory and financial mechanisms, and the courts. The nature and form of the provincial relationship with municipalities varies from province to province, but there is a general mismatch between the role of municipalities and the level of municipal autonomy. Provincial downloading and delegation of provincial functions and federal withdrawal from some policy areas has stressed municipal capacity and finances and entangled the relationships. From time to time, provinces and municipalities engage in disentanglement exercises, based on the principle of subsidiarity, to try to clarify roles and accountability and to often save money. The federal government has an informal and ad hoc relationship with municipalities that has varied in intensity and focus over time, depending on the political orientation of the party in power. Both the provincial and federal governments need strong and effective local governments. There are two main paths for new intergovernmental relationships: Changing the rules that govern the relationship formally negotiated change through constitutional or other legislative change Working around the rules informal change through municipal-led initiatives for collaboration and partnership with a range of government, business, and civil society partners Pressure is growing for formal change in intergovernmental relationships while at the same time municipalities are working informally to address local issues. Municipalities have longstanding relationships with other municipalities, although research suggests that the number of inter-municipal relationships may be smaller than one might expect. Next week we will focus on the complex and increasingly important local government relationships with Indigenous governments and peoples.. Evidence from a multi level survey of Canadian elected officials Gabriel Eidelman 1 Jack Lucas 2 Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, University of Toronto Department of Political Science, University of Calgary Correspondence Dr. Jack Lucas, Department of Political Science, University of Calgary. Email: Funding information Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, Grant Award Number: 890 2018 0 Abstract While past research suggests that informal processes of dialogue play an important role in municipal inter- governmental relations in Canada, we currently know very little about their character and frequency. Who do local elected officials communicate with, and through which channels? And which municipal voices carry the most weight in these conversations? This article answers these questions from the perspective of elected politicians themselves, using a pan Canadian survey of municipal, provincial, and federal elected representatives. Our find- ings confirm that municipal intergovernmental relations depend heavily on informal institutions and personal relationships and highlight the key role of municipal mayors as spokespersons and advocates for municipalities in Canadian federalism. Et quelles voix Par Nos r sultats INTRODUCTION Canadian political leaders routinely acknowledge that municipalities deserve a seat at the table when federal and provincial governments meet to discuss issues relevant to cities and local communities. But Canada's federal institutions do not include any formal mechanisms for intergovernmental collaboration or shared decision making with municipal governments . processes and personal relationships between municipal mayors and councillors and their parliamentary counterparts . We currently know very little about these informal mechanisms of elite intergovernmental communication and advocacy. How often do mayors and councillors actually interact with provincial and federal officials? Who do they communicate with most frequently? Which municipal voices carry the most weight in these conversations? In this article, we aim to answer these questions using a new survey of municipal, provincial, and federal elected representatives across Canada. We use the survey data to describe municipal provincial and municipal federal relationships from the perspective of municipal mayors and councillors themselves, while also comparing municipal representatives' perceptions to those of their provincial and federal counterparts. We begin by reviewing the academic literature on Canada's federal institutions, both formal and informal, then explore the historical and present role of municipalities and municipal elected representatives within these institutions. Next, we present survey results that help illuminate the mechanics and defining features of multilevel governance in Canada. Our findings demonstrate the importance of informal processes of intergovernmental communica- tion and advocacy in the Canadian municipal sector, and highlight the especially important role of mayors as spokespersons and advocates for their municipalities. We show that provincial and federal politicians generally share municipal representatives' perceptions of these relationships, further cementing the importance of informal relationships in municipal intergovernmental interaction. Throughout our analysis, we also find that municipal population size is strongly associated with municipal representatives' perceptions of both the quality and the character of intergovernmental interaction in Canada. See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License INFORMAL INSTITUTIONS AND INTERGOVERNMENTAL REL ATIONS Institutions are systems of rules, practices, and narratives that govern political behaviour . Formal institutions, such as written constitutions, laws, and contracts, are codified or recorded and enforced by the courts. Informal institutions, such as constitutional conventions and other rules that guide government behaviour without being spelled out in law, are products of social norms, customs, and traditions, and enforced in the political arena. Whether formal or informal, institutions establish, and arguably determine, how political choices are made and conflicts resolved. This is particularly apparent in federal systems of government, and the practice of intergovernmental relations in these systems. Canada is a highly decentralized federation. The Constitution (British North America) Act of 1867 originally concentrated power in the federal government. But over decades of changing legal interpretations, political practices, and public narratives, Canadian federalism has evolved to the point that jurisdiction over many consequential policy domains, such as health care, education, and, most relevant for our purposes, urban and municipal affairs, are now principally controlled by provincial governments. This transformation has been shaped, in part, by Canada's unique mix of formal and informal intergovernmental institutions. Formally, sections 91 95 of Canada's written Constitution explicitly enumerate the division of powers between federal and provincial governments. In practice, these areas of responsibility are rarely watertight. Although the courts are often called upon to resolve jurisdictional confusion or conflicts as formal matters of constitutional law, in truth, the vast majority of intergovernmental relations take place informally, in the political arena. This is what federalism scholars such as Gauvin and Papillon mean when they characterize Canadian federalism as a loosely institutionalized system of government. Coordination and collaboration between governments are not spelled out by the formal rules of Canadian federalism. Unlike other federal systems, such as Germany, Canada's Constitution does not require, for example, provincial representation in federal parliament. Rather, cooperation emerges through the prevailing informal practices of intergovernmental dialogue. Actors demonstrate the rules of intergovernmental relations through their conduct in, say, bilateral and multilateral meetings that result in negotiated agreements between federal and provincial political leaders. Official mechanisms of intergovernmental relations, such as First Ministers Meetings and other high level political summits involving the prime minister and provincial premiers, attract attention from media and scholarly observers. But these meetings are, in fact, quite rare. Outside the recent COVID 19 pandemic emergency, there have been only 13 first ministers' meetings over the past 22 years.1 Intergovernmental councils and ministerial conferences organized by sector or departmental portfolio, such as the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment or the Council of Ministers of Education , are more common and meet on a semi regular basis. But they still only total about thirty five in number (Schnabel, 2020; 19). The vast majority of intergovernmental relations in Canada take place behind the scenes, through countless unofficial channels between the executive branches of both federal and provincial governments. This form of executive federalism follows the unwritten rules and procedural norms of federal provincial diplomacy, as Simeon famously described fifty years ago, typified by issue by issue negotiation and bargaining: Then as now, the process had no statutory or constitutional standing. There was no set schedule for first ministers' meetings; 80 EIDELMAN AND LUCAS17547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License there were no formal decision rules; and intergovernmental agreements and accords had no formal status or mechanisms for enforcement (Simeon, 2006 : 326). If all goes well, intergovernmental diplomacy may lead to non binding political agreements (e.g., joint statements, memorandums of understanding, and the like). Yet each success is the result of its own fragile, difficult to replicate political process. MUNICIPALITIES IN CANADIAN FEDERALISM Where do municipal governments fit within this system of intergovernmental relations? In the shadows, more or less. Lacking formal constitutional standing, municipalities are largely afterthoughts in Canadian federalism. Legally, municipalities are subordinate to federal and provincial governments, and thus generally overlooked in conventional understandings of intergovernmental relations. In ordinary practice, municipal politicians have no direct line to affecting provincial and federal decisions (Hachard, 2022; 9). Mayors and local elected officials have long demanded a seat at the table when it comes to intergovernmental negotiations (Bradford, 2016; Doberstein, 2013). In our survey of more than 800 municipal representatives in 2022 for which we provide detailed technical information in the next section 95 of respondents agreed with the statement that municipalities should have a seat at the table in intergovernmental discussions relevant to their communities. When asked the same question, more than 100 provincial and federal parliamentarians (85 ) also overwhelmingly agreed that municipalities should have a seat at the table. In reality, however, they rarely do. Fewer than one third of mayors and councillors in our survey reported that federal (28 ) and provincial (32 ) governments treat municipalities as equal partners in the policy making process a sentiment that was echoed by federal and provincial respondents (32 ). In recent years, promises from federal and provincial elected officials to work hand in hand with municipalities have become routine, especially when those leaders are invited to address Municipalities, or the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. Even so, municipal elected officials are rarely invited to first ministers' meetings or intergovernmental councils, and are generally excluded from federal provincial negotiations even on issues that directly affect municipal operations. Municipalities in British Columbia and Ontario, for instance, own and operate many child care centres, yet local elected officials were not directly involved in the series of bilateral Early Learning and Child Care Agreements recently signed by provinces and the federal government (Canada Government of, 2022). Similarly, the Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program flows through 13 separate bilateral agreements with provinces and territories, even though municipalities own the majority of public infrastructure assets (Infrastructure Canada, 2018). The Safe Restart Agreement between the federal government and the provinces in the early months of the COVID 19 pandemic included 2 billion for municipalities to offset COVID related operating costs, even though municipal representatives, such as the Big City Mayors Caucus, were not formally invited to the negotiating table . This is not to say that municipalities are completely ignored by senior governments. Slowly but surely, provincial governments have gradually expanded the scope of authority delegated to local governments via natural person powers, new spheres of jurisdiction, and increased fiscal and administrative capacity. This includes an emerging duty to consult with HOW DO MUNICIPAL MAYORS AND COUNCILLORS COMMUNICATE? 8117547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License municipal officials before making decisions that affect them. British Columbia and Ontario, for example, have enshrined a duty to consult in the Community Charter and Municipal Act, respectively, while Quebec and Alberta have signed MOUs with municipal associations and individual municipalities committed to the principle . Likewise, the federal government has acknowledged the growing importance of cities through direct federal municipal programs such as the Smart Cities Challenge, Innovation Superclusters Initiative, Urban Programming for Indigenous Peoples initiative. Most recently, in response to the COVID 19 pandemic, the Trudeau government established the Rapid Housing Initiative, which provides 1.5 billion in direct funding to build affordable housing, and expanded the Canada Community Building Fund (formerly known as the Gas Tax Fund) into a permanent 2 billion annual fund to directly support municipal infrastructure spending (even though it technically flows through provinces and territories). However, these collaborative steps have centred primarily on dialogue between administrative, rather than elected officials. Direct engagement with municipal elected representatives is limited, first, by the sheer variety of municipal governments in Canada some small, with limited resources and administrative support to engage in intergovernmental relations, others large, with obvious economic and strategic importance to provincial and federal governments, and municipal budgets that rival some provinces ; and, second, by the diversity of municipal responsibilities in different policy fields. The City of Toronto, for example, claims to provide more than 150 public services from affordable housing, to transit, to long term care homes all of which depend, to a greater or lesser degree, on intergovernmental coordination, cooperation, or investment. Yet each is rarely overseen by a single elected equivalent to a federal or provincial minister. The question who speaks for cities? seldom comes with a simple answer (see Feldman and Graham, 1979). As a result, the nature of intergovernmental dialogues between elected representatives across the three orders of government vary profoundly by policy domain (Lucas and Smith, 2020; 427). Local services that are closely regulated by provinces, as well as cases where municipal governments deliver or implement provincial policy, such as land use planning, policing, and water and waste management, are typically characterized by systemic partnership between provinces and municipalities (Sancton and Young., 2009; xi) that is to say, ongoing, day to day interaction between administrators and routine reporting. More complex files, such as services for urban Indigenous populations, exhibit a range of intergovernmental sophistication. On one end of the spectrum is immigrant settlement policy, where one observes regular discussions between federal, provincial, and municipal politicians facilitated by dedicated forums for intergovernmental dialogue, such as the Municipal Immigration Committee established under the Canada Ontario Immigration Agreement . On the other end is homelessness policy, which until recently, has long floundered due to institutional barriers to intergovernmental coordination . All in all, intergovernmental interaction among elected representatives in Canada is loosely organized and highly dependent on personal relationships between municipal, provincial, and federal politicians. To be sure, dialogue between elected officials is just one component of the larger system of intergovernmental relations in Canada, which also includes frequent communication between public servants and appointed officials. But as Bradford notes in his exploration of Canada's short lived experiment with trilateral Urban Development Agreements, at the end of the day, intergovernmental arrangements in Canada depend on political champions. RESEARCH DESIGN The literature summarized above suggests that the informal processes of provincial municipal and federal municipal interaction among elected representatives at all levels are a crucial yet under explored component of the Canadian municipal intergovernmental system. Past research has generally explored these informal relationships and intergovernmental dialogue using case study and interview methods across several municipalities and policy domains (Feldman and Graham, 1979; Horak and Young, 2012). Our analysis builds on this work, using survey methods to offer a pan Canadian look at municipal intergovernmental relations from the perspective of hundreds of municipal, provincial, and federal elected representatives engaged in these processes. We focus on five research questions. First, what channels do municipal representatives use to communicate with federal and provincial governments? politicians communicate with most frequently in provincial and federal governments? Third, who do they see as the most common spokesperson for municipalities? Fourth, whose voice is most important in these conversations? Finally, how does this form of intergovernmental advocacy by municipalities vary across political contexts and types of municipalities? To explore this final research question, we focus particular attention on three variables. First, we expect that ideological and partisan dynamics will shape municipal politicians' perceptions of the relationship between their municipalities and the provincial or federal government. Even in non partisan municipalities, a substantial fraction of Canadian municipal politicians have partisan identities and ideological preferences vary substantially across Canada among both elected representatives and the general public . We expect that municipal politicians who are more favourably disposed to their provincial government in political terms more ideologically proximate to the government and or connected by shared partisanship will have more positive assessments of their Our second variable of interest is municipal population size. Traditionally, local and urban politics researchers have tended to assume that smaller municipalities and big cities are very different worlds (Oliver, 2012; Peterson, 1981), and recent work in Canada has shown that municipal population size is an important factor for understanding local policy priorities . At the same time, other recent work in Canada and the United States has municipal voting behaviour, political representation, and policy responsiveness are considera- bly less pronounced than traditional research might have led us to suspect (Lucas and Armstrong, 2021; Tausanovitch and Warshaw, 2014). In the realm of intergovernmental relations, however, we have good reason to expect that informal practices vary substantially across small and large municipalities because of differences in the municipal council role itself (full time political careers vs. part time positions), differences in staff capacity devoted to intergovernmental relations, and important differences in the policy needs and responsibilities of Canada's largest cities. Our final variable of interest is government audience. Although there is growing interest among Canadian scholars in federal municipal interaction , the HOW DO MUNICIPAL MAYORS AND COUNCILLORS COMMUNICATE? 8317547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . DATA AND METHODS To provide a broad picture of intergovernmental interaction among municipal provincial and Barometer, an annual survey of mayors and councillors in every municipality above 9,000 population in Canada. While this sampling frame includes nearly 450 municipalities and covers the overwhelming majority of the Canadian population, we note that additional research will be required to understand if our findings extend to the large number of smaller municipalities across Canada below the 9,000 population threshold. We designed the 2022 edition of the survey with a special focus on intergovernmental relationships, including detailed questions of municipal politicians about channels of intergovernmental interaction, intergovernmental spokespeople and advocacy, and the health of municipal provincial and municipal federal relationships. The survey was fielded in January and February of 2022 and received a total of 867 responses, for an overall response rate of 23 a very strong response rate for a survey of North American elected political elites. Survey responses are broadly representative of the larger population of municipal politicians on observable characteristics including population size, province, region, and gender. We provide a detailed breakdown of these characteristics and further discussion of the survey's representativeness in the supplementary material (see Appendices). Alongside the 2022 survey of municipal mayors and councillors, the Canadian Municipal Barometer research team also invited every provincial and federal elected representative in Canada to participate in a shorter survey about provincial municipal or federal municipal relationships, soliciting provincial and federal perspectives on many of the same questions we The provincial and federal survey was fielded during the same dates as the municipal survey and received a total of 107 responses, for an overall response rate of 10 . While the provincial and federal survey data are more limited, they still interaction from the provincial and federal sides of those relationships. As we noted above, we are especially interested in understanding how municipal politicians' perceptions of the municipal provincial and municipal federal relationships are shaped by political dynamics, population size, and government audience. To measure municipal politicians' perceived ideological distance from their provincial or federal governments, we use data from the Barometer on each respondent's ideological self placement along with the ideological placement of their premier and the prime minister. On this measure, ideological distance is simply the absolute difference between the politician's 84 EIDELMAN AND LUCAS17547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License ideological self placement on a 0 10 left right scale and their placement of the provincial and federal leaders on the same scale. We also calculate the partisan match between the municipal politician and the party in power at the provincial and federal levels using politicians' self reported provincial and federal party identification in the Barometer survey. Our other variables of interest municipal population size and government audience are much simpler. We measure population size by matching each municipal respondent to the 2016 census population of the municipality in which they are elected. Because we ask separate questions in our survey about provincial and federal relationships, we generally present our findings on government audience separately, noting differences in the distribution of responses as well as the underlying relationships for each of the two other levels of government. Full wording of survey questions is presented alongside descriptive results in the next section. Finally, because we are interested in relationships that occur at both the individual level (ideological distance, party match) and the municipal level (population size), our research questions require a multilevel model that can properly estimate individual and municipal relationships. Bayesian multilevel models are well suited to this task, enabling straightforward multilevel specifications and producing appropriate 95 credible intervals for variables at both the For this reason, we employ multilevel models with varying municipal level intercepts in all models below. To account for possible heterogeneity in response rates and politicians' socio demographic characteristics, all models also include controls for politicians' age, gender, and level of education. We focus on our variables of substantive interest in the main text, but provide full tables of results for all models in the supplementary material. RESU LTS To set the stage, we asked municipal mayors and councillors to describe their relationship with respective provincial and federal governments. Responses are reflected in Figure 1, which offers a big picture overview of Canadian municipal politicians' perceptions of municipal provincial Data in the figure are drawn from all three waves of the Canadian Municipal Barometer survey (2020, 2021, 2022) and incorporate responses from more than 1,500 distinct municipal politicians. In the top panels of Figure 1, we see that municipal politicians' perceptions of intergovernmental relationships are very similar, in the aggregate, across the two levels. About one third of respondents describe provincial municipal and federal municipal relationships as fair, and nearly half describe the relationships as good. The only notable difference between the two levels is the slightly higher proportion of politicians who describe the relationship as excellent about 11 for provincial municipal relations, in contrast with about 7 for federal Overall, however, perceptions of both relationships are very similar. In the bottom panels of Figure 1, we summarize the correlates of these perceptions. As discussed above, these correlates are drawn from multilevel models that include socio demographic controls (age, gender, education) and also account for the fact that our respondents are clustered in municipalities and provinces. The coefficients in Figure 1 offer strong evidence that both partisan dynamics and population size are important ingredients for understanding municipal intergovernmental interaction in Canada. The first relationship in each panel, which captures the politician's perceived ideological distance from their provincial premier (on the left) or the prime minister (on the right), is substantively large and negative, which means that politicians who are more ideologically distant HOW DO MUNICIPAL MAYORS AND COUNCILLORS COMMUNICATE? 8517547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License from the premier or prime minister tend to score their provincial municipal or federal municipal relationship more poorly. The relationship is large enough to be substantively meaningful: more than 0.7 points, in both cases, on a four point scale from poor to excellent. The second relationship in Figure 1, party match, is also notable: politicians who personally identify with the party in power at the provincial or federal level are more positive in their assessment of the intergovernmental relationship than those who are non partisans or who identify with a different party a difference of about 0.2 points in both cases. This relationship is particularly noteworthy because both ideological distance and party match are included in the same model; perceived ideological distance and partisan identities are each independently related to intergovernmental assessments, suggesting that both ideological preferences and partisan identities are important predictors of a municipal politician's assessment of intergovernmental relationships. Finally, Figure 1 suggests that municipal population size is strongly related to politicians' assessments of provincial municipal and federal municipal relationships, but the direction of the relationship varies across levels of government. relationship is negative, suggesting that big city politicians tend to have less favourable impressions of relations with the province than politicians from smaller municipalities. For federal municipal relations, the coefficient is positive, suggesting that precisely the opposite holds: big city mayors and councillors tend to have more positive impressions of relations with the federal government than politicians from smaller municipalities. These findings illustrate that municipal politicians' perceptions of their relationship with their provincial and federal counterparts is strongly related to the level of government under consideration and the size of the municipality that the municipal politician represents: we are dealing not with a single relationship, but rather with many relationships, the character of which vary substantially across municipalities and level of government. With regard to provincial municipal relations, elected officials in large municipalities feel most able to act on their own, and hence feel most constrained by their provincial governments. It is thus not surprising that the so called city charters conversation is dominated by the country's most populous cities. With regard to federal municipal relations, on the other hand, the federal government's apparent work with big cities on major infrastructure investments and pressing policy challenges like housing perhaps combined with the fact that the federal Liberal government's own base of support rests primarily in the country's big cities means that the relationship is reversed. DISCU SSION AND C ONCLUSION Our goal in this article has been to provide a big picture and pan Canadian perspective on elected representatives' perceptions of municipal provincial federal interaction, with a particular focus on the informal institutions of municipal intergovernmental advocacy. Using data from more than 800 mayors and councillors across Canada, combined with insights from provincial and federal parliamentarians, our survey results lead us to the following conclusions.5 First, we found clear evidence that, for municipal mayors and councillors, personal relationships with local MLAs and MPs are the central mechanism for municipal provincial Informal institutions, in other words, are at the heart of municipal intergovernmental interaction in Canada, much like with federal provincial relations. This is an important finding, because it reminds us that the same conceptual tools used to understand federal provincial relations may prove useful to understand municipal provincial federal relations and multilevel governance. At the same time, it also highlights various idiosyncrasies not least, that municipal elected representatives see their interactio 7 Federal and provincial perceptions of municipal advocacy strategy. 92 EIDELMAN AND LUCAS17547121, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License with provincial and federal parliamentarians as intergovernmental relations, whether or not those representatives actually represent federal or provincial governments as a member of Cabinet. Second, our findings underscore the crucial importance of municipal mayors as the chief spokesperson and advocate for municipal governments in Canadian federalism. Formally, Canada's weak mayor system does not bestow mayors with any special authority or statutory responsibility for intergovernmental affairs. Nevertheless, a large majority of elected politicians across all orders of government agreed that when it comes to intergovernmental relations, mayors rule especially in larger municipalities. As chief executives of their respective governments, mayors take a lead role in the sort of informal diplomacy that has long typified Canadian intergovernmental relations. This opens new lines of scholarly inquiry regarding mayoral participation in executive federalism, including measuring the performance of mayors as chief municipal advocate in the intergovernmental arena. Third, our quantitative analysis suggests important variation in municipal inter- governmental processes across differing political contexts. For example, we find that municipal politicians' perceived ideological distance from their provincial or federal governments, as well as their shared (or differing) partisan affiliations, is related to assessments of the health of This finding follows from Lucas and Smith , who found that municipal politicians were aware of the advantages of partisan alignment, and also connects to important recent work from outside Canada on the ways that partisan match or mismatch between municipal and provincial federal governments can shape the advocacy strategies that municipal governments choose to pursue . Registered lobbying by Canadian municipal governments is quite rare, a striking contrast to the United States (Goldstein and You, 2017; Payson, 2022). But as discussed above, personal lobbying regular communication with elected counterparts in provincial and federal parliaments appears to be a crucial mode of municipal engagement in intergovernmental relations in Canada. Future research would do well to explore the ways that municipal non partisanship may give Canadian municipal mayors and councillors more flexibility in these relationships. Finally, we found that municipal population size has considerable influence on the characteristics of municipal intergovernmental relations, particularly when comparing For example, intergovernmental engagement with federal officials is more common in bigger cities than in smaller municipalities, and the role of the mayor as the municipality's chief intergovernmental advocate is especially heightened in bigger cities. Further research should explore these patterns in municipalities below the Canadian Municipal Barometer's population size threshold (9,000), with a particular focus on the role of municipal associations as advocates for small 6 Additional research could also help to illuminate if the population size patterns we have found are due to greater political profile enjoyed by big city mayors, or support from dedicated intergovernmental advisors and staff that strengthen municipal intergovernmental capacity.
