A Multifaceted Relationship The module introduction described three types of relationships between municipalities and the public. Let s look at them in a bit more detail. Services Municipalities provide services to people who live in the municipality in a customer-type relationship. Municipalities are concerned with accessible and responsive services and measure customer satisfaction of the people who use their services. Municipalities have introduced enhancements to respond to need and demand. People living in municipalities will access core services, like water or sewage, all the time but will use other services, like swimming lessons, parks, or libraries, as needed. If these services involve user fees, the customer relationship is even stronger. Source: mohamed Hassan from Pixabay Source: Wokandapix from Pixabay Representation Municipalities have a democratic citizenship-based relationship with eligible municipal voters. They are accountable to those citizens for acting in their best interests, while in office, and must seek their support at election time. Municipalities have broad democratic relationships with the public related to municipal policy and determining the nature, priorities, and rules that shape the quality of life and how people live, work, and play in municipalities. The public is a stakeholder and partner in the community and in the democratic institution of local government. Taxpayer Local governments also have an accountability relationship with the public about the use of municipal resources and a more direct relationship with those that pay the property tax. For some, this is the most visible of the three types of relationships as people have strong opinions on municipal spending, taxes, transparency, and accountability. Source: Nattanan Kanchanaprat from Pixabay Pause and Reflect As you work through this module, please reflect on these relationships. Which do you see reflected in the various ways that municipalities consult and engage the public? What are the implications for services, citizenship, and accountability of the different ways that municipalities connect with individuals, groups, and communities? Relationships are Political Local government is about politics. Decisions about how communities develop, how land is used, which services are provided and how they are provided, and what priorities are included in municipal budgets are inherently political. Municipal councils must assess competing interests and perspectives and make difficult decisions about complicated issues. The theories from Module 2 (see Introduction to Theories of Local Government) describe the relationships between municipalities, the public, and various interests and how these relationships shape Some are particularly relevant to our discussion of municipal- public relationships. For example, community power theories recognize that while elites have significant influence on decision-making, multiple groups and interests also exert power on municipalities. Urban regime theory considers how coalitions form among diverse groups around particular issues of shared interest. We can also think about political relationships in terms of influence of local decision-making structures, processes, rules, and values. Instead of influencing how an issue is framed and voted on, as in the community power and urban regime theories, system power theories focus on how the elite influences the context for making decisions. They exert influence on the process by shaping the structures and processes through which decisions are made. For example, elite influence could be exerted on the process for public deputations about municipal issues this might include whether deputations are allowed, the length of time for a deputation, limits on how many deputations, rules about advance registration to make a deputation, and timing (day or evening) of the meeting that hears deputations. Assessing the Relationship It is difficult to assess the municipal relationship with the public. Each of the three relationships involves different elements and measures. For example, the customer relationship would include effectiveness, service quality, and accessibility, while the taxpayer accountability relationship would include efficiency and transparency. Trying to bring them together into a standard measure is challenging. The Argyle Public Relationships Index looked at the relationship that local government had with the public in July 2019. : Click here to see the measures that were used in their index. The Argyle Public Relationships Index measures the quality of the relationships between organizations, including governments, and the public, based on six measures: trust, satisfaction, commitment, caring for customers, concern for people, and the public s ability to influence the organization. . The good news is that there is an opportunity for stronger relationships at the local level with 58 of respondents, increasing to 68 for those born outside Canada, reporting that they were interested in having a relationship with their local government . Another Approach to Assessing the Relationship Municipalities often measure their performance through evaluations, performance measures, benchmarking, and value for money audits. These tend to focus on service quality and financial health, rather than assessing the complex governance relationship with the public, which has received less attention. Zack Taylor suggests that local governance measures should include process and output elements. Taylor reflects that measuring governance outcomes is less important because municipalities have less control over outcomes due to their relationship with provinces, the dispersed authority over the many special purpose bodies at the municipal level, as well as external economic, social, and environmental pressures. Participation It is important to understand the relationship that municipalities have with the public and the roles that the public plays in municipal decision-making processes. Participation and engagement processes have evolved over time and include both statutory or required consultation and optional engagement processes to discuss policy change, development decisions, budget priorities, and more. Activism and Demands from Local Voices The 1960s and early 1970s were a time of growth and development as well as activism and protest. Not surprisingly, municipalities encountered public opposition to development plans that resulted in frustration and wasted time and energy. Municipalities determined that the processes could be more efficient and smoother if community input was solicited earlier in the process rather than at the end. At the same time, there was growing interest in community development and how to involve the public in local decision-making processes as a means to connect residents to their local government, develop capacity in local communities, and support local democracy . : Ladder of Citizen Participation You are probably familiar with Sherry Arnstein s Ladder of Citizen Participation, originally published in 1969, which offers a framework through which to consider engagement and participation. Arnstein argued that effective participation required a redistribution and sharing of decision- making power the ladder connects different stages of participation with levels of citizen power, beginning with the empty ritual of participation and ending with citizen control. Arnstein s ladder highlighted gaps in past efforts at participation and strengthened calls for more community power and participation. It also identified roadblocks in the way of higher levels of participation, including government paternalism, racism, resistance to change, mistrust on both sides, lack of community capacity and knowledge, community alienation, and difficulties organizing an accountable citizen s group or representative . Long Description Sherry Arnstein s ladder of citizen participation has eight stages of participation, which are grouped into three levels of citizen power. Nonparticipation includes: 1. Placation Degrees of citizen power includes: There is continuing interest in citizen participation and since the ladder was published, it has been estimated that at least 53 other participation models had been developed . Jane Jacobs Activist Jane Jacobs fought expressway plans in New York before moving to Toronto to live on Spadina Road in the middle of the route for the planned Spadina Expressway. Jacobs joined with other many Toronto activists in the Stop Spadina Save Our City Coordinating Committee. Metro Toronto, the upper tier of the metropolitan government in Toronto, had proposed the Spadina Expressway to help address growth-related traffic pressures. It was consistently opposed by both the City of Toronto and the Borough of York (both local municipalities in Metro Toronto), which contributed to ongoing tensions between the two levels of municipal government in Toronto. Stop Spadina Save Our City Coordinating Committee pressured Metro Toronto and Ontario to stop the planned expressway from proceeding past Eglinton Avenue in Toronto. In 1971, the premier of Ontario, Bill Davis, overturned Metro Toronto s decision to continue with the project. In the early 1980s, Ontario leased a three-foot wide piece of land at the end of the current expressway (now called the Allen Expressway) to the Borough of York, so that York could prevent any further efforts to build the expressway. Jacobs wrote about the importance of vibrant, mixed-use neighbourhoods and called for a stronger role for community members to contribute to government decision-making processes. Two of Jacobs books, The Death and Life of Great American Cities and The Economy of Cities, were hugely influential in shaping urban reformers efforts to make city hall accessible and open to community input and opinion. Jacobs opposed big development that would destroy the character of communities, arguing for more local decision-making that engaged residents and focused on neighbourhoods and communities. Want to learn more? You may be interested in two resources: TVO. (2016, December 1). Jane Jacobs Revisited . The Agenda with Steve Paiken. Citizen Jane: Battle for the City is a film-length documentary about Jacobs work. 6. Partnership 7. Delegated Power 8. Citizen Control One of the results of the emphasis on public participation and the mounting frustration with decision processes was that public participation became required or mandated in municipal services like planning. Interestingly, as public participation became routine, it moved away from its community roots and became more professionalized local governments hired planners and others specialized in facilitation and consultation . The Spadina Expressway was just one example of local community efforts across the country to stop development that wasn t in keeping with the community. The formal opportunities to participate in planning processes didn t stop local communities from using their voices to oppose development, leading to the phrase NIMBY, or not in my backyard. New Public Management and Emphasis on Customer In the 1980s, different perspectives emerged on the role and function of government, and new public management became the dominant approach. The fiscal crisis in the 1980s meant that there was less money for public services, funding was cut, and services were downloaded and offloaded to municipalities. Alternate service delivery was promoted as a way to reduce the cost of service provision through nonprofit or for-profit providers. Governments pursued a range of initiatives that supported innovation, service quality benchmarking and measurement, and improvement. The focus on customers paid off and levels of public satisfaction with service quality increased from 64 in 1998 to 72 in 2008, according to national surveys that looked at 26 government services across all levels of government (Hughes, 2013, 98). Few of us would disagree with a municipal focus on service quality and responsiveness to need. But the shift to the public as a consumer of service emphasizes a relationship with community members as consumers of service in a market-type relationship. Opportunities for Participation Municipalities engaged with the public in different ways in the 1980s and 1990s, but the relationship and forms of participation focused on getting input and consulting about issues. As you will see, municipalities didn t give the community much power to make recommendations or to make decisions. Deputations All municipalities allow deputations from individuals at the committee level on policy and program issues, municipal budgets, and governance processes and practices. Some municipalities have a public portion of the regular council meetings, where residents can make deputations on local issues. The Toronto Environmental Alliance and the Toronto Youth Food Policy Council have developed guides to deputations at Toronto City Hall that provide valuable advice for those interested in deputations at any Canadian municipality. Statutory consultation Municipalities are required to inform and provide opportunities for public input on planning developments and zoning changes. Direct contact with councillors and the mayor This takes place through email, social media, phone, or letters. Councillors may invite community members to public meetings to discuss key developments or issues in the community. Townhall meetings Many municipalities hold regular town hall meetings. Referendum Canadian municipalities don t use referenda very frequently. Vancouver had a referendum in 2015 on a new transit tax to fund transit improvements and residents voted 61.7 to 38.4 to reject the tax proposal. There was a lot of controversy over the referendum with some arguing that the referendum question was poorly developed. There was concern about giving more resources to TransLink, the Metro Vancouver transit authority, with many arguing that they needed to show a more efficient use of existing resources and greater accountability for how money was currently used. In October 2018, Winnipeg held its first referendum in 35 years as part of the municipal election. The intersection of Portage and Main had been closed to pedestrians since 1979 when an underground pedestrian concourse separated cars and people. In 2018, voters were asked whether they supported the removal of pedestrian barricades and the opening of the major Winnipeg intersection to pedestrians. Sixty-five percent voted against opening the intersection to pedestrians (CBC News, 2018). There was similar reaction to the Vancouver vote, with some advocates for pedestrian access commenting that voters didn t have enough information, while others questioned why all the voters in the city, rather than those in the Portage and Main area, were invited to vote on the intersection referendum question (CBC News, 2018). Surveys, polls, focus groups These are one-time measures of public opinion on key municipal issues and services. Appeals There are a number of appeal options available to interest groups who have been unsuccessful with their issue at the municipal council. Individuals and groups can take the municipality to court if they believe the municipality has broken the law. Groups can appeal a municipal land use decision to the Local Planning Appeal Tribunals (and to similar appeal bodies in other provinces), which have the power to overrule a municipal decision. For example, in 2005, a group of citizens challenged the City of Toronto s decision to build a dedicated right of way along St. Clair and won at the Ontario Court of Appeal; the court ruled that construction work should be halted. The city appealed and the original decision was set aside because of the perception of bias of one of the three judges involved in the original decision. Like other forms of interest group strategies, appeals are expensive and require significant financial resources and understanding of and connection to the subject and legal experts. Advisory committees As discussed in Module 4 (see Committees of Council), the establishment of advisory committees and working groups provides opportunities for ongoing citizen input in municipal decision-making. There are many examples of advisory committees that bring important voices and Public boards There are also citizen representatives on some municipal agencies, boards, and commissions. These members of the public must go through an appointment process before they are recommended for a seat on a municipal special purpose body. Shift to Citizen-based Relationship By the mid to late 1990s, the focus on customers and clients shifted to a focus on citizens. This was a result of a growing recognition that governance was a two-way relationship and citizens and communities had rights and responsibilities in that relationship (Graham and Phillips, 13). There was a complementary shift from consultation for receiving input on an issue to engagement of the public in resolving the issue. Municipalities continued to grow and urbanize. Demographic shifts, diversity, and an increasing gap between the rich and poor have influenced the shape of urban areas as well as the relationship that municipalities have with the public. Municipalities are challenged to develop relationships with and engage diverse communities. Communities may be challenged in how they respond; increasingly, community members want to tell their own stories rather than being represented by a community leader who brings a generic voice. The politics of difference (Crosby, Kelly and Shaeffer in Graham and Phillips, 1998, 15) put pressure on municipalities to support diverse voices and help communities develop capacity to engage in municipal processes. Technology has influenced the relationship between municipalities and the public by providing easier access to information and decision makers, but it also introduced additional barriers for some members of the community who are not tech-connected or tech-savvy. New Approaches to Engaging the Public The shift to citizen participation introduced some different ways of engaging the public directly for municipal issues. Participatory democracy, deliberate engagement, and accountability increasingly shaped how municipalities connected with citizens and local communities. This new relationship between municipalities and the public included: Community Councils Community councils, also called neighbourhood councils or community boards, have been established in Toronto and some other Canadian municipalities. These councils provide some focus on local issues in the municipal decision-making process and help to manage the number of agenda items appearing before city councils. As you remember from Module 4 (see Committees of Council), the powers and levels of community participation on the councils vary among municipalities. Toronto community councils, composed of elected councillors, are largely focused on planning and zoning issues and play a limited role in issues of community interest or in engaging the community (Flynn and Spicer, 2017, 17). Community councils tend to react to staff reports, homeowner requests, or community complaints; one of the recommendations from a review of community councils was to expand the opportunity for community members to take a direct role in shaping their city by putting unelected community members on the councils along with the elected councillors (Flynn and Spicer, 2017, 19). This would bring more diversity to the councils as well as engage new perspectives and dire
0|dashboard  | ctly involve community voices in local decision-making. Ward Councils Municipal wards vary in size; in some municipalities, a ward may be larger than the size of another municipality. Calgary averages 78,345 people per ward; Vancouver averages 60,350; and Winnipeg averages 44,241 (Toronto, 2014, 30). Toronto wards now range in size from 94,579 to 129,081 people, following the 2018 provincially imposed changes . These municipal wards are the size of medium-sized cities Cities that size are normally governed by a mayor and multiple councillors. Why not consider having a residents council for each ward, to deal with small, local issues? . Ward councils are similar in idea to a community council but would be more locally focused and composed of community members, rather than elected councillors. Engagement Policy Municipalities are developing more comprehensive and integrated approaches to public engagement that include formal policy statements, expectations, and supports for engagement. Here s an example from Edmonton. The Municipal Government Act in Alberta requires municipalities to develop and adopt a public participation policy. The video Public Engagement Share Your Voice Shape Our City describes the Edmonton experience developing their policy on public engagement and shares the perspective of community members, staff, and elected representatives who contributed to the initiative. Edmonton describes their approach as creating opportunities for people to contribute to decision making by City Council and Administration about the city s policies, programs, projects, and services, and communicates how public input is collected and used ). Edmonton has an Office of Public Engagement whose work is informed by a council-approved public engagement policy, a handbook for public engagement, standards of practice for public engagement as well as a web page that includes details on engagement opportunities, surveys and polls, and results of past research ). Citizens Panels Municipalities have also been using citizens panels, or a type of jury, to consider a policy issue in depth over time, identify options, and provide advice recommendations on the issue. These are a form of deliberative democracy, where members of the public are given the opportunity to learn about an issue and engage in a facilitated process of analysis, discussion, and reflection over a period of time. Engagement Practices Municipalities try different ways to engage members of the community in municipal issues. Here are a few short examples that show the variety of creative approaches to public engagement in Canadian municipalities. The Region of Waterloo in Ontario produced this amusing video as part of efforts to engage the community in discussions about the Waterloo biosolids strategy . Surrey, British Columbia engaged the public in contributing to the development of a new parks, recreation, and culture strategy . : Edmonton, Alberta Kamloops, British Columbia engaged the community in continued efforts to develop an inclusive and accessible community PDF . The project provided the opportunity for citizen-led input and development in community space and creat ion of a sense of shared ownership between residents and the municipality . Here are examples from Duncan and North Cowichan, B.C., and Toronto, Ontario. The City of Duncan and the municipality of North Cowichan, B.C. wanted to explore the idea of amalgamation and a structure for the new municipality. They decided to establish a citizen panel to research the issue. A civic lottery identified 10,000 people (from both municipalities) who received an invitation package about the initiative. Of the 10,000 invitations, 144 people volunteered to attend an information session and 36 were selected to sit on the panel. The panel was kept busy. They developed a set of values for good local governance PDF that guided their deliberations (take a minute to compare these values to the measures of good governance discussed earlier in this module). The panel developed a list of issues that needed to be resolved by the municipalities in order to proceed with amalgamation discussions, and they identified eight lenses through which amalgamation should be examined, including consistency of services, governance and leadership, economic development, environment, culture and identity, land use and planning, taxes, efficiencies, and savings. In the end, the 36 members reached consensus and endorsed amalgamation of the two municipalities the panel believed that the two jurisdictions will be better able to manage future growth, afford quality public services and infrastructure, and attract outside investment as a unified municipality . Toronto used a similar process to develop recommendations on short-term actions that could be taken to meet greenhouse gas emission targets and implement the TransformTO plan. They engaged a panel of 30 members who met for three full days. We are a diverse group of 3 Torontonians from throughout the city who are concerned about the future of Toronto amid the global impacts of climate change. Selected through Civic Lottery, our diversity is a strength it is a diversity of opinion, of age, of gender, of geography, and of life experience (Toronto, 2019, cover). The panel made recommendations related to housing, transportation, financial tools, and engagement. Planning and Priority Setting Municipalities are also engaging community members in broad, strategic planning and priority setting processes. The Alberta handbook for elected municipal officials Munis 101: The Essentials of Municipal Governance (Elected Officials Education Program, 2017) describes working with others and public input as critical elements in the process for adaptive planning. : Duncan and North Cowichan, British Columbia : Toronto, Ontario Adaptive planning includes input and feedback from community stakeholders as part of a continual process of reviewing and adapting strategy and plans based on learnings of what worked (and didn t), feedback from the community, and changes in the environment. Interests and Interest Groups The first part of the module referred broadly to individuals and groups in the discussion of the citizen local government relationship. This part of the module will focus on the role that interests and interest groups play in local government. Paul Pross defines interest groups as organizations whose members act together attempting to influence public policy in order to promote their common interests (1995, 252 3). Policy communities form when all the interests, agencies, individuals, businesses, and nonprofit organizations in a particular area join in efforts to influence policy. They have dominant voices in the political process because of their experience and specialized knowledge. Each of us belongs to a number of communities of interest they may be based on our gender, sexual orientation, racial and or cultural background, disability, profession, neighbourhood, cultural and sport interests, socio-economic background, etc. They relate to how and where we work, live, and play and to our background. We may not take out memberships in these groups but we are drawn together by our shared, common attributes. There are many situations where groups with shared interests attributes become active in response to an issue or challenge and develop a position or set of preferences. They may dissolve after the issue or evolve into an interest group around their shared goals. When we think of interest groups, we typically think of a group of like-minded individuals or organizations who are supporting or opposing a recommendation or decision or lobbying for something that local government doesn t provide. It is important to recognize that interest groups may also work collaboratively with both the political and bureaucratic elements of local government toward a common goal. Often senior staff or councillors will work with an interest group or policy community on an issue; the group brings legitimacy and support to the councillor or bureaucrat s recommendation and they work together to achieve their shared goal. Interest groups working in this way are referred to as reverse pressure groups. Many different interest groups are active in municipalities. Some are locally based, like residents associations, while others have broader interests that are applied at the local level, such as professional associations, policy think tanks, etc. We will briefly review key municipal interest groups. : Business Interests Many interest groups emerge from businesses and development interests that form part of the local economy. Municipalities are centres of complex economic activity and decisions of local governments can have a direct impact on the competitiveness and profitability of businesses. There are different types of business interest groups, including those with a municipal focus like the board of trade, chamber of commerce, or labour council, and those at a neighbourhood level like a business improvement area. Business interest groups may focus on different sectors, for example, restaurant and hotel associations, or particular types of businesses, like the Black Business and Professional Association. Individual business interests also lobby for their own interests, particularly land developers. Local Groups Neighbourhood-based interest groups are unique to local government and include ratepayer groups, residents associations, community groups, citizen groups, and tenant associations. Homeowners want to make sure the value of their investment in their property is maintained, and neighbourhood groups are strong advocates for preserving and enhancing local neighbourhoods. Their orientation is often defensive in that they react to plans or changes proposed by local government, developers, or other interests. They typically oppose a change or development and are often described using the term NIMBY not in my back yard. Strong neighbourhood groups can be exclusionary to new interests and non-traditional members. Identity-based Groups Identity-based interests can be ethno-cultural or based on faith, gender, age, and sexual orientation. Like other interest groups, identity-based groups participate in municipal processes, working to achieve access and appropriate programs for members of their group and to bring diverse voices for change in municipal policies, programs, and practices. Institutionalized Policy Communities Institutionalized policy communities are groups that join around a shared issue. They could include professional associations, groups like the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, the Ontario Association of Municipal Clerks and Treasurers, policy think tanks, and planning organizations. These groups may advocate for change, however, they may also be called upon for advice and input and, because of their unique knowledge and experience with a municipal policy issue, they can exercise significant influence. Unions Unions of workers, particularly municipal public sector unions, are active interest groups. They tend to have two areas of focus protecting jobs and compensation issues and lobbying on issues related to alternate service delivery (contracting out). Some local unions may contribute to other issues, for example, municipal licensing standards, policies, and processes and municipal policies regarding providers (e.g., Uber directly impacting taxi driver associations). Consumer-focused Groups Clients bring important voices to the decision-making process. Client consumer groups often form in social services, recreation, and affordable housing to advocate for their specific interests. Municipalities have advisory or similar committees involving consumer members contributing to the decision-making process. While consumer-oriented groups provide valuable input into service design and delivery, Tindal . caution against the focus on customers and service delivery. There is significant concern that the emphasis on a customer-service relationship between local government and its citizens narrows the relationship and reduces the scope for involvement in policy and priority setting as citizens of local government. Resources Available to Interest Groups Interest groups have different types and levels of resources available to them. This has a direct impact on the strategies they can employ to influence municipal councils and often, but not always, on their success. Membership, leadership, and public support are important to interest groups; groups that can demonstrate public support for their issue are likely to be more successful than those that do not have the support. Groups with larger membership can speak on behalf of a broader constituency and can command greater resources and volunteers to support their efforts. A strong and effective leader is also important to lend legitimacy to the group. Information is a valuable resource for interest groups. They need to understand the inner workings of local government, how to influence decisions, who the key decision makers are, and when and where they are meeting. They also need to be knowledgeable about the issue they are addressing, often requiring some technical knowledge of the complex issues. Having connections to people with knowledge of the issue area, contacts in the media, and social media presence are assets for an interest group. Resources, both money and in-kind, are critical to the success of an interest group. They can be used to fund the various expert help, communications, opinion polls and research, and staff or volunteers needed to do the work of the interest group. Interest Group Strategies Interest groups employ different strategies to advocate for their position, including lobbying, public appeals, elections, formal legal appeals, and direct action. There are many formal and informal opportunities to present a position to municipal decision makers. Councillors engage with residents, businesses, and other interests at events in the community and will hear perspectives and learn about issues. Interests and interest groups may mount public relations or communications campaigns in traditional and social media. Or they may use direct action, such as resistance, marches, petition campaigns, or protest to try to influence municipal decision-making. Interest groups may endorse candidates in a municipal election or support them through donations and volunteer labour. Legal challenge of municipal decisions is also an option for interests that have exhausted other routes. Lobbying describes direct communication between an interest group and a political decision maker. Many municipalities have rules about lobbying and may require registration with a municipal lobbyist registrar. Codes of ethics and other oversight bodies and policies have influence on how different interests access decision makers and how public and transparent that access is (see Accountability Structures and Officers). Reflections on Interests and Interest Groups Before we leave the discussion of interest groups at the municipal level, let s consider some common questions that are asked about the role and value of interest groups in decision-making processes. Please consider your answer to the question before you click on the green button. This is an interesting question. Does the answer depend on the context, the issue, the other interests that are involved in the issue, your opinion on the interest group or its position, or the decision-making process? Is the answer a no because it slows down and makes decision-making processes overly complicated or perhaps because you disagree with the position advocated by the interest group? Or is the answer a yes because you believe that a plurality of interests at the municipal level makes the process richer and more robust? Some observers believe that interest groups are essential to municipal democracy while others regard them as a threat to good governance. Interest groups give people a voice in politics between elections and provide a vehicle for individuals and organizations to communicate with decision makers and share information about local needs and issues. On the other hand, interest groups can negatively influence decision-making by imposing their unique position or need. They can interfere with decision-making processes and timing, raising issues associated with NIMBYism (not in my back yard). Public policy refers to the decisions governments make and don t make and the services, programs, and regulations they establish. Local government decisions have a direct impact on residents. It is not surprising then that people will attempt to convince government to make decisions that are favourable to them and their interests. There are lots of interest groups because there are so many different interests, including people and businesses at the local level. Interest groups can t be limited; it is important to provide space for diverse perspectives that are often left out of municipal decision-making. The politics of difference, discussed earlier in the module, has resulted in more interests and voices. In addition, interest groups help keep the decision-making process open and accountable for example, a local neighbourhood group may act to counterbalance the interests of a property developer. The process of decision-making is inherently political elected councils must choose between competing ideas or options and do what they think is best for the municipality. They may also do what is best for them politically, remembering that the next municipal election is never far away. Depending on how the councillor defines their role trustee or delegate they may lean toward local community interests. : Do interest groups enhance local democracy? : Why are there so many interest groups at the municipal level? : How should municipal decision makers balance the needs and demands of the different and many interests in a municipality? Citizenship and Voting Elections are a prime means by which citizens participate in the municipal political process. Voter turnout is low in all elections, but it tends to be lowest in municipal elections. Why is there little interest in voting in municipal elections, the most basic form of direct participation? The rational voter is one who calculates the cost (and amount of work it will take) and the benefits of voting and make a rational decision based on the results . These costs and benefits may be influenced by whether the person thinks that their preferred candidate will win and or whether they are interested in the issues being discussed by the candidates. For example, limited voting locations and hours and the anticipation of long lineups to fill in a paper ballot can lead to a decision not to vote. Limited connection to the issues and candidates can lead to disinterest. Social capital builds on the importance of social capital or connection to other people in voting. Voters with low social capital, who aren t engaged in discussions about the election, and who aren t encouraged by others are less likely to vote . For example, the slate of candidates for local office may not be representative of the voting population in terms of gender, ethno-racial and cultural background, age, background, and economic status. Voters may not identify with the candidates and may choose not to vote rather than vote for a candidate who they do not feel can adequately represent them. In addition, the print and broadcast media treat local government differently, reporting less on local issues and policy than politics and personality. The lack of party politics makes local government harder to understand; there is fragmented leadership and no identifiable group to vote in or out. Municipal ward size has similar implications for voter turnout the larger the ward, the less connection a voter will have with the candidates and the attachment to the community. Political efficacy refers to voters understanding and measuring the internal and external significance and effect of their voting . Internal efficacy is when voters consider whether their ballot will make a difference to the candidate they support or the issue that interests them. External political efficacy relates to whether there is trust in the system and whether it reflects the values held by the voter. If both internal and external efficacy are positive, then there is a higher likelihood that the person will vote. For example, some voters view the municipal role as relatively unimportant compared to the provincial or federal level. Most of the big issues (health care, education policy, etc.) are under provincial or federal jurisdiction and there is limited interest in local matters. There is fragmentation in policy and program delivery and funding between the province and municipalities, which adds to the complexity of the municipal franchise. In other areas, the province has responsibility for standards and regulations that affect municipal services, such as in planning, finance, public health, and policing. Voters may prefer to influence policy and programs by voting provincially rather than locally. In addition, the municipal structure and roles may be fragmented, for example in a two-tier local government system, leading to voter confusion. Special purpose bodies limit the municipal control over areas of significance and interest to voters like police and education. Voters question the impact of voting when the result won t affect these program areas. looked at some of the structures of municipal elections, including term limits and ward versus at-large elections (see Municipal Elections). These have an impact on voter turnout. Municipalities with no term limits may have more acclamations of incumbents, and at-large elections can be harder to follow and learn about all the candidates; both may serve to discourage voters. Municipalities have made efforts to address each of these, but it can be hard for municipalities to address low voter turnout. They don t have access to detailed demographic data about who votes and have limited research on the barriers that get in the way of voting. Citizenship and Other Election-related Issues Voting Franchise Voting is the cornerstone of public participation in our democratic system (Siemiatycki and Marshall, 2014, 3). Eligibility to vote in municipal elections defines citizenship rights for people who live in municipalities. In Ontario, municipal voters are those who are eligible to vote in provincial and federal elections over 18 years old, a Canadian citizen, who lives in (is a tenant) or who owns property in the municipality or is a spouse or same sex partner of a person who is a tenant or property owner. In a city like Toronto, these requirements exclude many immigrants who pay property taxes as a tenant or owner and may have lived in Canada for many years but are not yet Canadian citizens. These voting rules also give the right to vote to non-residents or part-time residents who own property in the municipality. This is an issue in cottage country because cottagers can directly influence the result of municipal elections but not participate or contribute to other municipal processes. Finally, the voting franchise has implications for municipal candidates and elections. Election rules require that candidates must be eligible to vote in the election, potentially restricting access to standing for office. Political Parties While political parties aren t very active at the municipal level in Canada, it is still important to reflect on the implications of municipal political parties for public participation in municipal decision-making processes. Would the political party process, which develops an election platform, including priorities for action, be open to ongoing public engagement and debate that may affect the platform once the party is elected? Or would the party only engage in discussions with the community about how the platform could be implemented? The party system is a feature of the parliamentary system of government. If the government can only rule as long as it has the support of a majority of elected members of parliament, then parties are required to assure the disciplined teamwork necessary to create stable government. This could potentially have implications for local issues raised by communities councillors may have to support the party rather than act on issues in their community. Campaign Donations Residents also connect with their municipality through election campaign donations. Toronto doesn t allow corporate or trade union donations and they have a cap on the amount of money an individual can donate to a candidate (which varies for mayor and councillor). Taxpayers can deduct the donation as a political donation when they file their income tax and some municipalities offer a rebate of a portion of the donation to encourage individuals to engage in the elections and to donate to municipal candidates. Limits in Citizenship Relationship The citizenship relationship excludes those who are not qualified to vote as citizens. This is an important limitation, discussed earlier, that isn t present in the other relationships. From time to time, there are situations involving elected councillors and mayors acting unethically or illegally and voters wanting to remove them from office. Municipal councils are different from the parliamentary system at the provincial and federal level where there is opportunity to hold a no- confidence vote and force an election; municipalities don t have this option. political parties, so the caucus can t fire the mayor as leader of the party or oust a councillor. Municipal voters don t have access to a recall process either the only recall process in Canada is at the provincial level in British Columbia. The process involves a recall petition signed by 40 of voters eligible to vote in the election that elected the member (Elections BC, 2020). In the case of Mayor Rob Ford, Toronto s municipal council was unable to remove the mayor from office and instead voted to remove many of the mayor s responsibilities, leaving Mayor Ford with limited statutory responsibilities as set out in the City of Toronto Act. Public pressure was put on Ontario to remove the mayor from office, but the legislation only allows that to happen in cases where a mayor has been found guilty of an offence, and the province didn t take any action. As noted earlier in the course, municipalities must establish codes of conduct for elected representatives as well as a policy on staff council relations. If these fail, voters can appeal to an integrity commissioner, if the municipality has one, but the commissioner is limited in terms of penalties. Activity If you re interested in learning more, you are encouraged to listen to this optional discussion from CBC s radio show, The House Firing a Mayor and Voter Recalls: Why You Can t Oust Rob Ford . Please note that this is an audio recording only. There is no transcription available. Taxpayer Accountability Relationships Traditional and social media headlines about property taxes are almost always negative warnings that taxes will increase. Few property owners can think of property taxes without wondering whether we are paying too much and there is always a vocal group that knows that they are paying too much! The taxpayer-municipal relationship is complicated. As you remember from Module 8, municipal finances are complicated, and it is often a feat of superhuman negotiation to get a balanced budget. It is very hard for municipalities to communicate the complexities of municipal budgets to the public in a way that supports a deeper understanding of property taxes; the conversation often stays at the rhetoric level. It can also be challenging to demonstrate that municipalities are using their financial resources efficiently. Municipal candidates often run campaigns on platforms against the gravy train, waste, and inefficiency. New mayors, or councils that experience a high degree of councillor turnover, often establish a citizen or expert panel to review municipal finances and services. independent auditor generals review municipal finances as well as municipal programs and services. Performance measures, benchmarking, and evaluations compare the costs of services with the quality and outcome of the services. Again, the results of these efforts can be hard to distill into media soundbites and plain language communications to taxpayers. All property taxpayers use municipal services (and are customers) although many forget the less visible, day-to-day infrastructure services and see themselves primarily as taxpayers. Property taxpayers also have the right to vote in municipal elections. This too is a secondary relationship with municipal government for many that is overshadowed by concerns over finances and accountability. Challenges in the Municipal Relationship with the Public There are many benefits of strong relationships between municipalities and their public. People feel a stronger sense of connection and belonging, they are more likely to vote in municipal elections, and they are more likely to engage in municipal processes . Municipalities benefit from the diversity of opinions and ideas, and while a multitude of groups can be overwhelming, they serve to reduce the dominance of certain groups and bring accountability to local government processes. But there are also some real challenges in municipal efforts to develop relationships with and engage individuals, groups, and communities. Globalization Globalization is reshaping relationships local community members may have stronger connections with people, interests, and communities across national borders than within their local municipality. On the other hand, globalization has highlighted the importance of place and community people, businesses, and investors want to live with a high quality of life in safe, dynamic, and engaged communities. Equity, Inclusion and Accessibliity There are other important challenges in the municipal-public relationship related to equity, inclusion, and accessibility. It s very common to hear citizens express interest in attending a public hearing or engagement session, only to be disappointed when they discover the day and time doesn t work with their schedule. Sitting through a four-hour hearing with a fussy baby or having to miss work to attend an engagement session is not a fair burden to place on citizens. More often than not, the people missing out are mothers, young people and working families, leading to a demographic misrepresentation at traditional forums for engagement. This is really a question of equity. (Salvador as quoted in Syvixay, 2019) Accessibility barriers prevent the public from participating in public processes. These can include: Technology barriers lack of access to computers and the internet, and or a limited ability to use them Barriers in physical access to public buildings and space Limited familiarity with municipal issues, concepts, and type of language used in municipal communication. This can be exacerbated in communities that don t have local media sources. Access barriers to either spoken, written, or social communication Fees and charges to access municipal data or documentation. The Saskatoon Star Phoenix and Regina Leader-Post conducted a review of the 774 municipalities in Manitoba. Watch the short trailer Fees May Apply or read the introductory article to their investigative series on transparency and access to information. Economic barriers, including transportation availability and cost, lost time, lost pay as a result of time away from work, and costs of child or elder care can prevent engagement in public processes. Legitimacy and inclusion barriers include: Engagement processes are not perceived as welcoming by all individuals, groups, and communities in the municipality There may be bias toward relationships with certain groups or communities, perhaps traditional neighbourhood groups versus newer interest groups or identity-based groups Some opinions and experiences are valued more than others relationships with younger or older adults may be less important to municipalities Municipalities face challenges developing relationships with at risk, homeless populations or people with transient living arrangements Municipal councils are not reflective of the diverse population they serve and councillors may not have relationships with some communities within their ward Municipalities also face limitations based on their internal capacity for new and more engaged relationships. They have limited resources and time and may lack experience in engaging diverse groups to discuss contentious or complex issues. In addition, wards are generally too large to be homogeneous and to have only one voice yet the need to include many voices may make an engagement process unwieldy. Opportunities in the Municipal Relationship with the Public Attention is being given to these barriers, and municipalities are broadening their toolkits and engaging more people in thoughtful, inclusive, and respectful dialogue about municipal issues. Online platforms present opportunities for municipalities to invite an unlimited number of people into discussions about their communities. Electronic voting could increase municipal voter turnout. Live streamed and archived videos of municipal council and committee meetings give residents the opportunity to follow issues and develop an understanding of municipal processes. Technology could provide more information and greater access to data and information. There is also potential for new forms of local news to replace the local newspapers, which have been closed by their publishers. Municipalities are developing engagement policies and building internal capacity to connect differently with diverse individuals, groups, and communities. Past consultation practices have been replaced by engagement processes and there are increasing examples of delegated decision-making to the community for example, citizen panels and participatory budgeting. Municipalities also have opportunities to build on recent social and environmental grassroots movements and harness some of the energy and ideas to improve municipal-public relationships, strengthen local governance, and improve local communities. A recent poll suggested that the COVID-19 crisis has opened up new possibilities for an enhanced relationship with municipalities. Forty-one percent of Canadians said that they enjoyed an improved relationship with their municipal government during the pandemic . Municipalities will need to build on this and connect with individuals, groups, and communities. The module looked at the multifaceted relationship that municipalities have with the public. Those relationships are political and relate to decisions about programs, services, policies, and the use of The module explored how municipal relationships with the public have shifted over time from consultation to participation and showed that they are grounded in a citizen foundation. It also looked at the expression of that citizenship through municipal voting and elections and engagement in public dialogue processes. Of course, the municipal public isn t a single entity it is made up of individuals, groups, and communities and the discussion of interests and interest groups showed how individuals and organizations work together in different types of interest groups to communicate and advance their issues. In the same way, local government isn t a single entity it includes municipal government as well as the many municipal agencies, boards, and commissions. The module ended with a discussion of some of the challenges and opportunities that will influence the municipal relationship with the public in the future. Municipal relationships with the public are complex and can be considered from three perspectives: a customer-type relationship, a citizenship-based relationship, and a taxpayer- accountability relationship. Relationships with the public are political and concern the use of limited resources and municipal authority. While there are service satisfaction and quality measures, there is not an accepted approach to measuring the overall municipal-public relationship. Public participation at the municipal level has broadened from consultation to engagement in The module described many forms of participation being used by Canadian municipalities. Review Table 10.1 in Chapter 10 of the textbook for some additional forms of participation. Interests and interest groups play an important role in the public-municipal relationship. Many different interests business, identity, local community, consumer, staff unions, and policy communities are active at the municipal level. Municipalities have direct relationships with many, but not all, of the public that meet the definition of citizen. Citizens have rights to run for local office, donate to candidates, and vote in municipal elections. Municipalities also have direct relationships with property taxpayers (property owners) that focus on accountability for the amount of taxes collected and how the money is used. Relationships that municipalities have with local communities are not as inclusive or accessible as they need to be to engage effectively with diverse individuals, groups, and communities. Online platforms and technology continue to influence participation processes and relationships with the public. Grassroots demands for more engagement and interest in better connections, suggests that there will continue to be development in municipal-public relationships. Module 11 will look at some challenges that municipalities face, like technology and the environment, that have implications for governance, sustainability, and quality of life in municipalities. The role of participation in global world cities Maureen M. Donaghy INTRODUCTION Participation in organized groups is often difficult, sometimes boring, and always time con- suming. Voting can also be unappealing, particularly if none of the candidates represents an ideal choice. But politics cannot be transparent, responsive, or accountable to citizens without public participation. This is what we as scholars, activists, and advocates believe to be true, but research on public participation of various forms and in different contexts over the past few decades has sought to provide evidence as to when and how participation matters in public policy making, electoral politics, and neighborhood development. In the urban context these questions are critical as cities are the sites of protest, advocacy, community organizing, and electoral contestation. Scholars, along with government officials, practitioners, and activists, need answers to questions about participation to guide public policy making and institutional design in the modern democratic city. This brief chapter, then, examines what I hold as one of the most central questions for urban politics: When does citizen participation matter? As the chapter will discuss, questions of impact often center on who participates in political activities, why these individuals and groups choose to engage with the state, and how they ultimately make demands or enact change, from the neighborhood to the global level. Over the past several decades, the clash between capitalism and democracy across all these levels has become clearer along with questions of identity, inequality, and who decides the future direction of cities. Citizens come into conflict with developers and governments are meant to mediate claims to urban space. The extent to which citizens particularly those traditionally marginalized from politics can influence government decisions in the face of pressure to generate profits and public revenues often guides central debates in research on participation in urban politics. But in the last two decades scholars increasingly rely on the principles of the right to the city as envisioned by Henri Lefebvre in the 1960s to measure the extent to which cities reflect the desires of residents rather than a small segment of elites. Building on the work of Lefebvre, Purcell argues for a conception of democracy as a tendential project in which people continually increase their desire to manage their affairs themselves . In the urban context this means that people seek to manage the production of urban space on their own terms. In addressing when participation matters, then, the impact may be defined by the extent to which people, rather than governments or corporations, hold power in deciding the tangible and intangible characteristics of cities that shape their everyday lives. But what does this participation look like? In defining democratic norms scholars gen- erally argue that those affected by official decisions should have the right to participate in making them, or at least having their voices heard at some point in the policy-making process. Participation enables transparency in that public officials have to defend their positions, responsiveness in that those most affected must be involved in order to get the policies right, and accountability when officials must report results of policy implementation. The role of participation in global world cities 287 we might now see participation as necessary in municipal governance this hasn t always been the case. The idea that citizens might be involved in planning only came about in the 1950s and 1960s when problems with top-down planning became apparent within slum clearance and urban renewal programs. Public officials at the time had not realized the problems these programs would cause to residents. In response, the 1960s War on Poverty programs required the maximum feasible participation of the poor in antipoverty programs. Today, almost all federally funded urban programs in the United States now have this requirement, formally institutionalizing the norm of citizen participation with the goal of incorporating the most vulnerable and often invisible individuals into decision making. But the form that citizen participation takes is certainly not static. Though participa- tion has become more institutionalized in global cities, in the past decade new forms of mobilization around issues of gentrification and displacement as well as race, migration, education, and public safety have renewed interest in research on what leads individuals to join collective movements, how these movements seek change, and what the outcomes of various claims-making strategies may be. As we move forward with research on participation, increasingly understanding when citizens influence the democratic process is key to innova- tions in institutional design and ensuring urban policies and programs respond to the needs of residents. The remainder of this chapter seeks to explore the threads of these arguments further, concluding with what we know about when citizen participation matters for determining the purpose and use of cities as well as directions for future research. WHAT IS PARTICIPATION? To understand when participation matters, of course we must first start with defining the vague independent variable of participation and how it has evolved over time. In global cities, participatory practices generally include: voting, running for office, engaging in open forums, taking part in street protests, debating on social media, contacting public officials, providing testimony, and writing letters, among numerous other possibilities. Dahl argued for the primacy of public contestation and participation as the bedrock of democratic polyarchy. Participation, in his view, was primarily defined by engagement with the electoral process through party formation, voting, and campaigning, and he argued that the opportunity for civic engagement was necessary to mediate conflicting interests in democracy, concepts that we mostly now take for granted. Verba and Nie then defined participation as behavior meant to influence the actions of government officials and policy-making decisions, broad- ening the concept from the electoral process to other types of lobbying and advocacy. Since then, other authors have found this definition too narrow, particularly outside of the United States context. For example, examining political events in five Western democracies, Barnes and Kaase , include all activities meant to directly or indirectly influence the political system, specifically incorporating protest and violent activities and not just elections or direct claims-making of the state. In the context of social movements, Sidney Tarrow framed participation in terms of contentious vs. cooperative activities, either meant to disrupt the status quo or work with public officials to achieve demands. More recently comparative urban scholars have included the means of influence, in which advocates seek power directly through formal institutions or Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K. Vogel, Edward Elgar Publishing Limited, 2024. ProQuest Ebook Central, Created from torontomu on 2025-01-15 . Copyright 2024. Edward Elgar Publishing Limited. All rights reserved. 2 Handbook of urban politics and policy mediated through efforts to influence voting and policy making from the outside . Eleonora Pasotti defines experiential tools embedded in cultural practices as repertoires of collective action, particularly in bringing attention to issues such as displace- ment and gentrification in cities worldwide. These types of performative activities often go hand in hand with voting and other traditional forms of protest to enable more voices to be heard, particularly from marginalized communities. Communities, themselves, also define what participation means to them. In the 1960s, Saul Alinsky urged urban residents to engage in community organizing, building on a community s power resources and assets to empower residents to bring about positive change. Since then, community organizations in the United States have largely turned away from protest towards more cooperative tactics, forming partnerships with public agencies to improve service deliv- ery and other conditions in neighborhoods. Community development corporations , which are neighborhood-based-non-profits, work with public and private entities to secure investments in low-income communities, and have had great success in generating and pre- serving affordable housing, health clinics, food banks, and other necessities. Working within these types of organizations may also be seen as a form of political participation in cities. In fact, Ostrom emphasized that communities have largely already developed ways of dealing with the challenges they face, and rather than imposing solutions from above the state should empower residents to further take charge. She developed the concept of co-production, in which citizens participate directly in the design and delivery of public services. Research by scholars such as Bovaird continues to emphasize the benefits of long-term relationships between public service users, community groups, and public sector bureaucrats through the process of co-production. Further, in the past two decades, research on participation has also shifted to understand the role of social media and new forms of participatory governance institutions as political partic- ipation. Social media serves as a platform for organizing in-person gatherings and events, but as Castells argues, it is also a mechanism for inciting participation through engaging with users emotions. Research continues to explore for whom social media influences par- ticipation and the impact of social media use on electoral choices, participation in advocacy campaigns, and other forms of individual and collective action. Continuing to calculate the balance between citizens and the state, the study of participation in governance arrangements has also evolved in the recent past. From public management literature, participation includes a broad range of governance activities, defined by Torfing . as the complex process through which a plurality of actors with diverging interests interact in order to formulate, promote and achieve common objectives by means of mobilizing, exchanging and deploying a range of ideas, rules and resources. Participation in governance processes is increasingly formalized in cities around the world. Literature on par- ticipatory governance institutions has proliferated over the last two decades, particularly since the installation of a participatory budgeting process in Porto Alegre, Brazil, which has served as a model for thousands of other cities. Scholars have sought to understand how par- ticipatory processes evolve, who participates, and how practices transfer to different contexts. Since the 1960s, our knowledge and understanding of what constitutes political partici- pation in cities has only grown as has our definition. The multitude of activities possible as forms of urban participation provides endless opportunities for research. But scholars must also be mindful to explicitly define participation in the urban context relevant to our places of study to clarify its meaning and impact for the population. The role of participation in global world cities 289 participation matters for shaping our cities, how we define participation must clearly move beyond electoral politics and traditional forms of protest to everyday forms of claims-making, cooperation, autonomous solutions, social networking, and shared governance. From the broadening definition of participation, we see the myriad ways that individuals and groups act, reinforcing the notion that there is no one set of actions that matters for shaping the lives of residents within cities. WHO PARTICIPATES? Though we see that citizen participation never takes just one form in any context, who par- ticipates should influence the voices that rise to the top of policy and decision making. For decades research and evidence as to who participates in politics in cities often focused on socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. From the 1960s questions of the relationship between income, education, and participation took priority. For example, Verba, Schlozman, and Brady found that lower-income and less educated citizens in the U.S. participated in politics less than those who were wealthier and more educated. Men (especially white men) have been more likely to participate in direct contact and collective action than women (Mansbridge 1983; Kittilson 2016). The elderly have higher levels of participation (Campbell 2003; Schlozman, Verba, and Brady 2012) as do people who have lived in their homes longer (Kang and Kwak 2003; Gay 2012) and own their homes . Wealthier citizens are also more likely to get involved in required participatory processes in the U.S. and there is evi- dence of voluntary participatory processes being dominated by middle- and upper-class urban residents in NYC , Minneapolis , and Los Angeles . All of these findings suggest a bias in conflict with the goal of enabling diverse voices in politics and policy making. Further, in recent challenges to spatial and resource distribution for housing in cities, researchers have found similar profiles for those who get involved in local politics. For example, Einstein, Palmer, and Glick compare individuals participating in planning and zoning board meetings on housing development to voter files in cities in Massachusetts, finding that people who are older, male, longtime residents, voters in local elections, and homeowners are significantly more likely to participate in these meetings. This group is also more likely than the general population to oppose new housing construction, leading to the conclusion that who participates in local politics has significant policy implications for development. From the studies above we see that who participates matters for shaping the city. And research on inclusivity in cities shows that neighborhood participation is key to providing voice to underrepresented groups and enhancing democracy (Berry, Portney, and Thomson 1993; Fung 2006; Michaels and de Graaf 2010; Stone and Stoker 2015). What we need is more research on how to ensure these groups do in fact get involved and that we design processes to meet diverse needs and interests in order to correct imbalances in power and representation. In terms of increasing diversity in who votes, research has shown mixed effects on specific interventions, such as early voting and initiatives to ease the burden of registration. Berinsky actually finds that these reforms are associated with an increase in socioeconomic ine- qualities in turnout. Burden and Neiheisel , however, finds that election day registration increases overall turnout, but early voting can decrease turnout without other reforms. So what does motivate urban residents to get involved in politics? Digging deeper, scholars have discovered further trends about why individuals choose to participate in political activ- ities. For example, economics and ideology often provide the motivation for mobilization around specific issues, such as financialization of housing and segregation of territory. Anger is also a powerful emotion associated with an increase in electoral participa- tion as are altruism and social identification associated with an increase in all types of political participation . Immigrants are also heavily involved in urban politics, often as opposed to formal and national politics, including partici- pation in local street life and engagement with the arts, often using media and communication technologies . Though Putnam blames declining social capital for lack of civic engagement by traditional means, he does find that citizens are increasingly likely to get involved in identity-based organizations, including non-profit advocacy groups. Individuals are also willing to get involved in political issues when they are likely to see a return on their investment of time and energy. This argument follows from the work of Olson , who found that where benefits to the individual are not so clear, people need selective incentives to participate in order to overcome the collective action
0|dashboard  | problem. In some instances, however, though benefits may not be individualized, residents can see collective rewards. For example, in participatory budgeting processes in Brazil, Goldfrank found that people were more likely to continue to participate if they saw tangible results from their efforts, such as new sidewalks or streetlights in their neighborhoods. Further research identified similar effects in participatory budgeting processes in New York City . In a study of three Western European cities, Bologna, Stuttgart, and Zaragoza, Manes-Rossi . found that citizens were more likely to continue participating when they perceived their role as effec- tive in the co-production of outcomes. Still, other scholars have criticized the focus on community participation as the solution to urban conflicts and challenges of service delivery. David Harvey writes, One of the aspects of much contemporary debate about the urban which I find particularly striking is the tendency when faced with all sorts of difficulties again and again to reach into this bag called community , on the assumption that community is going to save us all. Community, endowed with salving powers, is perceived as capable of redeeming the mess which we are creating in our cities A lot of community construction projects are, in the end, a recipe for isolation. They isolate groups from the city as a whole. () Harvey recognizes that the community cannot be separated from the structure, logic, and institutions of the whole city, but when we rely on communities to solve local issues we often seem to forget this, leaving the individuals within a specific location responsible for the fate of their own development. Further, in global development literature, Cooke and Kothari make the case that participation represents a new tyranny in which the most powerful in communities often are the only voices to be heard, reinforcing existing dynamics. Additionally, they argue that local knowledge and decision-making processes are often overridden by outsiders who bring their own toolboxes to manage projects. In the U.S. context, marginalized groups also report what Sally Nuamah describes as a a type of mobilization fatigue that transpires when citizens engaged in policy processes are met with a lack of democratic transparency and responsive- Handbook of Urban Politics and Policy, edited by Ronald K.
