Key Issues the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in the video Brock Carlton: Looking into the future of Canadian municipalities . We can approach the question of identifying the key issues from different perspectives: Municipal service issues are related to service volumes, quality, levels, and costs of existing services provided by municipalities, including housing, transit, waste, arts, parks, children s services, public health, roads, water, culture, security and police, recreation and sports, and seniors services (see Key Service Issues) Broader system issues related to access, including geographic access ; financial access (user fees); hours of service access; barriers due to ethno-cultural background, age, gender, sexual orientation, and disability; and linguistic access Structural issues related to financing funding and the underpinnings of local government as well as the structure and jurisdictional boundaries of local government Governance issues related to municipal accountability, engagement, participation, voting, representation, and special purpose bodies Sustainability issues related to the environment, economy, finances, cultural, and social aspects of municipalities Technology issues Globalization Physical growth, size, and sprawl-related issues Intergovernmental issues regarding the relationships with different government and First Nations Relationship issues with community members, civil society, other municipalities, Indigenous peoples, agencies, boards, and commissions We have touched on many of these in the course content, readings, and discussions and you should have a broad sense of the scope of the issues. Key Point Municipal issues are complex and interconnected and some feel almost impossible to resolve. Rittel and Webber described two types of problems in public policy wicked problems and tame problems. Wicked problems are unique and complex; they are hard to define and are connected to and constrained by other complex problems. Wicked problems have multiple stakeholders with different ideas on both the problem and the solution, both of which may change over time. Because they are hard to define, it is difficult to get agreement that they have been resolved as a result, wicked problems usually don t go away or end (and they are never solved). Tame problems can be complex and challenging problems, but they are different from wicked problems in that they can be resolved through analysis and problem solving. A typical problem- solving process could be expected to develop a workable solution to a tame problem. Think back to the list of issues facing municipalities. Are there any you would define as wicked problems ? What about poverty or climate change? Also think about the tame problems and consider progress on those issues. Why has there been progress and or why has progress stalled? Municipal Capacity As you reflect on the range of issues facing municipalities, also think about the capacity of the municipality to address the problems. Earlier modules in this course looked at financial resources and autonomy municipal authority, which act as both constraints and opportunities for municipalities. Leadership mayor and council Capable public sector Relationships with the community Partnerships with the private and nonprofit sector Partnerships with other levels of government, Indigenous governments, and other municipal governments External influences, good practices from other municipalities Technology and Local Government E-government refers to the delivery of information and services online via the internet or other digital means. Municipalities are interested in e-government initiatives because they allow them to streamline : What other constraints and enablers are there? existing processes, reduce costs, improve services, increase access to information, and better connect with communities and community members. It is generally felt that these initiatives will lead to an increase in satisfaction with municipal services, greater economic competitiveness, and increased efficiency. E-government has evolved from the early stages of static, one-way provision of information to community members, through a municipal website where residents access information but don t interact with the municipality (Lenihan and Hanna, 2002, 8 10). Over time, this evolved to support basic online transactions, such as a municipal 3-1-1 service, payment of parking tickets, registration for recreation courses, and applications for permits. Mobile apps to report potholes or find out the next date for recycling pickup fall into this category. Further changes supported greater interaction through online communities, engagement exercises, and access to municipal data that contribute to understanding and assessing issues. Of course, technology continues to evolve and influence municipalities. We sometimes talk about smart cities that are networked, transparent, provide leadership, share information, innovate, and support new forms of democracy through artificially intelligent, electronic means. Others refer to Government 2.0 a more open, social, communicative, interactive and user-centred version of e-government that has the potential to reshape the relationship between government and citizens, in a sense that services, control and policy formulation are designed through a cooperation of citizens, governments and civil society , a TEDxCollingwood presentation by Innisfil CAO Jason Reynar. Other municipalities are using technology in unique ways. The City of Durham, North Carolina is using Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant to provide a verbal alternative to communication for community members, initially about development in the municipality but with plans to expand to Lawrence Abeyta, one of the partners in the initiative, predicts that in the coming years every home will have some kind of IoT internet of things device and therefore cities should engage with their citizens or want to engage with their citizens in that very easy, natural way of speaking in a natural language (Municipal World, 2018). The Little Burgundy area of Montreal is a food desert an area that doesn t have easy walking access to fresh food. l innovation (supported by the City of Montreal and other levels of government and universities) have plans to test a self-driving shuttle bus that will take community members to a grocery store (CBC News, 2020). Will the internet be the next municipal service delivered as a utility through a municipal special purpose body? That suggestion was made by two partners from KPMG, Alex Benay and Stephen Beatty, who argued that 5G the next-generation mobile network required for such advanced technologies as artificial intelligence, which will drive killer apps like self-driving vehicles could be managed like a public utility developed by a municipality . It would be developed through partnerships and would serve to support economic development and innovation, increase global competitiveness, and provide more equitable internet to unserved and underserved communities. Openness, Transparency, Engagement Municipalities are also using technology to be more transparent and open and to offer opportunities for greater and different engagement with community members. Shape your City Halifax is an online engagement hub developed by the Regional Municipality of Halifax to get input and solicit ideas on policies, plans, services, and municipal decision-making. Many municipalities have open data initiatives whereby municipal data is available to researchers, communities, businesses, and innovators. Edmonton was one of the first municipalities to make data available, through an open data catalogue in 2010, an open data policy and framework in 2015, and in 2017, the municipality had approved a strategy and made 1,300 datasets and visualizations available for public use . While the focus is on the open data, the goal is for the data to provide opportunities for municipal service innovation, information sharing, and greater transparency and accountability to community members. An Open Cities Index measured the openness of municipal open data initiatives, provided tools and resources for municipalities, and produced regular report ranking cities based on governance, data infrastructure and quality, and community and organizational impact (psdcity wide, n.d). The 2020 results for North America include many Canadian cities. Open data is a good first step that needs to be supported by attention to engagement and Making information and data available and providing more meaningful connection and engagement prepares municipalities and communities for co- production where they work together to develop new approaches to challenges . E-Democracy E-democracy uses technology to engage community members in democratic processes, including voting, shaping priorities, and engaging in decision-making processes. The Town of Markham was the first major municipality in Canada to pilot internet voting in the 2003 municipal elections 194 of 4 Ontario municipalities offered online voting in the 2 Online voting is also used by about 20 self-governing First Nations (it isn t available to those under the Indian Act) for chief and council elections as well as to ratify agreements or vote on issues through a referendum . Municipalities are interested in online voting to help increase voter turnout by making voting more accessible and convenient. There may be cost and administrative savings to the municipality and e-voting may be more attractive to younger voters as well as voters who don t live in the municipality (i.e., cottagers). Smaller municipalities may replace in-person voting with online and telephone voting. But the technology of online voting has challenges and Toronto, London , and other Canadian municipalities have decided not to offer an e-voting option because of security concerns as well as the lack of common standards . Earlier modules explored how some municipalities are using technology to support greater engagement in municipal budget decisions. The City of Toronto had an extensive participation process for the 2004 and 2005 budgets that included an online budget simulation where residents were asked to try to develop a balanced budget. Halifax has a budget allocator available on its Shape your City web page that provides similar information about the municipal budget and an opportunity to both balance the budget and share budget preferences with the municipality. As noted earlier, community members are regularly asked for input on a range of municipal topics from broad policy to local changes like intersection improvements. Innovation Municipalities are using technology, data, and connections with community members to become more innovative in what they do and how they do their work. Edmonton held the first formal apps competition in Canada in 2010, which resulted in the development of 32 municipally focused apps. These bottom up approaches contrast to the top down approach of an initiative like Sidewalk Labs in Toronto. This development was an effort to use technology to develop and maintain a new community that was affordable, sustainable, climate-positive, and comprehensive in approach . The project was controversial in its use of technology and while initiatives like intelligent air quality measurement were welcomed, many criticized the tradeoffs of personal privacy and data that would have been needed to support the innovative and intelligent development. Ultimately, the project was cancelled in 2020. Innovation can be in other forms. Municipalities are increasingly supported and influenced by innovation hubs Vancouver has an independent CityStudio, an innovation hub that brings together city staff, students, faculty and community to co-create experimental projects that make Vancouver more sustainable, liveable and joyful . It receives funding from the City of Vancouver and other sources but is an independent charity. The City of Montreal has the Laboratoire d innovation urbaine de Montr al which includes a multidisciplinary team that fosters and supports innovative solutions to major urban challenges and is a space for exploration, experimentation and reflection . This urban innovation lab is part of the city of Montreal. Code for Canada is a collaborative initiative between the City of Toronto and Civic Hall Toronto to use technology and design to build better digital public services and improve life for residents . Other municipalities hold designjams and charettes to engage others in a process of innovation and outside-the-box thinking. There are also associations, networks, and collaboratives that focus on innovation at the municipal level. For example, Future Cities Canada is a national organization that brings together people, ideas, platforms, and innovations from across sectors and focuses on climate change and inequality in cities (Future Cities, 2020). Future Cities Canada offers a range of programs, supports a fellowship initiative, partners with other organizations, and provides resources and learning events that foster local innovation and change. Implications for Municipalities Opportunities Technology has implications for how local governments provide services, programs, processes, ways of working, administration, and governance, and there will be more change to come. Technology-inspired changes will also require significant up-front investment of money, time, and expertise all of which are in limited supply at the municipal level. This doesn t mean that change won t happen. Gord Hume, an expert on municipal government, predicted that by end of the 2020s, cities will routinely have autonomous vehicles on the streets, robots in city hall and machines to handle some administration (Hume, 2017, 27). Municipalities will clearly need to think differently and pursue initiatives that bring new risks. Cities need the courage to be audacious in a too-often beige government world. Municipalities must seek new ways of business Municipal leaders need to break through traditional barriers because change is arriving now (Hume, 2017, 27). Some of the change will include partnerships and multi-level governance. The Regional District of East Kootenay, British Columbia, successfully negotiated a regional electronic vehicle-charging network with partners such as the federal and provincial government, three regional districts, 24 municipalities, two national parks as well as corporate partners, businesses, and local residents (Union of BC Municipalities, 2018). Technology has broadened the number and type of groups we belong to. In the past, these groups were grounded in geography a meeting had to be held in a physical location, accessible to local members but now we can participate in dialogues with other communities across the world and our connections with local places are weaker. McAllister raises questions about the implications of the loss of geographical grounding for local governments . Pause and Reflect Do you think there will be a weakening of municipal governance and influence if boundaries blur and geography becomes less important? The processes through which municipalities engage community members in local government and decision-making is evolving. Many municipalities are adapting consultation and engagement practices to online or technology-supported processes, while others are making efforts to engage differently with communities in community spaces through social media. Proponents of e-democracy suggest that municipalities need to do broader and wider engagement in community spaces. In addition to cost and expertise challenges, engaging with communities in different spaces may result in a loss of municipal control over the process and have implications for municipal governance and decision-making. Digital governance may well be the central challenge facing governing institutions and societies in the coming decades where no one owns information, power is dispersed and authority and accountability need to be reconceived (Institute on Governance, 2020). Technology supports the engagement of individuals to share their opinion, but unlike town hall meetings or consultations at a local community centre, technology reduces the need to listen to others opinions or to try to come to community consensus on issues. This raises the potential for the balance to shift away from community and a public interest focus to a more individualistic perspective at the local level . On the other hand, e-government initiatives are seen as ways of strengthening the connection between citizens and local governments. They are tools for greater local government accountability to their constituents and provide much more information in a more accessible form than ever before. E- government initiatives are considered essential to economic competitiveness and to the economic stability of local communities, and they provide a different, more convenient vehicle for participation and engagement. Implications for Municipalities Challenges and Barriers Of course, there are some significant barriers and challenges to the adoption of new technologies. Some community members resist change; they prefer human connection to an impersonal internet connection. Despite the ease of accessing information and business through the municipal website, Toronto reported that 90 of total contacts between community members and the municipality were still through the phone . The digital divide, a term used to refer to barriers in the use of new technologies based on income, education, race, age, ethnicity, and gender, continues to be a challenge for the greater use of technology at the local level. Language may also be a barrier for some, as English is the language of the internet. Many argue that technology will widen the existing divide and disadvantage members of marginalized and unconnected communities. During the COVID-19 shutdown, one of the first Toronto Public Library services to reopen was access, albeit limited, to the computers and related equipment. The divide is evident among municipalities most of the unconnected communities are rural municipalities, where barriers to internet access persist. Saskatoon StarPhoenix provide a unique perspective on the real challenges facing many small, rural municipalities. The Sidewalk Labs example, described earlier in the module, raises the issue of ethics. Big data, the use of technology to deliver services, the use of artificial intelligence to inform services and decisions, and the security of electronic files and records open up new and serious challenges related to privacy and public interest. Discussions continue about the right balance between technology-supported innovation and the public interest, privacy, and governance. Nonetheless, many see enormous potential for local governments. I think there are people who are starting to understand that cities have the power to affect real societal change, reflected Mayor Dawn Arnold, from Moncton, N.B. (Hume, 2017, 27). Local governments are well positioned to play important roles in e-government; they have a strong service delivery role, and community members have more contact and transactions with municipal governments than other levels of government. This provides greater opportunity for improving information, access, accountability, and opportunity for engagement and co-creation. Globalization and Local Government Globalization is a process of increasing connection and interdependence of countries, economics, and people, enabled by rapid transportation, accessible and inexpensive communications technology, and processes of international economic finance and trade. In essence, globalization has removed physical space as a barrier to the movement of ideas, information, economic activity, communications, and culture and to the concentration of economic management, finance, and control functions in global cities. Former Winnipeg Mayor Glen Murray stated that the planet is becoming an interconnected network of urban economies and local governments and that cities are increasingly important political and economic centres (Janigan, 2002, 22). Globalization and the process of greater integration has created new international political arrangements and changed the structure of government. Agreements like the 1 North America Free Trade Agreement , the 2 Canada United States Mexico Agreement , or the 2 Canada European Union: Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement created policies and governance structures that cross national boundaries. Internationalization of Cities Cities have influence at the national and international levels. In our increasingly urban world, cities find themselves at the forefront of some of the most pressing issues of our time, such as climate change and the integration of migrants into communities (OECD, 2019, 43). But they are also seen as an important and relevant form of government, small enough to react swiftly and responsively to issues and large enough to hold economic and political power . This growing influence of cities has led to calls for the addition of a committee of local government to the governance structure of the United Nations Habitat . Urban areas face many similar challenges climate change, poverty, ageing infrastructure and increasing connections through global city networks to share, learn, and advocate brings attention to these shared issues. The graph below shows the significant growth since the 1990s in the number of global city networks that have developed to partner and collaborate on these shared issues. Source: OCED, 2019, 37 of cities and local, regional, and metropolitan governments and their associations from 1 UN member states that focuses on increasing the role and influence of local government in global government . United Cities and Local Governments describes the global association and explains why local governments need a stronger voice in shaping and contributing to the international agenda. Impacts of Globalization Municipalities are affected by the challenges of globalization, the struggle between the external opportunities of globalization, and the internal consequences of globalization including growth, how limited resources are used at the local level, and increasing polarization (Lightbody, 2005, 510). Within municipalities, a divide exists between those who participate in the global economy and those that don t, but there is also a distinction between municipalities that are connected to the global economy and those that aren t active. Globalization and urbanization are mutually reinforcing (Clark and Moonen, 2017, 203). Larger globally connected areas grow at a higher rate than other areas Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal census metropolitan areas grew by 1.7 in 2019, compared to 0.6 for the rest of the country (Statistics Canada, 2020, 1). This growth also leads to increasing concentration of population in the urban centres Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal CMAs are home to more than one-third of all residents of Canada (Statistics Canada, 2020, 1). There have been changes in the shape and size of our cities. As cities grew, the central model of a strong downtown core was replaced by increasing low- density sprawl and the development of employment and cultural nodes in the suburbs. Edge cities is a term used to describe sprawling outer suburbs that gradually become cities with their own retail and business centres. The footprint of the urban area has expanded and with it, there has been a loss of farmland, ecological impacts, pollution from commuting, and inefficient forms of development. While the urban spread continues in cities like Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal, there is a counter force of professionals moving back to inner cities, displacing poorer residents and gentrifying inner city neighbourhoods (Statistics Canada, 2020, 1). In Toronto, this has resulted in a donut shape of low-income communities surrounding an inner core or donut hole of high-income neighbourhoods. There has been a shift in jobs and employment. Industry, manufacturing, and production jobs have become much more mobile, moving to the periphery or to other regions of the world based on cost of labour and production. Jobs at both ends of the employment spectrum have grown lower paying service and part-time contract jobs have increased, as have professional jobs further adding to the income inequality. In addition, jobs are not evenly distributed. Canadians should not underestimate the nature of the transition that is underway. Most if not all national job growth has been concentrated in a small number of major cities, adding to the differences between large urban areas and smaller municipalities. (Coates, 2019, 11). There are divisions between Canadian cities participating in globalization and those not participating. The impact of globalization is different for different types of municipalities. Graham, Phillips, and Maslove note that Canada s capital cities are at a comparative disadvantage because of the challenge of provincial-city relations in those cities . Smaller cities, towns, and villages are also at a disadvantage, particularly single manufacturing communities and those dependent on resource-based industries. Canada s growth is attributed to immigration (Statistics Canada, 2020, 1), most of which is focused in major urban centres and further exacerbates the gaps between large and small municipalities. Economic success from globalization is not equally shared. There are significant inequities between different cities in the world and within cities; there are differences between neighbourhoods and communities. There are growing inequities between individuals and groups of people based on income, education, culture, and race. Globalization has led to increasing polarization, based on income and education. Growing income inequalities in Canadian cities have received increasing attention in research studies and are a greater consideration in municipal responses to strengthen neighbourhoods and provide more support to individuals and groups that don t enjoy the benefits of globalization. Education is identified as a critical enabler to participate in the global economy; those without education are being left behind. Intergovernmental Relationships and Globalization Municipalities have a limited scope for policy and other actions needed to be globally competitive because of provincial control over local government responsibilities and level of authority (Graham, Phillips and Maslove, 1998, 10). Municipalities are also limited in their ability to respond to the education and income polarization challenges of globalization by the scope of their responsibilities and financial capacity. Provinces define the boundaries of municipalities and this directly affects the ability of a municipality to compete in the global economy. The fragmentation of local government, for example in the Toronto area, makes it difficult to achieve a strong and effective international presence and to develop in the global context (Clark and Moonen, 2017, 212). The urban area is spread over a number of separate municipalities (City of Toronto and the Regions of Peel, York, Durham, and Halton) with few formal structures or mechanisms for cooperation. Nearly always in the evolution of globally oriented cities, existing governance arrangements come to be insufficient to sustain and develop their lead roles within a fast-moving global economy (Clark and Moonen, 2017, 207). The federal government holds many of the policy levers in the international arena, including international finance, economy, trade, and foreign affairs. Municipalities have limited input into the negotiation and application of international agreements, even though these agreements may create real barriers or operational challenges for municipalities. For example, the World Trade Organization General Agreement on Trade in Services applies to services provided by or on behalf of municipalities, including public-private partnerships, contracting out, development design build arrangements, and privatization (Tindal ., 2017, 20). The North American Free Trade Agreement allowed U.S. or Mexican firms to sue municipalities if their actions restricted current or future profits. Canada s municipalities are impacted by the level and type of support that provinces and the federal government give (or don t give) to support municipal competition in the world economy. Globalization has placed pressure on all levels of government to reduce and downsize their operations to reflect the more competitive environment demanded by the international community. In the context of limited support from the provincial and federal levels of government, local governments must find other ways to respond to increasing international competition. Municipalities tend to have reduced bargaining power and hold limited financial carrots to attract global investors. Given their fiscal challenges, municipalities are reluctant to negotiate away property tax revenue or to change the structure of property tax to make it more of a location incentive. On the other hand, urban centres have many international relationships with other cities and interests that are independent of the provincial or federal government. They increasingly have influence and voices at a global level. Cities represent a large share of the national economy and population, and their strengthening political clout could help address some of the challenging issues facing the country. The growing influence of urban municipalities has implications for national and sub-national (or provincial and state) governments. More than twenty years ago, sociologist Daniel Bell observed that these were difficult times for countries since the nation state has become too small for the big problems of life and too big for the small problems of life (as quoted by Ignatius, 1999). Similarly, provinces are poorly positioned between the national government which has authority for trade, finance, immigration, and international relations and municipalities, which are dealing with issues on the ground. Intergovernmental antagonism can result when increasingly powerful and connected cities interact with other levels of government in their country (Clark and Moonen, 2017, 26). Local governments in Canada have responded to globalization in different ways. The early focus was on forging partnerships and twinning with other international cities. Sometimes these partnerships included economic development goals; other times it was expected that economic opportunities would result from the new relationships. Municipalities also focused on developing competitive advantage in certain sectors. For example, Vancouver has a strong connection to southeast Asia; Ottawa has a technology sector; and Toronto is a financial capital and benefits from the connections of its large immigrant population. Some municipalities pursued international events the Olympics, world games, international conferences, and expositions as a means of showcasing their advantages and potential. Municipalities have developed increasingly important connections with interests and groups within their boundaries. Private businesses, nonprofit organizations, and community groups are important partners in addressing global issues at the local level, such as in collaborations to promote the municipalities in the local and international arena, like Calgary Economic Development or the Halifax Partnership. In the absence of structural change to the boundaries, municipalities must work with other municipalities, regions, and levels of government to address issues and opportunities that cross boundaries and require multi-level governance. This suggests that there needs to be agreement around common priorities and leadership at the municipal level. Regional partnerships and pooling of resources are both important for smaller municipalities. In some cases, cities are connecting directly to global agreements or commitments . The 2 Paris Agreement on climate change to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions was adopted by 195 countries as well as cities and businesses. The C Cities includes 96 cities, which represent 25 of the global GDP and 1 in 12 people in the world . When President Trump announced the U.S. withdrawal from the 2 Paris Agreement, cities and other municipalities made formal commitments of support for the agreement. The Sierra Club reports that over 1 U.S. cities, 10 counties, and 8 states, representing over 100 million people, have clean, renewable energy goals and plans consistent with the Paris Agreement (Sierra Club, 2020). Canadian municipalities are active in sustainable development initiatives, based on global standards. Peg, was developed by advisory committee including the City of Winnipeg, Alberta, First Nations,foundations, nonprofits and businesses, worked with 800 members of the Winnipeg local community to develop a set of indicators to measure community well-being. Peg is expanding their indicators to reflect the 1 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals . Three Future Globalization Scenarios What will the future bring for local governments in Canada? Tindal imagined three different types of futures: The first scenario is a flat internationalized world where countries and businesses can compete on a level playing field, as described in the works of Thomas Friedman. This imagined future includes international free trade, no national boundaries between countries or jurisdictions, and governance rules developed by non-elected organizations like the World Trade Organization . This is consistent with the idea of world cities, global competition, and the involvement of more non-governmental partners in governance (Clark and Moonen, 2017, 25). The second imagined future is based on Richard Florida s research, which focuses on geographic concentrations of people, economic activity, and growth or spikes that support innovation in cities and city regions. Some places have more advantages than others and can use those advantages to achieve higher growth and concentration of innovation. The third possible scenario predicts the end of globalization and a shift to a more focused, local future. Jeff Rubin argues that the cheap oil and fuel supporting the current levels of global trade and growth can t last and when demand for goods increases, supplies of fuel diminish, and or costs increase, there will be adjustments that bring the focus closer to home, within national or regional boundaries (as referenced in Tindal, 2009). While each has different implications for municipalities, Tindal argues that municipalities have the ability to respond to each of the scenarios: Whatever constraints and challenges a potentially changing world economic order may bring, municipalities need to start by shaking off self-imposed constraints. The old notions of helplessness and dependency however familiar, even comfortable must no longer be an excuse for inaction (Tindal, 2010, 26). Municipalities have demonstrated leadership in the area of climate change. do more if resources were available and they had greater authority to act, but the example of municipalities and climate change that follows in the next section suggests that municipalities are following Tindal s advice and taking action despite constraints and challenges. Municipal Role in Climate Change Mitigation Canadian municipalities face some real challenges, as discussed throughout the course, but they are also taking initiative in key areas like climate change. David Miller, former mayor of Toronto and now head of the C Cities Climate Leadership Group, describes cities as unique incubators of interesting ideas and actions on climate change . About 70 of the world s greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to the generation of electricity, heating and cooling buildings, transportation, and solid waste in cities (Miller, 2020, 6). Cities and municipalities have significant control over those emissions the Federation of Canadian Municipalities estimates that municipal governments have direct or indirect control over 50 of Canada s greenhouse gas emissions: Municipal governments are fundamental to achieving local, community-based emission reductions since they have significant influence on development and land-use decisions that shape the pattern of energy use within communities. Municipal governments are also the order of government that is the closest to citizens and can most easily engage households and businesses to implement local projects to reduce GHG emissions. Municipal governments can affect GHG emissions as a regulator, facilitator, partner, program deliverer and educator (EnviroEconomics, 2009, 1). Municipalities have direct control over their own operations, facilities, vehicles, and spaces as well as indirect control through bylaws, regulation, building codes, land use, and services like public transit. While it may be a global problem, people and businesses in local communities experience the effects of climate change increasing temperatures, exceptional storms, floods, droughts, and fires. Local governments have a closer relationship with community members than other levels of government and can more easily connect and encourage participation and support for decisions to reduce greenhouse emissions and address climate change . There are no national requirements related to climate change planning. European countries tend to require municipalities to develop plans to mitigate change and to plan to adapt to change, but in Canada, climate change planning is highly uneven (Guyadeen, Thistlewaite and Henstra, 2019, 122). British Columbia is recognized as having more ambitious climate change actions than other provinces or the federal government . B.C. and Ontario require municipalities to have policies on climate change in the official municipal plan, but at the time of a 2017 study, only Nova Scotia required municipalities to create climate change plans. While provincial requirements for municipalities to develop plans form part of the municipal response to climate change, municipalities also develop policies and take initiatives independent of provincial requirements that have significant influence and impact. In addition, municipalities are able to test ideas and approaches to assess what works this learning trickles up to other levels of government and across to other municipalities where responses can be adapted to the local context. A Range of Municipal Responses Municipalities have taken action on climate change through a wide range of actions: Module 6 described the Hudson, Quebec municipal bylaw that banned pesticides and was tested in the Supreme Court. Following the Supreme Court decision in favour of the municipality, and in the absence of any federal or provincial action on pesticides, other municipalities across Canada enacted similar bylaws. In 2022, the City of Vancouver voted to join other B.C. municipalities in a Sue Big Oil class action lawsuit in an effort to recover costs associated with climate change impacts at the municipal level. One estimate puts the cost of municipal climate change costs at 5.3 billion a year (Insurance Bureau of Canada as quoted by Logan, 2022). the The city is levying a special 1 per resident tax that will go towards their legal costs. In 2017, Ottawa was the first Canadian city to issue green bonds to finance their light rail transit system, connecting economic development with climate change. In 2019, Ottawa joined Vancouver, Montreal, Halifax, Kingston, and many other municipalities in declaring a climate emergency. Watch Climate Emergency Rally at Ottawa City Hall where Councillor Shawn Menard addresses the public before the municipal vote on a climate emergency. Guelph, Ontario developed a secondary plan for a 1,000-acre sustainable, innovative development of a section of in the municipality previously owned by the province. The community will be carbon neutral and will take advantage of the existing district energy system. Guelph described their plan for the land and accepted the 2 FCM award for Sustainable Neighbourhood Design in this video. The B.C. Climate Action Charter is a voluntary agreement between the province and the Union of B.C. Municipalities about action on climate change. Since the 2007 launch, 187 of 190 municipalities in British Columbia have signed the voluntary agreement to become carbon neutral, measure and report on greenhouse gas emissions, and develop more energy efficient communities . Toronto City Council approved a plan to reduce greenhouse gases in 2007 called Change Is In the Air. By 2012, Toronto had achieved a 15 reduction in emissions, and by 2017, the greenhouse gas emissions were 33 below the 1990 levels (Miller, 2020, 10). North Vancouver passed a business licence bylaw amendment in 2015, the first in North America that required gas stations to put information labels about greenhouse gases on all fuel pumps. Our Horizon, a national nonprofit organization, worked with the municipality to introduce the change. Watch This Is an Idea that Will Change the World to learn more. Source: Our Horizon, 2 Long Description This is a photo of a red gas pump. On the pump is a sticker of an adult moose followed by a baby moose in the snow. There is a large Warning below the photo and further text that says: Use of this fuel product contributes to climate change which may put up to 30 of species at likely risk of extinction. To learn more, go to WeCanDoBetter.Me. Pause and Reflect These are just a handful of the many examples of municipal leadership in the environmental and climate change areas. Take a few minutes and look at what your municipality is to reduce greenhouse gases and mitigate climate change. Four barriers to greater municipal action on climate change are experienced by most all municipalities in Canada and are described below. Capacity and Resources The most significant barriers for municipalities taking action on climate change are resources and capacity, including staff expertise and availability, time, and budget. There is a lot of information about the need for change and many examples of municipal action when funding is available; the challenge that municipalities face is accessing the resources to act (Dale ., 2020, 869). Funding is also needed to support new technologies to measure and monitor change and to test and introduce new systems, materials, and approaches to reduce and eliminate emissions. This could include infrastructure costs related to electric buses and solar power as well as the technology and programs needed to manage reduction efforts. Local Governments for Sustainability and the FCM established Partners for Climate Protection in 2014. This network includes more than 350 municipalities that have committed to reduce greenhouse gases and take action on climate change. The ICLEI FCM partnership makes information, case studies, tools, as well as support from program advisors available to municipalities to develop climate change plans. discussed the Green Municipal Fund, a federal fund administered through FCM that includes funding for municipal energy efficiency. Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy is an international group of cities and local governments that commit to action to combat climate change and shift to low emissions. The OECD-led initiative supports local solutions to climate challenges (OECD, 2019, 51). Political Priority Municipalities must juggle many issues, and some municipalities may not rank climate change as a priority. Changing leadership as a result of elections at all orders of government can result in shifting priorities and programs and can lead to a lack of policy coherence over time (Dale ., 2020, 869). A study in B.C. found that a reduction in climate-related innovation at the municipal level corresponded to the election of a new political party and premier that was not supportive of action on climate change (Dale ., 2020, 869). Intergovernmental Relations Intergovernmental issues and division of responsibility among the levels of government is a formidable challenge to municipal action on climate change (Robinson and Gore, 2005, 115). Not all provinces are providing consistent leadership, and the federal government has been constrained by the absence of a formal relationship with municipalities. When action happens, it is often not consistent or coordinated (Dale ., 2020, 877). Municipalities need to look at climate change mitigation reduction strategies through a long-term lens and to play a trustee rather than a delegate role. This isn t easy for municipal councils that have traditionally focused on the short term, on service delivery and property tax issues, and who see themselves as representatives of their constituents views. There is also a need for municipalities to play a leadership role in helping the public understand the need for change and engaging the public in the change public perception is important to shifting political culture. Reflection on Municipalities and Climate Change The discussion of climate change highlights the barriers and constraints local governments face in taking action on climate change as well their ability to work around them. While there are national and international networks to support change, local municipal action is incremental and dependent on a supportive political culture and the resources to develop municipal capacity, including technology. Nonetheless, municipalities have demonstrated leadership in developing and adapting initiatives to meet their unique needs and situations. This module focused on three of the key issues facing Canada s municipalities technology, globalization, and climate change and reflected on possible paths for local government for the future. Municipalities face a variety of issues, including issues with service delivery, access, governance, sustainability, technology, globalization, and growth, and structural, intergovernmental, and relationship issues. Municipal capacity to address these issues is limited and enabled by financial resources, formal municipal authority and autonomy, leadership, the public service, relationships, partnerships, intergovernmental relationships, and external influences. Local governments use technology to improve services; support transparency, openness, and accountability; support democracy and engagement; and to engage in innovation. The digital divide within communities and between technology-enabled and technology-restricted municipalities presents a significant barrier to greater use of technology. Municipalities also face ethical challenges related to records, data, and use of technology. Urban areas and cities are gaining influence through globalization processes. Urbanization is concentrating populations in cities, which are responsible for increasing shares of the national economy and national visibility. Like technology, globalization brings challenges and opportunities. Municipalities are challenged to compete globally and respond to the impacts of globalization, like growing inequality, at the local level with their limited resources, formal authority, and autonomy. Climate change is an example of a global issue that is experienced at the local level. The discussion highlighted challenges faced by municipalities as well as some ways that they are working around these constraints and barriers and playing a leadership role. Technology, globalization, and climate change represent some of the important issues that municipalities are faced with today and that will directly affect the municipality of tomorrow. The module discussion continues to explore opportunity for municipal leadership and action within the context of limited resources, structure, and autonomy. Module 12 provides an opportunity to review the key messages in the course content and to reflect on some of the themes that have emerged in our study of local government. Please do not redistribute CHAPTER Future Prospects for Municipal Governments T he future for local governments in Canada will be more activist. Frances Frisken once noted that Canadian municipalities often used the lack of jurisdictional authority as an excuse for inaction. 1 The past decade has suggested a significant attitudinal change in such local governmental thinking. Examples, large and small, abound-from the commitment to \"fair trade\" in Wolfville, Nova Scotia, to the establishment of North America's first official supervised injection site in Vancouver, British Columbia. Leading up to the 2015 federal election, Canada's municipalities stepped forward offering to take and help settle Syrian (and related) refugees- though municipal fiscal reality meant that many local governments acknowledged that their offers were partly contingent on federal immi- grant settlement aid. On environmental matters, many municipalities have signed on to Kyoto targets on emissions, not waiting for senior governments to lead with their own action. Municipalities, such as Burnaby, BC, have indicated they will take whatever local action they can-including civil disobedience-to stop the development of Kinder Morgan's Trans Mountain Pipeline and oil sands bitumen shipping in their communities. Apart from the designation as Canada's \"best run municipality,\" Burnaby Mayor Derek Corrigan and his fellow Burnaby Citizens' Association councillors stand out as dedicated, committed, local representatives and as electoral examples with a history of democratic success through this local engagement. 1 Frances Frisken, ed., The Changing Canadian Metropolis: A Public Policy Perspective, Introduction, Berkeley, CA: Institute of Governmental Studies Press, University of California, 1994. 3 In 2014-2018, British Columbia became the last Canadian province to institute four-year terms of office; given the senior trend of fixed- usually four-year-terms provincially and federally, this longer local governmental planning horizon may push the political professionalism of councillors and councils from a more part-time orientation. While sometimes adding recruitment challenges for smaller municipalities, the shift to longer council terms also raises questions about ensuring accountability, a feature largely answered with the development of local political parties. While for most Canadian local governments, this latter development remains uncertain, there is no doubt that local governments in Canada will be more engaged. How well municipalities fare in the 21st century will depend, as always, on how successfully they maintain a balance between their two primary roles: representative political and administrative service delivery (see Box 12.1). The tension between these two roles is reflected in two contrasting images of municipal government-as a democratic institution that responds to community concerns, and as but one of many players in a competitive marketplace in which individual interests prevail. This book began with fanciful suggestions about the 21st century belonging to Canada's municipalities. What have we learned in the more than 400 intervening pages that support or detract from this optimistic outlook? NEl Chapter 1 Future Prospects for Municipal Governments 3 What needs to happen if this new century is to bring greater municipal significance? Taking a New Look The best way to start, especially for those in municipal government, is to turn upside down the usual way of looking at municipalities, a perspec- tive that has them on the bottom of several levels of higher jurisdiction, as in Figure 12.1. According to this traditional view, municipalities are subordinate and subservient creatures of the provinces to which they owe their existence. They are also dependent on the federal (and provincial) levels for financial assistance that-in practice-is limited and elusive, and they are significantly affected by senior federal government actions (and inaction). They are also increasingly constrained by international agreements and organizations and by global competitive pressures and a prevailing neoliberal ideological paradigm. There is, however, an alternative way of looking at municipalities and their place in the world, unaccustomed as we are to considering it. What if we invert the traditional hierarchical view, as in Figure 12.2? What if we see local governments as the first order of government? Let us con- sider the significance of such a reversal. Globalization and the accompanying free trade regime are certainly forces to be reckoned with, but we shouldn't overstate their impor- tance for day-to-day municipal operations. Not all firms are completely mobile, and most would think long and hard before pulling up stakes and setting up shop in another country where culture, language, and other barriers may present quite a challenge. Since the terrorist attacks Figure 12.1 The Traditional Hierarchy International Agreements and Organizations I I I Federal Provincial Government Goverment I Municipal Government Figure 12.2 The Inverted Hierarchy Local Citizens I I Provincial Government I Federal Government I International Agreements and Organizations of September 11, 2001, many actions have been rationalized or justified \"because of 9 11\" or \"ISIS\" and its equivalents-no matter how tenuous the link. The attacks have become an all too convenient cover or excuse for actions (especially adversely affecting individual rights and free- doms-as in Canada's C-5 Anti-Terrorism Act of 2015) that would not otherwise be tolerated. In much the same way, globalization is constantly invoked as the reason why something must be done or cannot be done. Without in any way denying its importance, we should not allow it to become an excuse for municipal actions or inaction. There is still consid- erable scope for municipal initiative within a global world. It is instructive to examine Martin Horak's analysis of the background to Toronto's New Deal campaign that ultimately led to the new City of Toronto Act of June 2006. 2 At first blush, one might interpret this devel- opment as the inevitable response of a global city seeking out additional powers to strengthen its competitive position. But Horak found that the forces of global economic competition were not the key factors driving 2 Martin Horak, Governance Reform from Below: Multilevel Politics and the \"New Deal\" Campaign in Toronto, Global Dialogue Series, , Nairobi, ON-Habitat, 2008, accessed October 30, 2011 and July 3, 2015, at aspx?publicationiD 2494. A similar dynamic might occur among Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Premier Kathleen Wynne, and Mayor John Tory for Toronto. Future Prospects for Municipal Governments 3 Toronto's New Deal campaign. Instead, he identified a number of devel- opments that came together to create the impetus and opportunity for change: The provincially imposed amalgamation that created the City ofT oronto; Provincial downloading of social programs that burdened the new municipality with substantial costs; and Elections at all three levels of government that resulted in leaders (Prime Minister Martin, Premier McGuinty, and Mayor Miller) predisposed to working together. The size of the amalgamated municipality gave it increased clout, and the disparities in downloaded cost burdens between the new City of Toronto and the suburban municipalities in the surrounding Greater Toronto Area provided further stimulus for those seeking greater powers for Toronto. The arrival of the \"three Ms\" as heads of the three levels of government provided the other major factor favourable to a New Deal for Toronto. Horak's research into the Toronto case demonstrates that even in cities that are highly integrated into the global economy, the exigencies of global competition are not the only or necessarily even the primary influence. He concludes, \"both the size of the new City and the sense of fiscal crisis that accompanied its birth were critical to the emergence of the New Deal campaign, in that they enabled and encour- aged the new City to move beyond the passive intergovernmental stance that Canadian municipalities have typically assumed given their weak standing in the constitutional order.\" 3 Once again, we have a welcome example of what \"eager beavers\" can accomplish. Though Meaghan Joy and Ronald Vogel offer caution in overinterpretation of the Toronto advantage. 4 Because the constraints imposed by globalization apply more to federal and provincial governments, it can even be argued that the net result is to liberate rather than to restrict municipalities. National borders are more porous and the nation state is challenged by international trade rules and agencies and scaled back by neoliberal preachings about the inherent superiority of private-sector operations. These global and ideological pressures affect the local level as well, but municipalities also have an opportunity to move into the vacuum created at the centre by the reduced role of the federal and provincial levels. In fact, the municipal capacity to capitalize on this opportunity has been strengthened, unwittingly, by the actions taken by the federal and provincial levels in response to global- ization and neoliberalism. This issue is rapidly evolving. In addition to our own monitoring and analysis, Alberta Municipalities is engaged with the Government of Alberta and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to align and amplify messaging where possible. We will explore the ways in which the new U.S. administration's actions will affect municipalities in the weeks and months ahead and at our Spring Municipal Leaders Caucus on March 6 in Edmonton. As your municipality is considering the impacts of tariffs on your community, some of the potential impacts could include: Reduced funding from the Government of Alberta Particularly because less taxable revenue will be generated from natural resource exports, which is what drives the provincial government s surplus or deficit budget position. Funding provided to municipalities via the Local Government Fiscal Framework is directly tied to the provincial government s revenues. Therefore, reductions in provincial revenue will result in less funding to municipalities. Reduced municipal revenues For example, higher unemployment will affect residents ability to access pay-for- use municipal services (e.g., transportation, recreation facilities). Reduced Investment Tariffs may cause businesses to slow or shutdown their operations (e.g., farming, agriculture, energy), along with limiting new economic development in municipalities. Stunted property tax growth Higher unemployment rates and increasing costs of living may increase pressure from residents to maintain lower property tax rates. Higher costs on goods and services In addition to tariffs goods, alternatives (including those produced in Canada) may be more expensive, resulting in municipalities having higher-than-planned costs for goods and services. There will also be instances where Canadian-made products become cheaper due to reduced demand (i.e., countervailing forces). Increased demand for social supports Recessionary economic factors may create (and exacerbate) issues pertaining to homeless, in-need , and new temporary Canadian populations (e.g., access to medical services, policing services). JUNE 9, 2 BY ENID SLACK TOMAS HACHARD Saskatoon, Sask. Shutterstock.com Municipalities have played a central role in Canada s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. They have provided economic relief to residents and businesses, instituted public health measures, delivered vaccines and begun planning for a post-pandemic future. The increased cost of this work, combined with decreased revenues particularly from user fees such as transit fares have resulted in significant, unanticipated operating deficits. Large cities with transit systems have been especially hard hit. Because municipalities are required by law to pass balanced operating budgets every year, they have not been able to resort to more borrowing. Instead, federal and provincial governments have stepped in to help them cover the shortfalls. Alongside fiscal deficits, municipalities have also faced a governance deficit. While they have been on the front lines responding to the pandemic, they nevertheless have been excluded in many cases from key decisions made at the federal and provincial level. Instead, municipalities have relied on advocacy to get heard, although public health units have in some cases made use of their authority to enact certain restrictions. All of this points to an underlying reality about Canadian federalism. Despite the important role that cities play in the federation, local governments are equipped with limited sources of revenue largely property taxes, user fees, and transfers from the federal and provincial governments. They also do not have any real role or voice in Canada s federal structure and are generally not included in federal- provincial discussions or negotiations. Both of these problems need to be addressed. Municipalities should have access to the revenue necessary to fund the services they must provide. There should also be regular trilateral meetings among Ottawa, the provinces and senior municipal leaders to address issues of common concern, while recognizing the different needs of large and small municipalities. Municipalities have too often been the forgotten partners or little siblings of Canadian federalism. Recent research has highlighted the challenges Canadian municipalities face in this respect. Municipalities have a semblance of authority in several policy areas, but often little actual power to make changes unilaterally, partly because provinces have shown little interest in ceding control. They have inadequate revenue sources and insufficient fiscal flexibility to meet their responsibilities. There is often unclear and overlapping jurisdiction between municipalities, provinces and the federal government. Finally, much of Canada lacks appropriate regional governance structures to encourage inter-municipal co-operation. Coming out of the pandemic, there is an opportunity to put municipalities and Canada on firmer footing by addressing fiscal capacity and flexibility, embracing municipalities as partners and taking municipal differences into consideration. Address fiscal capacity and flexibility Provincial governments determine the revenue sources available to municipalities. They also hold municipalities to balanced budgets for operating purposes, and restrict how much they can borrow for capital expenditures. This high degree of provincial control ensures that municipalities maintain good fiscal health, but it can obfuscate real fiscal problems. Balanced budgets, for instance, can hide the fact that a municipality is unable to pay the cost of maintaining and building new infrastructure, including public transit and affordable housing, using revenue sources at their disposal. The limited number of revenue sources available to municipalities also means they lack fiscal flexibility. If transfers from government are adjusted downward, or property tax revenues decrease, they have few other places to turn for revenue. Without a mix of taxes, they are less able to respond to shifts in the economy, evolving demographics and changing expenditure needs. In this respect, big cities in Canada compare unfavourably to the rest of the world. In a study of eight international cities, only London was found to have access to fewer taxation options than Toronto. In response, a reconsideration of who does what in Canada particularly with respect to provincial-municipal relations is needed. Such a process should ensure two things. Saint John, N.B. Shutterstock.com First, municipalities should have revenues that allow them to deliver effectively This may entail giving municipalities access to new revenue sources, or uploading responsibilities to the provincial level. Second, municipalities should have appropriate revenue sources for the services they deliver. For instance, both in response to provincial downloading of responsibilities and to resident demands for action on issues like the opioid crisis and mental health, municipalities are increasingly being tasked with redistributive services such as social housing, public health and social assistance. These are best funded by progressive taxes, such as an income tax or a sales tax with mitigation for low-income individuals. Embrace municipalities as partners A new vision for municipalities in Canada should also address intergovernmental relations. In Canada, there is no formal mechanism for ongoing, formal federal-provincial- This is despite the fact that decisions taken by provincial and federal governments on immigration, infrastructure and public health, to name a few examples, have significant effects on municipalities. In cases where there is insufficient funding for programs, municipalities often bear the cost of filling gaps in services. Even in cases where municipalities have a semblance of authority for instance, land-use planning and elections provinces can often second-guess and or overrule their decisions. Many of Canada s policy challenges require increased co-ordination and co- operation among all three orders of government. As Gabriel Eidelman has noted, Urban governance is not simply municipal governance. Urban policy-making necessarily involves all levels of government. Municipalities should not need to wait to see what arrangements are made by the provinces and Ottawa in areas with municipal impact. Just as the provinces and the federal government meet regularly, without regard to whether there are particular issues that need to be discussed, so should cities, provinces and the federal government have formal avenues for regular meetings and collaborative governance. Instituting more formal trilateral relations, however, runs up against the issue of fragmentation. Canada has approximately 3,750 local governments. It is unfeasible to involve them all in intergovernmental discussions. Ensuring that Canada s major economic regions have robust metropolitan governance structures through which municipalities can co-ordinate on shared policy challenges and, when possible, speak as one voice, can help address this issue. Take municipal differences into consideration Canada is a largely urban and suburban country. Nevertheless, around a quarter of Canadians live in a municipality with a population of less than 20,000. Small and large municipalities are distinct in many ways. Larger municipalities generally can draw more revenue from their tax base and also have a larger and more sophisticated public service. As a result, policies and decisions tailored to large cities may not work for smaller municipalities. Instead, asymmetrical arrangements may be preferable. This might mean large cities and metropolitan regions take on more responsibility and gain access to new revenue sources, while smaller municipalities stay as they are and rely more on transfers. In such a scenario, greater disparities may emerge among municipalities, so new or enhanced provincial-municipal equalization transfers may also be required to ensure that all municipalities can provide at least an average level of local public services by levying an average standard tax rate. COVID-19 has shown us once more that municipalities play a fundamental role in the country s policy-making. It is equally apparent that municipalities will be critical to address climate change and tackle the affordable housing crisis, among other challenges. Reforming our fiscal and governance structures would be the next step in reflecting the key role of municipalities in the federation. This article is part of the Reshaping Canada s Cities After the Pandemic Shockwave special feature. Enid Slack Enid Slack is the director of the Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto. How are Canadian municipal leaders expected to lead when the future is so unclear? Perhaps it is best to look at what we do know and extrapolate from there. Keynesian economics tells us that the best way to restart and sustain a battered economy has been public spending, bolstered by public borrowing. In response to the COVID-19 shutdown of the economy, we have seen federal debt balloon to the highest it has been in decades. That effort, complemented by provincial and municipal fiscal initiatives, and unprecedented infusions of credit from the Bank of Canada, headed-off an economic disaster for millions of Canadians. But it will leave a legacy. In the short term, government support is positioned to cushion municipal operating deficits caused by extraordinary expenditures and revenue losses in 2020. This support includes the recent 19 billion Safe Restart Agreement announcement, which in the case of Ontario s 7 billion share will include 2 billion for Ontario municipalities and 2 billion for public transit authorities. Many local leaders wonder what levels of support will be like for 2021 as they begin their budget planning process, with significant question marks about both the revenue and cost side for next year. Longer-term, it may result in renewed efforts to boost infrastructure spending, if capital budgets at all three levels of government can be preserved. Before the end of this municipal council term in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada, the fiscal hangover will lead to belt-tightening, coupled with efforts to ensure that the economy grows sustainably and that further public spending is constrained. As we know from history, when constraint is adopted by other orders of government, the prospects for significant financial help for municipal governments from traditional sources will dim. Municipalities will all be urged, in UK journalist Ann Leslie s colourful phrase, to kill your own snakes . If there was ever any doubt before the pandemic, we are now firmly facing a structural deficit, particularly in local government finance. Much is anticipated for the new normal . We await a COVID-19 vaccine and the reinventing of the complex global supply chain for the goods and services that we use (and produce) every day. Some developments are with us to stay, such as remote working and telecommuting, more online retail and on-street product fulfillment, social distancing, and the increasing vagaries of a global marketplace. Many of these developments had been predicted but were expected to happen over the course of a few decades, not months. It now appears that we may face a municipal version of Moore s Law (which in the Information Technology field has accurately predicted a disruptive doubling of technological capacity every 18 months). In parallel with the pandemic, we have also seen a global response to the death of George Floyd. Public demonstrations have led to demands for fundamental reform of policing. The Black Lives Matter movement has spurred re-thinking societal issues such as racial discrimination and response to calls for emergency assistance for incidents related to mental illness, addictions, and domestic violence. As these economic, fiscal, and social developments continue, both from COVID- 19 and other factors, some things are certain like the continuing financial challenges facing municipalities while we may also see pressure: To increase productivity, to be more tax-competitive and to reduce public sector costs, which means reduced labour costs To accommodate autonomous vehicles, ride sharing, smart transportation, and more so-called active transportation To absorb the land-use and tax impacts of fundamental changes to retail, office, parking requirements, and new models of housing for the elderly To address environmental sustainability, housing costs and social inequality in our communities and in our workplaces on an accelerated timetable To reform policing and society s response to emergency calls-for-service for incidents related to mental illness, addictions, and families in crisis; and, Making the leap to 5G mobile digital service delivery. All of this, while simultaneously lifting the burdens of cost and uncertainty caused by traditional regulation and approvals and borne by those to whom we are looking to create and sustain employment and to revitalize economic activity. So where does all this leave municipal governments? What does the future hold? What items need to be on the agenda of municipal governments? There are at least eight likely outcomes. Two are outlined below and another six will be addressed in a subsequent article: The municipal workforce will transform, as artificial-intelligence and machine- learning applications and monitoring technologies are used in all manner of repetitive or inspection-related processes, especially those guided by rules, established policies, standard conditions, and precedents. Just as asphalt-laying crews and meter-readers were displaced by paving machines and automated meter reading in the 20 century, technology will improve productivity in labour-intensive functions. Whether it is incremental change, like replacing site visits with digital video inspections, or more structural change, driven by AI and remote-monitoring technologies. Process reforms will produce quicker, more consistent, and less idiosyncratic decisions on everything from business licensing and re-zonings to asset management and inspections. Mirroring the banking and travel industries, which have displaced much of their routine in-person interaction with clients, municipal workforces must reskill. Fewer but more productive municipal employees will serve an increasingly larger and more sophisticated online clientele. The workforce that remains should be more diverse, in all aspects of that term. Fortunately, the 21 century needs of municipalities will make diversity objectives much more achievable than they were with a 20 century workforce built around seniority, fixed employee benefits, employment guarantees, and traditional skills. Finally, municipal governments should adopt the so-called commissioning model in the UK and EU, a model described in an excellent 2017 article by Taylor and Migone, then at Institute of Public Administration of Canada. With commissioning , municipal governments play their role by ensuring that services and infrastructure are available on reasonable terms to their communities, their residents and their businesses, rather than assuming they must be provided by direct, monopoly delivery employing municipal facilities and municipal workers, financed by taxpayers. New models of policing and public safety Nineteenth century models of policing and fire suppression will need to evolve delivery models that reflect today s public safety priorities. For example, responding to preponderant incidence of health-related emergencies, especially as the Baby Boomer cohort ages. These new delivery models will also be needed to address social, mental illness, substance abuse, and family crisis situations with responses more suitable for those calls for emergency assistance. Rather than defunding police, we can expect to see measures to produce a new workplace culture in policing. This new culture should begin with embedding within the police workforce staff who have other professional perspectives on dealing with public safety and calls for service. Modernizing policing will need to reflect four pillars of reform: Becoming a learning organization that aligns its values and leadership priorities throughout the staff complement, and dissipates the informal education of front-line constables Re-engineering the hierarchical structure of police organizations to reflect contemporary priorities (mental health issues, technological advances, etc) A risk-based approach to planning and staff deployment, with a focus on community collaboration, public health and social services (e.g., the comprehensive approach successfully employed by Karyn McCluskey with violent crime and gangs in Scotland) ; and Despite reallocation of some police resources and the introduction of new contemporary priorities, preserving within policing a robust capacity for th st th effective law enforcement and criminal investigations, with a focus on value- for-investment, outputs and outcomes. We could also see an overdue and successful societal effort, led by municipal councils with recently announced federal support, to reduce the level of urban handgun possession. Success in treating the scourge of handgun deaths and injuries, as more of a public health issue than a criminal matter, would certainly change the character and reduce the risk-profile of many urgent responses by both police and other agencies. In our next article, we will look at another six developments on the post-2020 action agenda for municipal governments. Dr. Robert P.
